Attention kernels optimize a specific tensor operator; they do not determine what an agent should remember. For one head, let , , and . With additive mask , attention is , where row by row. The mask can encode causality, padding, sliding windows, or a more specialized visibility relation. Changing the mask changes the operator. Changing its implementation while preserving the same mask and arithmetic target is an optimization of that operator. These cases require different correctness tests .

For dense equal-length sequences and , forming scores and multiplying probabilities by values requires approximately floating-point operations when one multiply-add counts as two operations. Causal structure can reduce useful score work by roughly half, but actual savings depend on whether the kernel skips masked tiles. Projection and feed-forward costs are additional. A dense kernel that uses less temporary memory still evaluates a quadratic set of interactions. FlashAttention is exact attention in this algorithmic sense; it avoids materializing the full score and probability matrices in high-bandwidth memory, rather than replacing them with a low-rank or sparse approximation .

Two regimes matter for agents. Prefill processes a supplied context and commonly has many query positions. Autoregressive decode often has one new query position per sequence, interacting with a long retained cache. A technique that improves a large square matrix computation need not produce the same gain for a thin decode operation. During a long tool pause, the cache may occupy accelerator memory without generating tokens. The workload consequently includes active computation, idle retained state, resumption, branching, and cancellation. Kernel benchmarks that omit those phases do not fully characterize a long-running agent service.

Correctness also has several levels. Algebraic equality assumes real arithmetic. Floating-point implementations reorder reductions and can differ numerically while targeting the same function. Randomized dropout requires consistent random-number semantics in training and recomputation. Mask alignment, positional offsets, and sequence lengths must match exactly. A kernel can pass average numerical tolerances yet fail at a rare boundary length or unsupported head dimension. For an agent, such a defect can appear as a semantic planning error many actions later. Operator-level verification should therefore precede task-level evaluation rather than relying on an aggregate task score to detect low-level mistakes.

The numerical role of the maximum is essential. Exponentiating arbitrary logits directly can overflow even when the normalized result is well defined. FlashAttention uses this reduction with tiles that fit in on-chip memory, minimizing transfers of large intermediate matrices between device memory and the processor. Its backward pass recomputes selected quantities rather than storing the full probability matrix . Recomputation exchanges arithmetic for reduced memory traffic. That trade can be favorable because arithmetic capacity and memory bandwidth do not grow in the same proportion. It is nevertheless conditional on tile dimensions, head sizes, register pressure, shared-memory capacity, and compiler scheduling. The asymptotic I/O analysis explains a mechanism; it does not replace measurement on the deployed accelerator.

FlashAttention-2 changes work partitioning and reduces non-matrix-multiplication work. FlashAttention-3 uses Hopper-specific asynchronous execution and low-precision techniques . Their author-reported speedups refer to specified GPUs and configurations. It is incorrect to transfer one of those multipliers to arbitrary inference traffic or to multiply it by an unrelated serving speedup as though the gains were independent. Both techniques may remove the same bottleneck, or one can expose another. End-to-end agent latency additionally includes communication, parsing, tools, queueing, and verification.

The cache is computational state tied to a particular model computation. It is not an independently meaningful semantic archive. A durable conversation log can survive a model upgrade while its old keys and values become unusable. A context summary can preserve the intended task while changing every downstream hidden representation. Conversely, retaining an enormous cache does not ensure that the model will attend to a decisive constraint. The system should therefore distinguish three questions: whether source events are stored, whether their computation can be reused exactly, and whether their information affects the correct action.

Long sessions introduce an allocation problem even when the per-token formula is simple. Each tool result can increase retained length; branches can share a common prefix before diverging; abandoned runs can leave caches resident until cleanup. A serving system must define ownership and reclamation for each block. Cancellation is not complete until resources are released or transferred to an explicit resumable state. A session identifier alone does not prove that the cache is durable, and a durable cache does not prove that the external tool state can be replayed. These are independent recovery contracts.

PagedAttention separates logical token positions from physically contiguous storage. Fixed-size blocks hold keys and values, and a block table maps logical positions to physical blocks. This avoids reserving one large contiguous buffer for the maximum possible length of every request. It also permits sharing of completed prefix blocks across related sequences, with copy-on-write behavior when a shared mutable region would otherwise diverge. The original vLLM paper attributes throughput gains to improved memory use and associated batching opportunities under its evaluated workloads. Those are author-reported results for that implementation and its baselines .

Let a block hold tokens. A sequence of length occupies token slots. Its internal slack is less than slots; across sequences the total slack is less than , before considering sharing or metadata. This bound explains one advantage over reserving each request’s maximum length. It does not imply zero overhead. Smaller blocks reduce terminal slack but increase block-table size and indirection frequency. Larger blocks can improve locality while wasting more space near sequence ends. The best block size depends on the length distribution, attention kernel, and sharing patterns.

Prefix sharing is valid only for an identical computation prefix. Identical visible text is insufficient if tokenization, positions, masks, model weights, adapters, or relevant execution settings differ. Even an identical token sequence can yield different keys and values when an earlier hidden input differs. A robust cache key therefore binds the complete computation identity required by the model implementation, together with tenant isolation rules. A semantic embedding match can suggest useful retrieval; it cannot justify substituting exact KV tensors. Confusing these mechanisms can create silent correctness failures rather than merely a lower cache hit rate.

Editing a prefix invalidates more than the edited tokens in ordinary causal attention. Representations at later positions depend on the earlier prefix through successive layers. Reusing their old keys and values after a deletion or replacement generally evaluates a different computational graph from a fresh forward pass. Safe reuse requires a proved invariant, a model architecture that supports the transformation, or recomputation of affected state. Context-editing systems therefore need explicit interaction with the cache manager. The compression service cannot be treated as a purely textual component whose output is transparently compatible with every retained tensor.

An agent often branches on uncertain plans or candidate patches. Shared prefixes can reduce physical memory duplication, but every divergent continuation still consumes computation and new blocks. A search controller that increases the branch count can exhaust capacity even while the cache manager is efficient. Admission control should reserve an envelope for likely continuation or support preemption with declared semantics. Recompute-on-resume and host offload are different policies with different latency and bandwidth costs. Neither can be ranked without the session length distribution, tool-pause distribution, and deadline requirements.

A simple lower-bound model distinguishes arithmetic and movement. If an operation requires floating-point operations and transfers bytes through a bottleneck interface with usable rates and , then its duration is at least under ideal overlap. This is a lower bound, not a performance prediction. Kernel launches, synchronization, indexing, cache misses, and queueing add costs. The relevant bandwidth is the measured rate for the actual access pattern, not an advertised peak. Small batches and scattered page accesses may fail to approach that peak.

For long-context decode, repeatedly reading keys and values can dominate the attention component. Grouping more sequences can improve weight reuse and hardware utilization, but also increases active KV traffic and waiting time. An agent service should report time to first token, inter-token latency, complete action latency, and end-to-end task latency. A tool call that takes seconds can hide a model optimization in the mean while the optimization still matters for the tail of interactive steps. Conversely, aggressive batching can increase the time before a safety-critical confirmation reaches the execution boundary.

Queueing creates another source of misleading comparisons. At low offered load, both implementations may have small queues. Near capacity, a modest service-rate difference can produce a large latency difference because requests accumulate. A benchmark that measures only completed-request throughput can conceal dropped or timed-out work. Report offered load, admitted load, completed load, error rate, and latency percentiles together. Open-loop arrivals are useful for exposing overload because the load generator does not automatically slow down when responses become late. Closed-loop tests answer a different question about a fixed client population.

Cache offload shifts the bottleneck. A host-memory cache can permit more paused sessions while introducing transfers on resumption. If bytes must cross a link with sustained bandwidth , transfer time alone is at least before overlap and scheduling effects. Compression may reduce transferred bytes while adding quantization or decompression work. A system that advertises more simultaneous sessions should disclose whether those sessions are immediately executable, offloaded, or represented only by a durable log requiring prefill. These states have different practical meanings for interactive agents.

These distinctions define appropriate ablations. Compare exact attention, reduced precision without eviction, eviction without quantization, and their combination. Measure tensor discrepancies, next-token distribution changes, action validity, and complete task outcomes. Include queries that make an old low-frequency constraint suddenly relevant. A cache method can maintain language-model perplexity while damaging stateful decision reliability. The converse can also occur when a task never uses the affected information. The experiment should identify that dependence rather than presenting one aggregate quality number as a universal cache-safety certificate.

A discriminating experiment crosses source phase, window origin, stride, width, and query location while holding the relevant fact and answer fixed. A test with uniform compression weights can further separate learned gate specialization from information mixing at boundaries.

For agents, a changed tool description, a harmless comment, or a memory summary can shift a decisive old constraint to a different phase. The compression policy should therefore be evaluated under realistic serialization changes and rare action-changing facts. A fixed benchmark placement can accidentally favor a strong phase. Random placement helps estimate average behavior, but worst-phase evaluation remains necessary when a constraint must survive independently of incidental token offsets. The source paper’s bounded retrieval evidence motivates this mechanism test; it does not establish a universal deployment failure rate.

The FlashAttention and vLLM repositories provide identifiable implementations, with immutable snapshots recorded separately from their associated papers . A current repository snapshot is not assumed to be the code used for an older paper’s measurements. The implementation audit should trace public interfaces to kernel dispatch, supported dtypes, head dimensions, mask conventions, block tables, and cache update logic. It should record fallback paths: an unsupported shape can silently invoke a slower implementation, changing the interpretation of a benchmark that purports to compare kernels.

Operator tests should compare forward outputs and gradients against a high-precision reference over a matrix of lengths, masks, offsets, and head dimensions. Include empty sequences, partially filled pages, shared-prefix divergence, and cancellation during allocation. For inference, compare fresh prefill with resumed-cache computation under identical inputs. For context edits, deliberately modify an early token and confirm that any claimed reuse matches a recomputed reference within declared tolerances. Numerical tolerance should reflect dtype and operation length, but a permissive tolerance must not conceal an incorrect visibility mask.

A concrete implementation chain connects Section 3.1 of the first FlashAttention paper to the public flash_attn/flash_attn_interface.py interface and its _flash_attn_forward dispatch. The Hopper snapshot additionally exposes flash_attn_func through hopper/flash_attn_interface.py. These names were checked in the pinned repository; they identify interfaces, not a claim that the Python wrapper itself implements the tiled CUDA arithmetic. For a hypothetical single head with , , and two-byte inputs, each of occupies 4 MiB, whereas one fully materialized FP32 score matrix occupies 1 GiB. Two FP32 running statistics per row occupy only 128 KiB. This arithmetic illustrates the memory mechanism without assigning an invented device runtime.

A numerical implementation constraint is visible in the pinned Blackwell path itself. In FlashAttentionForwardSm100.softmax_loop, the probability scale offset and permitted running-maximum lag are checked against the largest finite probability-storage value :

This is a finite-range condition for the scaled probabilities before the value product, not an attention-quality bound. The corresponding correction_loop restores the scale when forming the output . A useful stress test varies logit maxima, dtype and head dimension while checking the actual dispatched path against a reference; changing only an average tensor tolerance can conceal this failure. The inspected code establishes the guard and dataflow, not a new runtime or accuracy measurement.

At the allocation layer, Section 4.2 of the PagedAttention paper can be compared with the pinned vLLM module vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_manager.py, whose KVCacheManager exposes get_computed_blocks, allocate_slots, and free. This later V1 implementation is not the original paper’s code version. A falsifiable integration check allocates two requests with the same eligible prefix, verifies their shared complete physical blocks, extends one request, and confirms that the other request’s logical sequence remains unchanged. It then frees both requests and checks that the allocator’s accounting returns to the initial state. This tests ownership and reuse independently of language-model quality.

The complete serving experiment should combine short and long prefills, varying output lengths, repeated prefixes, branching, tool pauses, and aborted sessions. Use a fixed workload trace for paired comparisons and a separate stress workload for overload. Warm and cold cache conditions need separate runs. Report accelerator count, available memory, precision, kernel versions, host-link characteristics, queue policy, and tenant isolation settings. Include allocation failures and recovery time in the outcome set. Throughput improvements are meaningful only when quality, admission, and latency conditions remain comparable.

The practical conclusion is a separation of obligations. Kernels must compute the intended operator; allocators must preserve logical state and ownership; approximation methods must justify their error; schedulers must satisfy service objectives; and the agent must use retained evidence correctly. Progress at one layer can enable progress at another, but cannot establish it by implication. This separation permits precise attribution while retaining the central interaction: a context policy that changes historical visibility also changes cache validity, resource demand, and the distribution on which the action policy operates.

The invalidation rule can be stated precisely for a deterministic causal decoder. Let be its input and let be the representation at position after layer . Suppose every layer may attend to every earlier position and its key and value projections are functions of the preceding-layer representation. If position changes, the original representations at positions are not generally reusable. At the input layer, changes. At the first attention layer, every later query may combine a changed value or a changed normalization term from position . At subsequent layers these changed representations produce changed keys and values. Induction across layers establishes a dependency path to every later cached position. This argument establishes possible dependence, not that every numerical value must change for every input.

Exact reuse therefore needs stronger evidence than a small edit distance. A special mask can remove the dependency path; an architecture can partition independent segments; a specific edit may leave a relevant representation unchanged. Each case requires a demonstrated invariant. Ordinary semantic similarity between the original and edited text supplies none of these conditions. The same reasoning applies to changing an adapter or a positional convention. Even if the visible token sequence is identical, the projection functions or their inputs differ. A cache manager should prefer a conservative invalidation rule to silently assuming equality that the model computation does not support.

There is a related distinction between prefix deletion and left truncation during generation. Removing old positions from the attention set while retaining representations computed when those positions were visible does not reproduce a fresh run on the shorter input. It evaluates a hybrid state: later representations already incorporate information from the deleted history, but future queries cannot access the deleted positions directly. Such a policy can be intentional, for example as an approximation that preserves some historical influence. It must be described and evaluated as that policy, rather than as exact execution of the shortened textual context. Training on a freshly shortened sequence would condition on a different computation again.

These observations motivate a three-way equivalence test. First run an uninterrupted reference trajectory. Second resume from a stored cache without editing; this tests serialization and restoration of computational state. Third apply the intended edit and compare with a fresh run under the edited inputs and mask. The second comparison should agree within the documented numerical contract. The third agrees only if the transformation claims exact equivalence; an approximate transformation should instead report its discrepancy and downstream effects. Holding the sampled continuation fixed through teacher forcing helps localize tensor drift before free-running outputs amplify it.

For an agent service, these tests should include a consequential old instruction that is later revoked, not merely irrelevant prose. If removed information survives indirectly in retained states, a textual audit may incorrectly conclude that it has been forgotten. If recomputation eliminates that influence, the cost can be larger than the nominal number of edited tokens suggests. This is a concrete interaction between computational memory, policy conditioning, and deletion semantics. It also explains why the durable event log, the visible context, and the retained cache must be inspected as separate state objects when diagnosing long-session behavior.

V-JEPA 2.1 changes the training target rather than merely scaling the original video encoder. Its Section 2.3 applies prediction supervision to masked and visible tokens, introduces intermediate-layer supervision, and uses modality-specific image/video patch embeddings. The inspected 2026 implementation exposes forward_target, forward_context, and loss_fn in app/vjepa_2_1/train.py . This is a current, identifiable objective-to-code case; the original I-JEPA discussion supplies its foundation rather than a claim about the frontier’s latest recipe.

The local-versus-global tradeoff has a useful optimization interpretation. Let measure prediction of masked targets and supervision of visible context features. Training minimizes in a simplified two-term view. A direction that reduces can increase when the gradient inner product is negative. Thus adding dense supervision is not guaranteed to improve every global metric. The scale and spatial weighting of the context term determine which distinctions receive pressure. This deduction explains why an implementation must retain the actual loss weights and scheduling, rather than treating the presence of an additional loss as a uniformly beneficial feature.

For agents, dense features are attractive because many operations depend on a localized affordance rather than a whole-scene label. The corresponding falsifiable hypothesis is that improved local representations reduce target-selection errors under a fixed policy and observation budget. Test that hypothesis with counterfactual layouts, small text, occlusion, and temporal changes. Retain a global-recognition diagnostic to detect whether the local gain trades away broader scene understanding. A classifier or robotics score from the source paper does not answer the computer-use question automatically; it identifies a mechanism worth testing.

Implementation inspection should follow the feature path across encoder layers, normalization, fusion, and predictor outputs. Multi-level features increase the amount of intermediate state that may be retained or recomputed. A frozen feature-extraction benchmark should include preprocessing and feature-transfer costs, not only encoder FLOPs. An agent that invokes the encoder on every observation may prefer a smaller distilled model, a crop policy, or event-triggered refresh even when a larger model has the best unconstrained representation score. Quality should therefore be plotted against complete decision latency and storage, with the action interface held constant.

The October 2026 revision of V-JEPA Policy couples a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder with an instruction-conditioned future-latent predictor and a flow-matching action expert. Its Section 3 connects future-informed context keys and values to action generation, while the experiments compare visual foundations under a common downstream framework . This is a more direct representation-to-action case than passive recognition alone. It still changes several trained components, so a result for the complete policy cannot be assigned entirely to the frozen encoder without the corresponding controlled comparison.

The actual coupling point matters for an ablation. The action expert reads the predictor’s layerwise context keys and values, not the final future-latent readouts. In the paper’s notation, its visual interface is

where are projections at context positions and only the keys receive the stated rotary transform . Changing an unused final readout would therefore not test whether the action path uses future-conditioned context. A more diagnostic proposed study holds the visual encoder and action expert fixed and intervenes on future-query-to-context interactions, preserving observed tokens, positions, tensor shapes and comparable compute. A performance drop after that intervention can support functional use of the coupling, while leaving its calibration and interventional validity open. Shuffling the whole context interface would conflate loss of present evidence with loss of future conditioning. Out-of-distribution corruption remains an alternative explanation and requires matched controls; no such experiment is reported here.
Figure separates latent prediction from the downstream control path whose validity must be tested.

Predictive representation training and control test different properties. The context branch uses positions ; the target branch processes the complete observation, selects positions , and blocks loss gradients through . An EMA parameter update is separate from gradient flow. The declared loss must match the selected JEPA variant. A downstream controller requires independent environment-outcome evaluation; small prediction loss does not establish action sufficiency.

A representation is useful to an agent when it preserves distinctions that matter for future decisions under the available interaction policy. This criterion differs from visual similarity, image classification accuracy, or reconstructing every pixel. Let be the current multimodal observation and an encoded state. An image encoder may discard lighting variation while preserving object identity; a computer-use agent may additionally need exact text, focus state, disabled controls, and the difference between a preview and a committed operation. These requirements depend on the action space and objective, so no representation can be declared generally sufficient from a single transfer benchmark.

For a one-step decision with loss , define the Bayes risk available from information as . If is deterministic, then : every policy on can be implemented on by composition, while the reverse need not hold. Equality holds when some optimal decision is measurable with respect to . This elementary proposition supplies the right direction of comparison. Compression cannot improve the ideal information-theoretic optimum, although it can improve finite-data learning, optimization, and computational feasibility. Those practical benefits should not be confused with creating information absent from the observation.

For sequential control, a sufficient state must support relevant prediction and reward decisions across future actions. A representation trained on passive video can preserve correlations that disappear when the agent intervenes. A representation trained on one action distribution can omit details needed by another. The complete state includes external records, tool state, and permissions; a visual embedding is only one component. Session continuity therefore requires synchronizing encoded observations with event timestamps and action outcomes. An excellent screenshot representation paired with the wrong browser tab or stale environment state is still an incorrect decision input.

Evaluation should separate representation learning from policy learning. A frozen-encoder probe asks what a restricted decoder can recover. Fine-tuning asks whether the representation is a useful initialization under additional supervision. Closed-loop evaluation asks whether the integrated controller succeeds while its actions alter the observation distribution. These are different experimental interventions. A linear probe can fail even when information is present in a nonlinear code, and a powerful policy can compensate for a weak visual encoder through repeated tool queries. Reporting the intervention prevents either result from being overstated as a definitive property of the latent state.

An abstraction can be evaluated more directly than through a generic probe score. Let be the complete permitted observation and let indicate a binary action requirement, with balanced. Construct two environments whose broad appearance is the same but whose required action differs because of a localized signal. If the encoder maps both observations to exactly the same representation and no additional evidence is available, the best downstream classifier has accuracy at most one half. This follows from the state-aliasing argument in Chapter . With approximate rather than exact collisions, the relevant object is the separability of the induced representation distributions under the actual decoder class.

For unrestricted binary testing with equal priors, the optimal success probability is , where is the representation distribution conditional on . The identity follows by choosing the decision region that maximizes . This is a standard probability deduction, used here to specify a diagnostic rather than to claim a new representation theorem. It explains why a low average reconstruction error or a high semantic retrieval score cannot alone certify preservation of a rare action-critical signal: those metrics need not control the total variation of these conditional distributions.

In practice, total variation in high-dimensional learned representations is not directly known. A fixed classifier with population accuracy gives , not an upper bound on the information present. A finite held-out accuracy estimate needs a one-sided lower confidence bound , valid for the sampling design, before reporting as a statistical lower bound. Tuning on those test outcomes invalidates that independent-test interpretation. A failed probe can therefore motivate stronger probes or a direct action test, while a successful probe still leaves policy access and calibration unresolved. The experiment should report encoder stochasticity, preprocessing, sample size, decoder capacity, and the precise intervention defining . Those details determine what conclusion can be drawn from the observed accuracy.

The resulting design principle is to preserve a recoverable path from task-critical observations to execution, while allowing abstraction of genuine nuisances. Multiple channels can provide complementary evidence, but agreement between two models trained on similar data is not independence. A robust agent records which channel supplied a fact, checks freshness before action, and seeks another observation when the distinction remains unresolved. Representation learning contributes powerful statistical structure; the surrounding system must still connect that structure to the exact state and action semantics of the task.

RC-aux changes two interfaces that one-step JEPA prediction leaves unspecified: recursive prediction over the planning horizon and a directed reachability estimate conditioned on remaining steps. Its Section 3 constructs positive and negative labels from observed trajectory offsets and also supplies predicted-latent inputs to the reachability head. Temporal-Distance JEPA’s current second version instead calibrates a nonnegative asymmetric cost from demonstration step counts, with a metric-residual head and horizon-matched rollout supervision . A distance between two embeddings is therefore no longer assumed to be the planning objective merely because the predictor was trained in that space.

The supervision has a precise epistemic limit. In deterministic state dynamics, let be the minimum number of feasible actions from to , with value when none exists. An observed valid segment from to of length proves . It does not prove equality. Consequently, labeling the pair unreachable at budget introduces possible false negatives whenever an unobserved shortcut exists. Cross-trajectory negatives are weaker still: two independently collected trajectories may pass through mutually reachable states. These are deductions from the labeling construction, rather than objections that invalidate every useful learned ranking.

Directionality is independently necessary when actions are irreversible. If a transition deletes an object and no action restores it, can be finite while is infinite. Every symmetric embedding distance assigns the same value in both directions. An asymmetric head removes that representational restriction, but does not establish calibrated reachability on unseen states. To distinguish the interventions, hold the encoder and rollout operator fixed while comparing symmetric and directed heads, then hold the scoring head fixed while changing recursive prediction training. Include observed loops and deliberately collected shortcut trajectories to measure label ambiguity.

For a stateful agent, the budget must count executable operations rather than an unspecified number of latent updates. A plan with three service calls and a required approval can be unreachable within three permitted actions even if its visual endpoint is nearby. Test changes in permission and resource availability while preserving the displayed scene. A reachability head that sees only pixels cannot resolve a hidden authorization change without another state channel. The strongest diagnostic therefore reports action feasibility, goal completion, and predicted reachability separately, including false acceptance of infeasible plans. Neither source’s trajectory-based supervision supplies a general certificate for that broader execution contract.

Latent Projection for Latent Planning fits an action-free linear dynamics operator to frozen representations and changes the goal cost through a selected subspace. Its Sections 3–4 assume joint Gaussianity, stationary standard-normal marginals, Markov dynamics, and a normal transition matrix . Writing with independent zero-mean innovation, stationarity gives

This follows by taking the covariance of the transition, not from an empirical assurance that a regularizer has made real embeddings exactly Gaussian. Normality further yields , so one orthonormal basis diagonalizes the innovation covariance at every positive integer horizon. Without normality, the preferred subspace can change with horizon.

The pinned implementation makes several consequential choices visible. NormalDrift in module.py parameterizes contraction and rotation blocks; its evaluation mode zeros configured static line blocks. LP2GoalMSE in cost.py selects left singular vectors of the evaluation operator and compares terminal features after projection . Thus the exact choice of dynamic planes, static lines, retained rank, and training versus evaluation mode belongs in the experimental configuration. A description that mentions only top singular vectors omits an implemented structural filter.
A counterexample limits any universal identification of predictable features with controllable goal progress. Let , where , and define hypothetical dynamics

with , orthogonal two-dimensional rotation , and independent . Under behavior actions independent of the current state, stationary marginals are standard Gaussian and the action-free fitted operator is . It is normal and its most predictable two-dimensional subspace is . Yet actions directly set , so a goal depending on is reachable in one step while a projected cost retaining only cannot distinguish candidate actions by that goal.

This constructed example is not a reported failure of the paper’s evaluated models. It proves that the stated statistical assumptions alone do not guarantee decision sufficiency, even when the retained predictable features are dynamic planes rather than static lines. A falsifiable test introduces an autonomous visual distractor and a less behavior-predictable but controllable target, then compares full latent cost, fitted projection, random projection, and an action-conditioned relevance control at matched search budget. Vary the behavior policy used to fit the projection. A change in the selected subspace can reveal dependence on exploration statistics rather than an invariant property of environment controllability.

A Vision Transformer converts an image into patch embeddings and processes their sequence with attention . For image dimensions and nonoverlapping square patches of side , the patch count is approximately when dimensions divide evenly. Reducing increases spatial sampling density and sequence length. In dense attention, the corresponding pairwise term grows as , while projection and feed-forward terms grow linearly in . The choice of patch size is consequently both a perception decision and a systems decision for agents that must read detailed interfaces.

As a calculated example, a 1024 by 1024 image yields 4096 patches at side 16 and 1024 patches at side 32. The patch count changes by four and the dense pairwise attention term by sixteen, before architectural details and implementation. These numbers do not predict a sixteen-fold latency difference: other operations, preprocessing, and memory effects remain. They do explain why uniformly increasing screenshot resolution can be expensive. An agent can instead request a local crop, use an accessibility tree, or extract text through a separate channel. Each strategy changes the evidence interface and can introduce its own omissions.

Small text illustrates a failure that semantic benchmarks can hide. A button label, decimal point, or negative sign may occupy a small fraction of the image but determine the correct action. Resizing can make that feature unrecoverable before the encoder sees it. No amount of later language reasoning can reconstruct the actual character reliably from an information-destroying preprocessing step. A model may guess correctly from context, which makes aggregate success deceptively reassuring. Tests should include counterfactual pairs whose large-scale layout is identical and whose correct action depends on the small feature.

Coordinates require an explicit transform. If the model receives a resized crop, a predicted point must be mapped back through scale, crop offset, display scaling, and possibly scrolling. A correct semantic target can become an incorrect click through a geometric conversion error. Record the image dimensions and transform alongside the observation, rather than reconstructing them from an assumed default. For browser agents, an element identifier from a structured interface can avoid some coordinate ambiguity, but the identifier must remain valid at execution time. A page mutation between observation and action can invalidate both geometric and structural references.
CLIP learns image and text representations through a contrastive objective on paired data . Let normalized embeddings be and and temperature . A directional batch loss is

The symmetric objective also predicts images from texts. This trains compatibility between paired modalities relative to the negative set. It does not by itself supervise a state transition, a tool argument, or the consequences of an action. A representation that matches a screenshot to a caption can still confuse whether a visible operation has already occurred.

Negative construction affects the learned distinctions. Two captions can both accurately describe an image while the batch treats only one as its paired positive. Conversely, dataset artifacts can make a pair identifiable without learning the causal structure relevant to control. These issues do not invalidate contrastive learning; they identify its objective. An agent evaluation should therefore test exact distinctions such as enabled versus disabled, before versus after, or selected versus merely visible. Generic image-text retrieval can be included as a diagnostic, but should not substitute for the closed-loop decision task.

Temperature controls the sharpness of the softmax over similarities. A smaller temperature concentrates gradients on hard alternatives and can magnify calibration differences between domains. The similarity score is not a calibrated probability that a proposed tool action is correct. Thresholding it as though it were one can yield unstable rejection behavior after a change in image style, prompt wording, or candidate set. Calibration should be measured against an explicit event, such as whether a retrieved frame contains the target control, under the deployment candidate distribution.

Cross-modal alignment also has a temporal dimension. A transcript can describe an earlier state while an image shows the current one. Combining them without timestamps can produce a fluent but internally inconsistent account. The representation pipeline should preserve modality, source, time, and transformation lineage. If an OCR engine and a vision-language model disagree, the agent needs a policy for seeking additional evidence rather than silently trusting whichever channel produces more confident language. Such disagreement is often an informative signal that the observation boundary needs another interaction.

I-JEPA predicts representations of target image regions from a context representation, using a predictor conditioned on target positions and a slowly updated target encoder . In schematic notation, a context encoder gives , a target encoder gives , and a predictor produces . For illustration, a squared representation loss takes the form

Here stops gradients through the target, and is updated from the online encoder through an exponential moving average. The mask distribution determines which contextual and spatial relations must be learned. This squared loss is a schematic analysis objective: the inspected I-JEPA implementation uses smooth , so reproducing that recipe requires its actual loss rather than substituting this expression.

Prediction in a learned latent space can avoid expending all capacity on unpredictable pixel detail. That is an attractive objective for agents whose actions depend on stable structure rather than every texture variation. However, which variation becomes irrelevant is learned from the data and objective. If a tiny visual indicator is weakly predictable yet action-critical, an abstraction optimized for broad semantic transfer may discard it. The appropriate question is whether the representation preserves task-relevant conditional distinctions, not whether it is more abstract in an unspecified sense.

The constant-representation solution clarifies a logical limitation. If both encoders output the same constant and the predictor outputs it, the schematic prediction loss is zero. Stop-gradient and a moving target change optimization dynamics but do not, by themselves, make this algebraic solution impossible. Actual JEPA training uses architectural, masking, normalization, and optimization choices that empirically avoid uninformative solutions in the reported settings. The existence of useful trained representations is an empirical result; a universal noncollapse guarantee should not be inferred from the abbreviated objective. This distinction is especially important when adapting the method to a new modality or action-conditioned domain.

V-JEPA extends feature prediction to video representations, learning temporal structure without reconstructing every observed pixel . Temporal predictability and interventional identification remain different properties. Consider a binary latent variable , an observational action , and two possible transition mechanisms: or . Both generate exactly the same observational pairs . Under , however, the first gives and the second gives . This constructed counterexample shows that perfect passive prediction does not identify the effect of an intervention absent additional assumptions or action-grounded evidence.

The 2026 progression from dense V-JEPA features to action-conditioned policy components should therefore be evaluated at two distinct interfaces: preservation of observation distinctions and prediction of consequences under the deployed action distribution . A changed action schema can break the second while leaving the first intact. Relevant controls retain the encoder while changing the policy or action expert, then retain the action interface while changing the encoder. A frozen visual backbone can supply useful state features without constituting an identified transition model or a complete controller.

A multimodal language model commonly maps visual features through a projection or adapter into representations consumed by a language decoder. Visual instruction tuning studies how such a system can answer or follow instructions involving images . For an agent, the output must eventually identify an executable target and arguments. This adds a grounding obligation absent from many question-answering tasks: the referenced object must correspond to the current environment, and the selected action must be valid there. Describing the correct button is not equivalent to clicking it, and producing a plausible screenshot description is not evidence that a state transition occurred.

Fusion strategies expose different bottlenecks. Early token fusion lets attention combine modalities directly but can consume a large context budget. A fixed-size visual summary controls cost while restricting recoverable detail. Cross-attention can separate language and visual lengths but adds its own compute and architectural assumptions. A tool-mediated approach leaves images outside the main model and retrieves structured descriptions or crops on demand. None dominates independently of task distribution. Exact document reading, spatial manipulation, and long video understanding demand different balances of detail, temporal coverage, and interaction latency.

The data pipeline must preserve the relation between natural-language instructions and observations. If a training example includes a final answer beside a screenshot taken after the action, the learner may exploit evidence unavailable when the action was chosen. A similar leak occurs when an evaluator supplies a full trajectory while judging a decision that should depend only on its prefix. Dataset construction should retain action timestamps and distinguish pre-action observations from post-action verification. The context-policy consistency issue is thus not restricted to text compression; it also applies to multimodal temporal alignment.

Untrusted visual content can contain instructions. A web page, document, or terminal screenshot can ask the agent to reveal secrets or change its objective. Converting that content to text through OCR does not change its authority. The system should retain provenance through every modality transformation and enforce authorization outside the model. A learned refusal policy can reduce harmful routing, but cannot replace an execution boundary that checks actual permissions. Evaluations should include task-relevant visual instructions and adversarial embedded instructions so that ignoring all image text is not rewarded as a successful defense.

Video and streaming interfaces require a choice of what to observe and when. Uniform frame sampling can miss short events; dense sampling can exhaust computation and context. For an event of duration observed by periodic samples spaced apart, a randomly phased event has detection probability under ideal instantaneous sampling and visibility assumptions. This is a calculated sampling fact, not a benchmark result. It shows why an agent that must notice transient confirmations or failures needs event-driven observations or a sampling rate matched to the event timescale.

Freshness is distinct from recognition accuracy. Let an observation be captured at time and the action execute at . Its age is . A correct recognition at can become wrong at when another actor changes the environment. Systems should retain observation versions and use preconditions or refreshed observations before consequential operations. A multimodal model cannot infer an unobserved concurrent change reliably merely because it can describe the previous frame. The control policy should decide when the expected cost of stale evidence exceeds the cost of another observation.

A simple decision rule formalizes that trade. Suppose refreshing costs and reduces expected action loss from to . Refreshing is beneficial when , with all quantities measured in a common utility scale. Estimating the loss reduction is difficult and task-dependent; an arbitrary confidence score is not automatically that estimate. Nevertheless, the formulation separates uncertainty about recognition from uncertainty about environmental change. A high-confidence image classification can coexist with a high need for refresh.

An observation policy can itself be learned, but its training distribution must include the consequences of missed events and unnecessary observations. Rewarding only final task completion may obscure excessive sensing cost. Rewarding fewer frames without a reliability constraint can encourage omission of rare but decisive events. Evaluate sensing decisions with retained raw streams where permissions allow, so that missed information can be distinguished from reasoning failure. For privacy-sensitive environments, an appropriately scoped event record may be preferable to storing all video, but the resulting evidential limits should remain explicit.

The I-JEPA and V-JEPA repositories provide concrete encoders, predictors, masking pipelines, and training configurations . A reproduction should identify the exact snapshot and trace the target update, stop-gradient boundary, mask construction, positional embeddings, preprocessing, and downstream adaptation. A learned checkpoint can be incompatible with a changed resize or normalization policy even when tensor shapes match. The implementation record must bind preprocessing, weights, and evaluation.

An abstract training step separates observation visibility, gradient flow, optimization, and target maintenance. Let be a permitted training example with provenance . Let select context and target positions from the example’s index set. Their admissibility and possible overlap are determined by the chosen JEPA variant. The view carries the selected observations together with their original position indices for the encoder’s positional embeddings. Using the encoder and predictor notation of Section ,

Here is the declared prediction loss on the selected target representation. The operator preserves its argument’s value while assigning zero derivative through the target branch. Write , with current value , and let be optimizer state. A fresh gradient and the declared stateful optimizer update are
The gradient contains no residual accumulation from the preceding step; optimizer state is retained according to . For the exponential-moving-average target update considered here,

The order uses the updated online encoder, while the current loss uses the previous target. At the target is unchanged for that update. Mask construction, loss, optimizer, and target schedule must match the inspected variant; these equations do not assert one universal JEPA recipe.

For I-JEPA, the paper’s Section 3 prediction loss is implemented through forward_target, forward_context, and loss_fn inside src/train.py; spatial target construction is exposed by MaskCollator in src/masks/multiblock.py. The pinned V-JEPA repository has corresponding training functions in app/vjepa/train.py and a VisionTransformerPredictor in src/models/predictor.py. These checked code locations allow a reproduction to inspect where the target is detached, which positions are predicted, and whether a mask includes information that should have been hidden. A mask bug can make representation loss excellent while destroying the intended predictive task. The inspected I-JEPA loss_fn calls F.smooth_l1_loss; the V-JEPA 2.1 path instead exposes an absolute-error power, per-target masking and optional distance weights. Its forward_target normalizes selected intermediate feature groups separately before concatenating them . The exponent, normalization axes, target positions and weighting schedule are therefore objective-defining variables, even when both implementations are called predictive representation learning.

The I-JEPA paper’s Table 7 reports 66.9 percent versus 40.7 percent for target-encoder versus pixel targets in a ViT-L/16 low-shot linear evaluation using one percent of ImageNet-1K labels. The corresponding pretraining budgets are 500 and 800 epochs . Those reported values support a useful target-space comparison in the authors’ setup; the unequal training budgets preclude describing the difference as a perfectly compute-matched causal estimate. An agent-specific follow-up should hold preprocessing, training compute, policy, and observation access fixed, then test exact small-text distinctions and action success rather than assuming the classification advantage transfers unchanged.

For a controlled agent study, compare a frozen contrastive encoder, a frozen predictive encoder, a fine-tuned version of each, and a raw-observation or structured-state oracle where available. Keep the language policy, tool budget, and action interface fixed when attributing a representation effect. Include a separate end-to-end comparison that permits each method’s best supported integration, but label it as a system comparison. Report training data exposure and adaptation compute: a method that uses action-labeled trajectories has a different information advantage from one trained only on passive images.

Task construction should include counterfactual visual pairs, temporal reorderings, altered themes, multilingual text, unseen layouts, and concurrent state changes. Split by application or environment lineage when template reuse could inflate transfer. Exact action outcomes should be verified through the environment rather than judged only from the model’s explanation. Human or model judgments can still assess ambiguous semantics, but their uncertainty and disagreement need reporting. A visually plausible explanation should never substitute for evidence that the intended external effect occurred.

Multimodal resource accounting should identify where compression occurs. If visual tokens are inserted into a language sequence of length , the unmasked pair-count increment is . Causal attention changes constants and visibility patterns but retains the interaction between old language context and new visual evidence. The vision encoder has a separate cost, and cross-attention architectures use a different accounting expression. Reporting only the final language-token count can conceal an expensive image encoder or multiple high-resolution crops. Reporting only image resolution can conceal aggressive visual compression before the language policy sees the result.

Persistent multimodal memory adds another choice: retain raw observations, retain encoder features, or retain textual interpretations. Raw observations permit later re-encoding after a model update but consume storage and may carry sensitive information. Features are compact but tied to an encoder and preprocessing version. Textual interpretations can be searchable and cheap to condition on, while irreversibly losing visual details that were not described. A memory system should preserve the distinction between an observed fact and an interpretation derived from an image. When an agent later needs a detail absent from the interpretation, confidence in the summary cannot restore the missing evidence.

A useful ablation fixes storage bytes rather than the number of stored items. Compare raw thumbnails, cropped evidence regions, latent features, and textual summaries under that envelope. Measure retrieval of action-relevant facts, successful re-grounding after interface changes, and the cost of re-encoding or additional observation. Include an encoder-upgrade condition to expose representation-version dependence. The outcome may favor different storage forms for different timescales; there is no reason to expect one universal visual-memory format. Keeping the original evidence for selected high-value events can be worthwhile even when most routine observations are summarized.

Finally, visual confidence should be calibrated after fusion, not inherited from one channel. A high image-text similarity, an OCR confidence, and a language-model token probability refer to different events and sample spaces. Multiplying them assumes a probabilistic model and dependence structure that usually has not been established. A decision-level calibrator can instead be trained and assessed against verified target selection or task outcomes, with separate evaluation under appearance and temporal shifts. Calibration then supports an explicit refresh or abstention policy rather than decorating an uncertain action with an unjustified numerical score.

LeFlow’s August 2026 method generates a latent path with rectified flow, decodes latent transitions into action chunks through inverse dynamics, and reranks candidates by rollout through a frozen world model. Its Section 3 separates these components and includes consistency between generated and realizable trajectories . This supplies a current counterpoint to solving an action-space optimization problem from scratch at every control step. The proposal distribution is learned offline, while verification still consumes online model computation.

An analytical cost comparison should keep that offline investment visible. If training the planner costs , iterative planning costs per query, and amortized generation plus reranking costs , the latter has lower total compute after more than queries when the denominator is positive and the compared quality constraint is satisfied. This is a break-even identity, not a claim about the paper’s measured crossover. It fails as a deployment prediction when the learned prior becomes stale or must be retrained for changed dynamics.

The distinction between a generated endpoint and a realizable endpoint is equally important. Conditioning a latent generator on the desired goal can force its proposed path to end there by construction. That does not establish that decoded actions produce the path under the dynamics. Scoring the generated endpoint alone would reward a tautology. A rollout-based score instead checks what the decoded controls actually induce in the model, while retaining the real-model discrepancy analyzed below. A strong evaluation reports both generated-path error and rollout endpoint error, followed by actual environment success under receding-horizon execution.

A world model for an agent predicts consequences conditional on actions and the information available before those actions. Let be environment state, an action, and an observation. A fully observed model estimates and a reward or task-progress function. Under partial observability it instead maintains a belief or learned latent state from . Predicting a plausible next screenshot is not sufficient: the prediction must distinguish the consequences of the agent’s available interventions, including failure, denial, and partial completion. A model that generates visually convincing but causally incorrect transitions can actively mislead a planner.

Observational data alone can leave the intervention effect unidentified. Suppose a training corpus shows a confirmation dialog followed by a completed purchase. The correlation does not establish which button was clicked, whether authorization was granted, or whether an unseen service completed the transaction. A controller using this correlation as an action model can infer success without performing the required operation. Action-labeled transitions, controlled interventions, and authoritative postconditions reduce this ambiguity. They do not eliminate every hidden confound, especially when external services contain state not exposed to the agent.

The model’s boundary should include failure semantics. A network timeout is not equivalent to a failed transaction: the remote operation may have committed while the response was lost. A useful transition model can represent this uncertainty and the value of a status query. A text generator trained only on successful demonstrations may instead fill in the expected success narrative. The distinction is operationally important for stateful agents because imagined certainty can cause duplicate execution, incorrect memory updates, or premature termination. The world model should support epistemic uncertainty about the actual external state, not merely stochastic variation in its rendered description.

World modeling also differs from a policy prior. A language model may know that tests usually follow a code edit, which helps propose an action sequence. That does not mean it predicts whether the particular patch passes the repository’s tests. A learned policy can exploit regularities without an explicit simulator; a simulator can be useful even when the final policy executes without online lookahead. The comparative question is whether adding the model improves decisions under matched data and computation, and whether the gain comes from predictive accuracy, additional supervision, or extra search.

Let be a stochastic latent variable and a deterministic recurrent state. A generic latent dynamics model uses a prior , an observation-conditioned posterior , and an update . Observation, reward, and termination heads provide learning signals. A variational training objective combines reconstruction or prediction terms with a divergence between posterior and prior. Its purpose is to make a state inferable from real observations while allowing future latent trajectories to be sampled without access to those future observations.

The two directions of information flow matter. The posterior can use the new observation to correct its state estimate. The prior must predict before seeing that observation. A training loss that allows the prior to condition on future information is not a valid test of imagination. Similarly, a replay dataset must distinguish what was known at action time from what was later discovered. The same temporal leakage that damages agent policy training can make a world model appear more predictive than its deployable interface permits. Saving full trajectories is not enough unless their causal visibility is retained.

DreamerV3 provides a concrete latent-world-model approach in which the actor and critic learn from imagined latent trajectories. Its reported method uses separate prediction, dynamics, and representation losses, with stop-gradient placement and regularization controlling their interaction. The deployed actor in the cited version samples actions without online lookahead planning . This distinction prevents a common category error: learning through imagined trajectories and searching a model at every decision are different uses of a world model. Both can improve control, but their computation and failure modes differ.

Representation pressure creates a tradeoff. Strong compression can make dynamics easier to predict while discarding task-critical detail. Weak compression can preserve observations while making the latent transition harder to learn. Reward and continuation predictions encourage retention of some control-relevant information, but their sufficiency depends on the training objectives and task family. A reward change can reveal distinctions the original representation ignored. A world model intended for reusable enterprise agents should therefore be evaluated under changed goals and tools, not only the reward function that shaped its latent state.

An uncertainty estimate should distinguish ambiguity in observations, stochastic environmental outcomes, and lack of model knowledge. Sampling multiple futures from one generative model does not automatically capture the third category. All samples can share the same systematic error. Ensembles, held-out transition tests, and disagreement across independently informed predictors can provide diagnostics, but dependence and shared training data limit their interpretation. The controller needs a policy for falling back to real observations or conservative actions when model evidence is weak; otherwise uncertainty remains an unused output rather than a control mechanism.

Dual-WM’s September 2026 construction assigns primitive transitions and macro-action transitions to distinct latent spaces. Its Section 3 encodes windows of low-level features into a high-level state, learns a regularized macro-action interface, and refines high-level subgoals by projecting low-level rollouts back into the high-level space . It does not require an inverse decoder from an arbitrary high-level state to one concrete primitive state. A final low-level goal phase restores distinctions that an abstract subgoal can omit.

The temporal units matter. If one low-level model action spans environment operations and one macro transition spans low-level steps, a high-level horizon covers operations. Comparing directly with a primitive planning horizon confounds abstraction with temporal reach. Moreover, a high-level transition is usable only if some allowed primitive sequence realizes its proposed subgoal. A normal prior over macro-actions regularizes search but does not prove that every sampled point has an executable refinement.

For an agent experiment, fix an overall operation budget and compare primitive planning, two-scale planning without refinement validation, and two-scale planning with observed subgoal checks. Hold the number of environment operations covered constant before comparing prediction depth or latency. Include abstract states that alias different permissions or irreversible changes. If refinement reaches the high-level embedding but violates a required concrete predicate, score it as a failed refinement. This separates useful temporal abstraction from a planner that merely hides execution error inside a coarser representation.

The effect of model error grows with the horizon over which imagined outcomes influence selection. Consider a finite-horizon Markov system, a common initial-state distribution, a fixed policy, and true and modeled reward functions taking values in . Suppose one-step transition total variation is uniformly at most and reward error at most on the union of state-action supports reachable under true and modeled dynamics. Couple true and modeled transitions so that, while their states agree, their actions agree and the next states disagree with probability at most . By a union bound, the probability of divergence before step is at most , capped at one.
Before divergence, rewards differ by at most ; after divergence their difference is at most because both functions are bounded. Summing a conservative bound across steps yields

This is an elementary simulation argument under uniform error and bounded rewards, presented as a deduction rather than a new theorem. The quadratic term explains why a small one-step error need not justify long open-loop plans. The bound can be loose, and its assumptions are often harder to establish than a low average prediction loss.

The uniformity condition is the critical practical limit. A model can have excellent average error on logged behavior while being inaccurate on the unusual action sequences selected by optimization. Search actively seeks trajectories with high predicted value, which can concentrate on precisely those unsupported regions. This is model exploitation. Increasing search breadth can therefore reduce real performance even when it improves the planner’s predicted objective. The relevant evaluation distribution includes states and actions induced by the planner, not only a random held-out subset of the original transition dataset.

If the return discrepancy is uniformly bounded by for every candidate policy and the model-based optimizer is at most below its model optimum, its true-policy regret is at most . To prove this, add and subtract the modeled returns of the true optimum and selected policy. The two true-to-model discrepancies each contribute at most , and modeled suboptimality contributes at most . This reduction makes the requirement explicit: improving search reduces , but does not reduce model error. Once model error dominates, more precise optimization of the same inaccurate simulator need not improve real performance. The result requires a common feasible policy class and a discrepancy bound over that class; a bound for one fixed logged policy is insufficient after selection.

Receding-horizon control reduces the interval over which the controller relies on uncorrected predictions. It plans for a horizon, executes a short prefix, observes the real outcome, and replans. This does not remove model error, but it can prevent an early mistake from propagating through an entire unobserved trajectory. The benefit must be balanced against observation cost, action latency, and irreversible effects. In a coding agent, running a cheap local test can correct a model of program behavior. In a payment workflow, an irreversible action may require stronger preconditions than replanning afterward can provide.

Denoising diffusion models learn a reverse process associated with a prescribed noising process. For a declared schedule , the standard Gaussian forward transition is . Writing and gives the directly sampled marginal

A network can be trained to predict the injected noise under a timestep-conditioned squared-error objective. The reverse parameterization, variance choices, and sampling procedure determine how that prediction is used .

For an agent, conditioning can include previous observations, actions, goals, or structured state. The resulting generator models a distribution of possible future observations under the training data’s conditional relationships. It does not become a causal simulator merely because actions appear in the prompt. The action labels must correspond to actual interventions, and the training data must identify the relevant effects. Otherwise the generator may produce what usually follows a textual description rather than what the external system would do. Visual realism can make this error harder to detect because the imagined outcome appears coherent.

Sampling cost is important when generation enters a planning loop. If a candidate trajectory requires denoising evaluations and the planner evaluates candidates over multiple rounds, model-call count can grow with both and . Batching can improve throughput while increasing peak memory. Reusing conditional features can save work but must respect changing actions and state. A comparison with a direct policy should include all generative sampling and scoring costs, not only the final chosen trajectory. A method that plans better with a much larger budget answers a different question from one that allocates equal computation more effectively.

Latent diffusion moves generation into a compressed representation produced by an encoder and decoded back into observations . The compression reduces the dimensionality of the denoising computation, while introducing an information bottleneck and decoder distortion. If a safety-relevant indicator disappears in the latent representation, the diffusion process cannot reliably preserve it. A control-oriented latent generator should therefore be evaluated on exact state properties as well as perceptual quality. A small average image error can coexist with a wrong text label, object count, or action affordance.

Diffusion Transformers replace the denoising backbone with a Transformer-based architecture and study its scaling properties . Architectural scaling results from image synthesis should not be promoted into evidence of reliable agent planning without a control experiment. The relevant bridge is whether action-conditioned generated trajectories improve verified decisions relative to matched alternatives. A generator can be useful for training diversity, counterfactual hypothesis generation, or visualization while remaining unsuitable as the authoritative source of environment state.

Flow matching learns a time-dependent vector field that transports a simple distribution toward the data distribution . For a simple illustrative path , with endpoints drawn from a chosen coupling, the conditional velocity is . A regression objective trains to predict that velocity. The marginally correct field is the conditional expectation of the target velocity given , obtained by the usual squared-loss projection property. This formulation separates a training path from the numerical solver used at sampling time.

The interpolation variable in this construction is not physical environment time. It parameterizes a transformation between distributions. Confusing the two can lead to an incorrect interpretation of an intermediate generated state as a physically possible step in an agent trajectory. A model can generate an entire action sequence or future video as one sample while its internal denoising or transport path passes through objects with no environmental meaning. Planning constraints must apply to the generated trajectory’s action and state coordinates, not to arbitrary intermediate solver iterates.

Numerical integration introduces another approximation. A learned vector field can be accurate under its training distribution while a coarse solver accumulates error or evaluates off-distribution states. More solver steps may improve fidelity but cost latency. The solver, tolerance, precision, and conditioning policy belong to the reproducible method. A claimed model improvement that changes both the learned field and the solver cannot isolate which component produced the gain. For agents, the complete outcome also depends on the external verifier that accepts or rejects the generated plan.

Action constraints can be enforced through parameterization, constrained sampling, projection, or post-generation rejection. Each changes the distribution or feasible set. Projection may alter a generated trajectory so that its predicted consequences no longer correspond to its actions. Rejection can require many expensive samples when feasible plans are rare. A parameterization can guarantee local bounds, such as a control range, while leaving global requirements unproven. These mechanisms should be tested against exact environment constraints where possible, rather than assuming that a high-quality generator learns every hard rule from examples.

Textual agents often operate in environments whose important state can be represented symbolically: files, database records, task statuses, permissions, and tool outputs. A world model can predict this structured state instead of rendering a visual future. Executable transition rules have the advantage that invariants can be checked directly. They have the disadvantage that a missing rule or hidden service behavior can invalidate the simulation. A generated tool response should be marked as imagined so that it cannot be mistaken for an actual observation and written into persistent memory as verified fact.

The separation between hypothetical and observed events should be structural. Maintain distinct event types or stores for simulation, proposals, and executed operations. A natural-language disclaimer embedded in the same untyped text is fragile: a later summarizer may omit it. If a planner imagines that a test passes and the memory writer records only the passing result, future sessions inherit fabricated evidence. The same problem appears when synthetic training trajectories are mixed with real traces without provenance. The system must preserve whether each transition was measured, simulated by executable rules, or sampled from a generative model.

Model validation should focus on transition invariants and counterexamples. For a file-editing environment, verify that reads reflect prior writes, path resolution is consistent, and failed operations do not silently mutate state. For a workflow environment, check allowed status transitions, authorization changes, and duplicate requests. A model that predicts common successful traces may still violate these invariants on rare branches. Such failures can be more consequential than an average next-observation loss suggests because planners deliberately explore unusual sequences.

The symbol denotes a point mass, not a model-predicted response. Let denote record append and let implement the inference map incrementally on the domain of observed interaction histories, including recorded denials. Then

The imagined trajectories never enter as observations. A real tool response may itself report failure or an uncertain external outcome; recording it preserves that evidence rather than certifying the described effect. The update from this actual response is the control loop’s anchor. Without it, the procedure can drift into optimizing its own narratives instead of the external task.

The inspected V-JEPA 2 repository separates passive representation training from action-conditioned robot training. Its current app/vjepa_droid/train.py exposes forward_target, forward_predictions, and _step_predictor, while the V-JEPA 2.1 training module has a distinct representation-learning path . This separation matters scientifically: a stronger visual representation and a better action-conditioned transition model are related interventions, but their effects should not be conflated. The available code enables a reader to inspect where actions enter the predictor and which targets supply supervision.

The contemporary Dreamer implementation similarly exposes Agent.policy, Agent.loss, imag_loss, and lambda_return in dreamerv3/agent.py . These checked function names identify the distinction between real interaction, model fitting, and imagined policy learning. A current repository snapshot may differ from the cited report’s experimental release; reproducing its headline results requires the original configuration as well as code. For diffusion, the inspected Diffusers DDPMScheduler.step and add_noise in scheduling_ddpm.py make the forward-noise and reverse-update conventions explicit . Swapping scheduler prediction types without changing the trained output interpretation is a concrete correctness error, not a harmless implementation variation.
