A single rollout can contain multiple action-time contexts. Each segment retains context , sampled tokens , behavior probabilities and learning mask . Terminal outcome may weight later learning terms; it is not an additional conditioning argument of the displayed action likelihood. The lower circles denote learning computations, not behavior calls. This schematic omits the full post-training objective and correction factors.

A terminal reward must assign credit to decisions separated by long tool delays and many intermediate tokens. Treating every token in a successful trajectory as equally good can reinforce redundant explanations and accidental workarounds. Tool selection, argument construction, context editing, and memory writing have different causal roles. A useful ablation removes or replaces one component while preserving resources and observes the outcome. Such interventions can inform training signals, but hindsight attribution remains uncertain when several actions jointly enable success.

Memory writing is particularly difficult because its value may appear only in a later session. Immediate task reward can favor a compact note that helps the current answer while discarding a rare future constraint. Conversely, rewarding every retrieved use can encourage excessive storage or irrelevant retrieval. The learning objective should declare the horizon and cost of retention, retrieval, verification, and conflict handling. Evaluation should randomize task order and distinguish within-session adaptation from cross-session transfer. Otherwise improvements can depend on a favorable curriculum that deployment will not reproduce.

Model updates also change the policy that interprets existing memories and skills. A procedure distilled for one checkpoint may become redundant, misleading, or incompatible after post-training. Evaluate retained skill banks before and after a weight update, including stale assumptions and changed tool schemas. Updating memory and model weights together without separate ablations makes it difficult to identify where a gain or regression originated. Compatibility tests should therefore be part of the learning loop, with rollback capable of restoring the relevant combination of policy and external state.

Post-training can improve reasoning and tool use substantially, but the claim must remain attached to a measurable behavior and evidence source. Preference agreement is not universal alignment, a higher automated reward is not verified task success, and a finite sequence of improving checkpoints is not accelerating recursive self-improvement. The scientific standard is stronger: correct conditioning, identified estimators, independent acceptance criteria, resource-matched alternatives, and retained regressions. These requirements make the resulting policy improvement interpretable and useful for a stateful agent rather than merely attractive on its training dashboard.

The September 2026 meta-reasoning study separates worker computation from a controller that assesses artifacts, proposes work, evaluates options, and dispatches context from persistent memory. Its analysis distinguishes whether a correct answer appeared, whether the controller recognized it, and whether it selected it. It reports gains alongside overhead that can hurt small-budget settings . The paper’s Appendix A explicitly limits component attribution and resource matching. Its shared budget allowance is not proof that every system consumed equal tokens, latency, or dollars. This is a current example of treating inference control as a mechanism rather than equating a larger reasoning transcript with better allocation.

An artifact graph supplies an observable account of the controller’s allocation. Nodes represent partial solutions, evidence, checks, and selected outputs; edges record derivation or reuse. Repeated restarts and refinement of verified partial work can have different cost and failure behavior at equal accuracy. Distinguish a copied assertion from independently obtained evidence, and record whether a computation changed the final choice. A verifier invocation that merely confirms the already selected artifact has a different causal role from one that rejects the incumbent and causes a successful replacement. Log both the selection before the check and the selection after it; a final graph without these decision-time snapshots cannot identify that distinction.

An appropriate ablation keeps workers, tools, task instances, and total actual expenditure comparable while varying the control policy. Compare direct control, independent sampling, structured reuse without explicit evaluation, and the full controller. Separately remove persistent artifact retrieval to test whether compact controller context depends on external memory. The resulting experiment can identify which interaction matters; the combined method’s headline score cannot assign causal credit to every named stage. The accessible paper specifies the algorithm and prompts; an executable reproduction additionally requires independently established, versioned implementation artifacts.

For stateful deployment, the controller’s compact state is itself a memory policy. Its summaries can omit constraints or misstate artifact validity. A worker should receive the evidence needed for its assigned subproblem, and its output should preserve unresolved assumptions. Version changes in workers or tools can invalidate earlier artifacts. The inference controller therefore needs the same compatibility and provenance contracts as other long-running agent components. A successful short benchmark run does not establish indefinite artifact validity or reliable cross-session reuse.

Inference-time reasoning changes the computation used to choose an answer or action while leaving some or all model weights fixed. A model can produce intermediate text, sample alternatives, invoke tools, or delegate subproblems. These mechanisms have different information and resource effects. Intermediate text extends the model’s conditional state; an external tool can supply new evidence; independent sampling explores alternative continuations; a verifier changes which continuation is selected. Calling all of them thinking obscures the intervention. Their contribution should be identified through the distribution they change and the evidence they add.

Let denote an intermediate reasoning sequence and the final action. A generative model defines , and its induced action distribution marginalizes over . Choosing one greedy sequence, sampling a sequence, voting across answers, and searching a tree produce different decision rules from the same underlying model. They need not rank actions identically. A system that reports only the final action without the generation and selection procedure does not fully specify its inference policy. The selected reasoning trace also need not characterize all alternative computations the model could have produced.

Chain-of-thought prompting supplies examples or instructions that elicit intermediate language before an answer, with reported improvements in the original study’s evaluated reasoning tasks . This is an empirical prompting result, not a guarantee that every generated rationale is a faithful account of internal computation. A rationale can contain a correct derivation, a plausible explanation of a guessed answer, or an error later corrected. For an agent, the distinction becomes consequential when a trace is stored as procedural memory. A fluent but invalid derivation should not become trusted guidance merely because the final answer happened to be correct.

The strongest reasoning evidence is an independently checkable object attached to a precise claim: an executable calculation, a proof accepted by a specified checker, a test demonstrating a behavior, or a trace of actual tool observations. Even these objects have scope limits. A proof checker validates a formal statement under its axioms; a test covers selected inputs; a calculator evaluates the supplied expression rather than determining whether it models the user’s problem. Reasoning quality therefore includes translating the task into the right formal object and interpreting its result, not only generating a long sequence of intermediate tokens.

Suppose independent attempts on one fixed task succeed with probability . The probability of at least one success among attempts is , while the probability that all succeed is . These quantities answer different questions. With hypothetical and , they are 0.992 and 0.512. The first describes solution coverage when an oracle can identify success; the second describes repeated-run consistency. Neither is the success probability of a practical selector unless the selector’s behavior is specified. Reporting pass-at- as dependable autonomous performance confuses these events.

Given recorded attempts with successes on a task, the conditional coverage of a uniformly chosen subset of attempts is exactly , with the numerator zero when fewer than failures exist. Under independent identically distributed sampling, this statistic is also an unbiased estimator of population pass-at- . The first statement is combinatorial; the second additionally depends on the sampling model. It estimates a sampling property of the candidate set; it does not account for the cost of finding and verifying those candidates. Tasks with different values should be aggregated at the task level rather than inserting a global average into the formula, because the nonlinear transformation changes the result.

Independence is often unrealistic. Samples share the same model, prompt, retrieved evidence, and training-induced misconceptions. Let correctness indicators have common mean , variance , and pairwise correlation . Then

This follows by summing variances and covariances. For an admissible correlation with , the corresponding variance-based effective sample size is . At zero denominator the sample mean has zero variance under this model, rather than a defined finite effective count. It is a diagnostic under the stated exchangeability assumptions, not a universal replacement for the full joint distribution. A hundred correlated attempts can carry much less independent evidence than their count suggests.

Self-consistency samples reasoning paths and aggregates their final answers, rather than trusting one path . It approximates the answer mass induced by the model and decoding procedure. The modal answer can still be wrong. Under independent binary correctness with , a majority vote has an error probability bounded by through Hoeffding’s inequality, with tie handling specified separately. If the model’s dominant misconception makes , increasing the sample count can make the wrong majority more stable. The bound’s premises are stronger than merely using different random seeds.

Answer equivalence is itself a component. Exact string voting can split mathematically equivalent expressions or merge ambiguous natural-language answers incorrectly. A canonicalizer may simplify arithmetic expressions, normalize units, or compare structured actions. That canonicalizer needs a correctness contract. For tool use, two actions that have the same apparent intent can differ in permissions, resource identity, or irreversible side effects. Voting on a prose description before argument validation can select an action family whose actual executable instances are all invalid. Aggregation should operate on a representation appropriate to the task’s semantics.

Diversity interventions include changing prompts, sampling parameters, decompositions, tools, or model checkpoints. Each can reduce shared errors while introducing new confounds and costs. A heterogeneous team is not automatically independent, particularly when all members read the same flawed summary. A useful study measures error overlap and the selector’s performance rather than relying on role names as evidence of diversity. When candidates have access to different evidence, retain that provenance so that disagreement can motivate another observation rather than being settled by a numerical majority alone.

In stateful tasks, candidates also need isolation. If the first attempt modifies a repository, the second is not a repeated trial from the same initial state unless the environment is restored. Shared persistent memory can make later attempts better informed, but the resulting process is adaptation rather than independent sampling. Both are legitimate experimental objects. They should be reported separately because their reliability, resource use, and deployment assumptions differ. A best-of-five outcome with accumulated memory does not estimate the same quantity as five fresh attempts.

More candidates increase coverage but also expose the selector to more opportunities for error. Let candidate have true utility and estimated score . Suppose each error has a sub-Gaussian tail . A union bound gives simultaneous error at most with probability at least across candidates. Independence is not needed for this union bound, though the marginal tail assumption must hold for the evaluated candidates.

If maximizes estimated score and maximizes true utility, simultaneous error control yields . Add and subtract the two estimated scores; their difference is nonpositive by selection, leaving two bounded errors. This elementary deduction formalizes a selection effect: the score accuracy required for a fixed regret tolerance becomes stricter as the candidate set grows. A method can discover better candidates while selecting a worse final answer. The correct diagnosis separates coverage, recognition, and final selection rather than treating all failure as insufficient generation quality. For a selector restricted to the generated candidate set, let be the event that the set contains a correct artifact and the event that the selected artifact is correct. Then and

This separates generator coverage from conditional selection success. A selector allowed to create a new answer changes the candidate set and must be evaluated under that expanded boundary; the inequality cannot be transferred silently to a different pipeline.

The assumptions deserve scrutiny in adaptive search. Candidates are proposed in response to earlier scores, so an error bound established on random unselected examples may not transfer. A reward model can be exploited by repeatedly searching for high-scoring artifacts. Calibration on ordinary completions is therefore insufficient evidence of robustness under optimization. Evaluate the judge on planner-selected candidates, preserve hidden tests, and record whether a correct candidate appeared but was rejected. These records explain whether additional compute should be spent on generation, verification, or a different scoring objective.

Binary validators have a related multiple-testing problem. If each invalid candidate has conditional false-acceptance probability at most given the prior search history, the probability of at least one false acceptance among at most checks is at most . This conservative bound does not require independent checks. It does require the conditional error guarantee, which adversarially selected candidates can violate. A validator with a small average false-positive rate can become unreliable when an optimizer targets its blind spots. Increasing the sample budget without strengthening verification can therefore worsen accepted-output quality.

Assume independent candidates are correct with probability , and a validator accepts correct candidates with probability and incorrect candidates with probability . Its acceptance probability is . Conditional on acceptance, correctness is when . If the system returns the first accepted candidate, unbounded retries have the same accepted-output correctness and mean attempt count . More attempts increase the chance of returning something; they do not improve the precision of this stationary acceptance rule. This deduction separates availability from correctness and prevents a retry loop from being described as verification improvement.

For hypothetical , , and , acceptance is , accepted-output correctness is approximately , and the mean number of unbounded attempts is approximately . With four attempts, the chance of any acceptance is . These are calculated examples, not measured characteristics of a model judge. They assume the validator’s errors and the candidate distribution remain stationary, with fresh independent trials. Real adaptive search often violates precisely these assumptions because later candidates are chosen to exploit previous scores.

The example also identifies which intervention matters. Reducing the false-positive rate can improve accepted-output correctness substantially even if candidate generation does not improve. Increasing sensitivity can reduce wasted rejection of good candidates. Improving helps both coverage and precision, but may cost a larger model or more computation per attempt. A scientific comparison should measure all three rather than crediting the generator for a better validator or describing a more permissive validator as improved reasoning. When true labels are expensive, audit a stratified sample of accepted and rejected candidates, with sampling weights that permit reconstruction of the desired rates.

Optional stopping requires care in evaluation. If the system repeatedly checks until a favorable score appears, reporting the final score without the number of checks introduces selection bias. The final artifact should be judged by a held-out acceptance procedure that was not used to guide the search. This does not require that every verifier be secret forever; it requires separation between optimization feedback and the evidence used to estimate generalization. For executable tasks, hidden tests and independent specification review can serve complementary roles. Neither resolves an ambiguous task specification automatically.

Stateful tasks make the stationary example especially fragile. A rejected candidate may have already changed files or consumed a one-time token. A repeated browser action can alter the environment even when the judge says it failed. The selector should either operate on isolated candidate artifacts before execution or explicitly model these transitions. Retaining the complete operation history makes it possible to distinguish improved solution search from repeated interaction with a gradually changing task. This distinction is essential when comparing self-correction, sampling, and planning under the same nominal attempt budget.
Figure isolates the mechanism and its stated information boundaries.

Search-time scores and report-only acceptance labels serve different roles. Under one fixed acceptance map , the displayed indicators satisfy when . The probability notation abbreviates and ; the decomposition requires . A fallible checker measures its declared acceptance criterion. Pruning attribution additionally requires stage-labelled candidate records; the selected artifact alone is insufficient.

Tree of Thoughts treats intermediate text units as search states and uses generation, evaluation, and traversal rules to explore alternatives. Its Game of 24 experiment reports 74 percent success for the evaluated method versus 4 percent for its chain-of-thought comparator . Those author-reported results establish a task-specific system comparison with additional search; they do not isolate a universal architectural capability or equalize every inference cost. The inspected repository’s src/tot/methods/bfs.py exposes get_proposals, get_values, get_votes, and solve . This makes proposal, evaluation, and search policy identifiable implementation components. In this snapshot, get_value caches evaluations by the rendered value prompt, while get_values assigns zero to repeated candidate strings within one evaluation call. These are not independent repeated checks. The sampled-selection branch in solve normalizes scores by their sum, so its mathematical domain requires nonnegative weights with positive total; an all-zero set needs an explicit fallback in an integration. Record candidate entries, unique artifacts, fresh evaluator calls and cache hits separately. Otherwise repeated or cached work can be mistaken for additional search evidence.

Granularity determines branching and verifiability. Token-level search has a large shallow action space and weak semantic boundaries. A complete-program proposal permits executable testing but can waste work when one early assumption is wrong. Intermediate structured states can expose constraints, but the state representation must preserve all information needed to continue. Merging two reasoning nodes because their summaries look similar can destroy an important distinction. Search-state equivalence needs a task-specific invariant, just as cache reuse requires a computational invariant in Chapter .

With branching factor and depth , an unpruned tree has nodes for . Beam search with width can reduce retained nodes while pruning a correct path based on an imperfect early score. Depth-first traversal reduces frontier memory but can spend a long budget on one unproductive branch. Search order therefore trades coverage, peak storage, latency, and susceptibility to evaluator error. Report the actual explored graph and pruning decisions. A nominal beam width alone does not identify how much model computation was used when proposals and evaluations have variable lengths.

For agents, branching can include real operations, not only text. A planner can safely explore hypothetical patches in isolated workspaces, but cannot assume every external action is reversible. A search method should distinguish simulated states from committed environment states and prevent one branch’s side effects from contaminating another. Replaying a tool call can be expensive or non-idempotent. The search graph should retain operation identity and observed outcomes; executor permission checks remain independent of controller confidence.

Inference budget allocation is a sequential decision problem. Let be the controller’s information state and the value of selecting now. Computation costs in utility units and returns evidence , producing state . Its one-step value is

Under calibrated Bayesian updating, unchanged external state, and retained access to all original actions, the unpriced information term is nonnegative by the expectation-of-maximum inequality. A learned judge or an irreversible external operation does not inherit these assumptions. Verification, retrieval, resampling, and delegation must be assessed by their effect on the selected artifact, including actual controller and worker costs.

Stopping when every one-step value is nonpositive is a myopic rule, not generally an optimal stopping theorem. In a constructed example, the correct binary answer is the exclusive-or of two independent fair bits. Either observation alone leaves optimal accuracy at ; both raise it to one. If each observation costs 0.1 in the same utility scale as correctness, each one-step net value is , while obtaining both has net value . Complementary computations can therefore justify continuing even when neither is individually valuable.

For a finite decision model with remaining resource budget , deterministic resource cost , a known computation-transition law, and terminal selection utility, let be the best continuation value. The recursion is

Set if no computation is feasible. These equations specify the ideal allocation problem; a deployed controller generally lacks its transition law and calibrated utilities. The 2026 meta-reasoning case in Section supplies a concrete harness and artifact-level observations, rather than solving this recursion exactly . Evaluate stopping against realized improvements and deadlines, including observation staleness induced by further deliberation. A model’s statement that more thought would help is not itself an estimate of the displayed value.

Repeatedly checking the same candidate can have little value when checks share a failure mode. An independent executable test may be more informative than another paraphrased self-critique. Conversely, a cheap local consistency check can eliminate an obvious error before an expensive environment call. The controller’s action space should therefore expose cost and evidence type, not just a generic request to think harder. A budget measured in model calls can be misleading because one call may replay a huge context while another evaluates a short expression. Report tokens, external costs, and wall-clock time alongside the call count.

One operational realization is a myopic recurrence over a candidate graph and remaining resource budget . Decision epochs are measured after the controller’s proposal and scoring costs have been charged. Let reserve resources for the terminal check. For each proposed computation , estimates selection-utility gain, its cost in the same utility units, and its total resource charge through the next decision epoch. Define
The choice is defined only for a nonempty finite candidate set; fix a tie rule. The continuation indicator and stopping index are

For , let be the artifact actually returned by an execution operator that applies the required isolation or current authorization. Its evidence record retains source provenance , observed execution and recording cost , and the applicable configuration . Let charge preparation of the next decision epoch:

Here adds the observed artifact and its evidence links to the graph. For finite , a declared acceptance map selects an artifact or returns the abstention marker . The bounded terminal checker returns a verdict and supporting record ; its domain includes , which produces an unresolved verdict and an abstention record:

The gain estimate remains a hypothesis to validate, and establishes only its specified property. Predicted resource feasibility does not guarantee ; caps or justified bounds on both execution and controller work are needed to preserve the reserve. This formulation makes those admissibility obligations explicit without identifying the myopic controller with the ideal Bellman solution.

Define comparison axes before allocating resources: single-attempt success, coverage at a candidate budget, selected-answer accuracy, repeated-run consistency, verified constraint violations, latency tails, and complete cost. Include a direct-answer baseline, ordinary intermediate reasoning, independent sampling, aggregation, and search with a common verifier where feasible. A stronger verifier is a meaningful system improvement, but should be named as the intervention. Oracle selection can estimate generation headroom and must be labeled nondeployable. It should not appear in the main autonomous-performance ranking.

Failure attribution should retain both candidate-level and task-level evidence. If no correct candidate exists, selection cannot solve the task. If a correct candidate exists but a weak judge rejects it, more generation may be wasteful. If an accepted program passes visible tests but fails a held-out requirement, the issue can lie in specification coverage. If a correct action is generated from a stale context, execution may still fail. These cases require different interventions. A single score labeled reasoning ability cannot identify them.

The practical role of inference-time computation is to convert available model competence and evidence into a better decision under an explicit resource envelope. Its limits arise from shared misconceptions, imperfect selection, stale state, and external effects as much as from insufficient token generation. The most informative studies expose those mechanisms with mathematical assumptions, implementation paths, and controlled outcomes. They establish where additional computation helps, where it merely repeats an error, and where another real observation is more valuable than another internal continuation.

The checked breadth-first search implementation offers a useful place to instrument these distinctions. Record every proposal before scoring, every value returned by the evaluator, the retained frontier, and the final selection. On a task with an exact checker, label all generated candidates after the run without exposing those labels to search. This yields separate estimates of candidate coverage, evaluator discrimination, pruning loss, and final selection loss. A correct candidate pruned early is different evidence from a candidate that never appears. The instrumentation should include cache hits and repeated proposals so that duplicated work does not inflate apparent search diversity.

For a fixed set of candidates, compare the deployed selector with random choice, majority answer, shortest valid artifact, and oracle choice. These are selector ablations, not alternative generators. Then hold the selector fixed while varying proposal count and temperature. This two-stage design identifies whether a reported gain comes from finding more correct artifacts or recognizing them better. When the task requires external execution, candidate checks should occur in isolated environments or on immutable artifacts. Otherwise the checker itself can alter the state that later candidates encounter, invalidating the fixed-candidate interpretation.

The score-error bound earlier in this chapter also suggests a calibration diagnostic. Partition candidates by whether they were sampled randomly, selected for high score, or generated adaptively after feedback. Estimate judge error separately in each stratum. A much larger error in the selected stratum is direct evidence that ordinary calibration does not survive optimization pressure. Recalibrating only on the selected examples can help within that regime, but a new adaptive optimizer can create another shift. Keep an untouched evaluation sample and record each judge revision rather than treating the judge as a stationary oracle.

Memory reuse should be audited at the assertion level. If three workers all repeat a conclusion derived from one unverified artifact, their agreement is one evidence lineage, not three independent observations. A provenance graph can collapse these dependent claims before aggregation. Conversely, two independent executable checks on different relevant cases provide distinct evidence even when their natural-language summaries are identical. The controller should reason about that dependence explicitly. Otherwise increasing the number of agents can make a weak claim appear more certain through repetition alone.

These controls support practical allocation decisions. If generation coverage saturates but selection remains weak, spend budget on a stronger checker or a more informative test. If the checker is reliable but no correct candidate appears, improve decomposition, evidence retrieval, or the model. If both are adequate but state changes invalidate the chosen action, reduce observation age and strengthen execution preconditions. The resulting diagnosis connects inference-time reasoning to the surrounding agent system instead of using additional tokens as the default response to every failure.

WorldEvolver’s September 2026 revision holds model parameters and the downstream agent fixed while revising world-model context through episodic transitions, semantic rules, and selective foresight. Its protocol permits five trials, with memory persistence affecting later attempts. The overlapping task-level intervals are not a paired difference test, and the point estimates alone do not establish population-level superiority. These are author-reported results, not independent reproductions.

Establish whether a forecast changes the action and whether the changed action improves the verified transition under a matched resource budget. Reset controls are essential when memory evolves. Clear state before every task to measure within-task adaptation; retain it across tasks to measure cross-task transfer; and separately reset between attempts if the objective is fresh-run reliability. Randomize task order and record the exact reset semantics. A best-of-five score under persistent memory is a valid outcome for a particular adaptive workflow, but it cannot be presented as the probability that one newly deployed run succeeds. The distinction matters directly for users who expect a system to complete a consequential task once.

Once a failure prefix is null, an earlier factor in the survival product is already zero, so this extension does not change the following chain-rule identity:

No independence assumption is required. Replacing every by one common success rate requires an additional stationarity claim that persistent memory can violate. This is a proposed diagnostic, not an explanation established for the reported point differences.

A plan is a policy for changing or learning about a task state, not merely an ordered explanation. Let be a goal predicate on environment state, an invariant on complete system state, and an action cost. A useful planning problem specifies which terminal states satisfy the user objective, which intermediate states are prohibited, and what resources are available. An agent that produces a convincing account of without establishing it in the environment has not completed that planning problem. The distinction is especially important when a language model can simulate the expected wording of a successful tool response.

Goal predicates can be partial or ambiguous. Passing tests may be an operational acceptance condition for a coding task without fully specifying intended behavior. A reservation can exist in a system while violating a requested time or budget. The planner should retain unresolved requirements and seek clarification or evidence when those distinctions affect action. Converting an ambiguous instruction into one confident internal goal silently changes the task. A practical goal representation therefore includes source instructions, interpreted constraints, acceptance checks, and unresolved assumptions, rather than only a short objective summary.

Multiobjective planning requires explicit priorities. Success, latency, monetary cost, privacy, and permission compliance cannot always be compressed into one unconstrained scalar reward. Some are hard feasibility conditions; others are tradeoffs within the feasible set. A planner should not spend an unauthorized action to gain a slightly higher task score. Let indicate whether trajectory contains a state violating the declared invariant . A constrained objective can require , in addition to statewise authorization. These formulations are meaningful only when the probabilities and predicates have an evidential basis. A model-generated confidence statement does not establish the risk bound.

The plan’s initial state is also a claim requiring evidence. A resumed session can contain stale memory, incomplete operations, or a tool schema different from the previous run. Before continuing, reconcile the durable event history with the current environment and permissions. The policy may need an information-gathering action rather than an execution action. This makes planning inseparable from context and memory: the planner’s apparent reasoning competence can be undermined by an incorrect state estimate before the first proposed step.

Under partial observability, a belief summarizes uncertainty in an ideal known model. After action and observation , Bayes filtering gives . Learned agents often use an approximate textual or latent state instead of an explicit distribution. That approximation should preserve which facts are observed, inferred, disputed, or unknown. A summary that converts uncertainty into an unqualified assertion changes the planning problem rather than merely compressing it.

Some actions primarily reduce uncertainty. Reading a file, querying transaction status, inspecting a browser element, or running a diagnostic can improve later decisions without immediately advancing the visible goal. Their value depends on what choices they can change. If two possible states require the same next action, distinguishing them has little immediate decision value; if they require opposite irreversible operations, the information can be decisive. This is the operational connection between representation sufficiency in Chapter and planning. The planner needs distinctions relevant to its action set, not an exhaustive description of every environmental detail.

Information-gathering can itself have side effects. A diagnostic test can modify files or consume a rate-limited resource. A read can expose sensitive information to a model or external service. A browser refresh can discard an unsaved form. The planner should therefore model observation actions with costs and permissions rather than treating them as free oracle access. A common evaluation error gives a research agent a privileged state-inspection tool unavailable to the deployed system, then attributes the resulting gain entirely to better reasoning.

The belief update should incorporate negative evidence carefully. A missing response does not necessarily mean the operation failed; a missing memory result does not mean the underlying fact is false. The planner should distinguish absence of evidence from evidence of absence using the source’s completeness contract. An authoritative database lookup can establish that no matching record exists under a defined query, while an approximate retrieval miss cannot. This distinction directly affects whether the next action should retry, search differently, or proceed with a state-changing operation.

For deterministic transitions, a local action contract can be expressed as : if precondition holds and the action terminates according to its specification, postcondition holds. A sequence is compositionally valid when each postcondition establishes the next precondition and the invariant remains true. The proof is induction over steps. This is a precise reason to represent preconditions and observed postconditions explicitly rather than relying on a fluent plan whose steps merely sound compatible.

The weakest precondition for a deterministic action and desired postcondition is the set of initial states from which executing guarantees , under the action’s semantics. Backward reasoning through a plan can reveal missing assumptions. If nontermination is possible, a weakest precondition for total correctness includes termination; a weakest liberal precondition describes partial correctness and does not require it. A planning contract must declare which claim is intended. For example, an update operation may require that a record exists, the version matches, and the user is authorized. A prior search that merely found a similar record does not establish those predicates. Natural-language planning can propose the chain, while executable checks verify the conditions at the actual boundary.

Stochastic actions require probabilistic contracts or conservative feasible sets. Suppose step preserves the required conditions with conditional failure probability at most , given that previous steps have succeeded. A union-bound argument gives total failure probability at most , without requiring independent failures. The conditional qualification is essential. An average failure rate measured on unrelated states does not supply a bound for a planner-selected action. If authorization is a hard constraint rather than a statistical reliability target, it should be checked deterministically where the system has authoritative state.

Contracts remain partial specifications. A schema checker can establish argument shape, not task relevance. A unit test can establish behavior for selected cases, not every possible input. A proof can establish a formal statement while leaving the translation from user intent wrong. Compositional verification is strongest when those boundaries are explicit: combine local guarantees with independent checks of the overall acceptance condition, and retain uncertainty where the available specification does not decide the matter.

Open-loop planning selects a sequence before observing intermediate outcomes. Receding-horizon execution repeatedly plans, executes a prefix, observes the real result, and replans. The latter can correct state estimates and avoid compounding prediction errors, at the cost of additional decision and observation overhead. The correct horizon depends on action reversibility, environment volatility, model accuracy, and latency. A plan for a deterministic local calculation can be executed in a larger block than a sequence of irreversible operations against a changing external service.

ReAct interleaves reasoning and acting with environment observations, providing a concrete language-model-agent design for this feedback loop . Its important boundary is that an action requests an external operation and an observation records a returned result. A model-generated continuation that imitates the observation is not equivalent. An execution harness should prevent these roles from being conflated in storage and training. A reasoning step can predict what a tool will return, but the prediction must remain distinguishable from the actual returned evidence.

Feedback has a source and scope. A compiler error identifies a problem relative to a language and configuration. A test failure identifies a violated assertion on an executed case. A human correction can clarify intent. A model critique supplies another statistical judgment. These signals should not all be assigned the same authority. A planner can use a weak critique to generate a hypothesis and then seek stronger evidence. Replacing an observed test result with a persuasive self-explanation reverses that hierarchy and can cause the agent to reason away a real failure.

Feedback should update the right state. A transient service failure may justify retrying without revising a general skill. A consistent schema mismatch may require changing the tool adapter. An incorrect remembered assumption may require invalidating a memory record. A failed plan can expose an error in the goal interpretation, world model, action implementation, or acceptance checker. If every failure produces only a new natural-language reflection, the system may accumulate explanations while leaving the actual defect unchanged. Retain diagnostic evidence sufficient to choose among these updates.

Self-correction is a transition from an existing candidate to a revised candidate based on feedback. Its value depends on both repair and corruption. Let the original candidate be correct with probability , let be the probability of repairing an incorrect candidate, and let be the probability of corrupting a correct one. Under these aggregate conditional definitions, revised correctness is , so the gain is . Correction helps only when repair benefit exceeds damage to already correct work. A high repair rate alone is insufficient evidence of a useful correction system.

With hypothetical , , and , revised correctness is , a decrease of 1.5 percentage points despite repairing 30 percent of initial errors. These are calculated probabilities, not experimental results. The example explains why evaluation should include initially correct cases and preserve their outputs before revision. A benchmark restricted to known failures can measure repair ability while missing the full system’s regression rate. A correction gate that accepts only independently validated improvements can reduce corruption, but inherits the validator’s own false-acceptance and coverage limits.

Reflexion uses verbal feedback and episodic reflection to influence later attempts without treating that textual update as a weight update . This is a useful mechanism for memory-mediated adaptation. Its success depends on informative feedback, appropriate retrieval, and a policy that interprets the reflection correctly. A reflection can overgeneralize from one failure, blame the wrong component, or become stale after a tool change. Store the supporting case and applicability conditions rather than promoting every reflection into an unconditional rule.

Multiple correction rounds can amplify shared errors. If the same model supplies the candidate, critique, and acceptance judgment, agreement need not indicate independent confirmation. A stronger experimental design crosses candidate generator, feedback source, and acceptance checker, retaining a common task set. Include no-feedback resampling to distinguish genuine feedback use from another chance to sample. Include misleading but plausible feedback to test whether the policy can reject unsupported corrections. The desired behavior is evidence-sensitive revision, not unconditional obedience to the latest criticism.

Hierarchical planning replaces some primitive actions with temporally extended procedures. An option can be described by an initiation set, an internal policy, and a termination condition. For almost-surely finite duration , bounded rewards and discount , a semi-Markov value expression is . The discount exponent records elapsed primitive time or steps under the chosen convention. Treating every skill as one equal-cost action ignores duration, tool expenditure, and failure exposure. A skill library can therefore make a plan shorter on paper while leaving its actual operational horizon large.

Reusable procedures need applicability conditions. A code-editing skill can depend on repository layout, language version, permissions, or a particular test command. A browser skill can depend on an interface that later changes. The planner should validate these conditions before invocation and interpret termination based on observed state. A natural-language skill description can help the model select a procedure, but it does not establish that the installed implementation satisfies the description. Versioned executable resources and tests provide a stronger connection between symbolic planning and actual execution.

Abstraction can also conceal conflicts between subgoals. Two procedures may independently succeed while writing incompatible state, consuming the same budget, or invalidating each other’s assumptions. A dependency graph should include shared resources and state versions, not merely an ordered list of textual tasks. Parallel execution is safe only when the relevant effects commute or are coordinated through an appropriate transaction or synchronization mechanism. Assigning different agent roles does not make their writes independent. This is a planning issue before it becomes a distributed-runtime issue.

A useful hierarchy experiment compares primitive control, fixed expert-authored skills, learned skill retrieval, and adaptive skill revision under the same external interfaces. Measure initiation errors, termination errors, task success, and complete cost. Hold out tool or repository variants to test transfer beyond memorized workarounds. A shorter generated plan is not by itself an improvement; it may simply hide more work inside a skill call. The scientific question is whether the abstraction improves decision quality and resource use while preserving the required constraints.

External operations can partially succeed. A file edit may commit before a test process crashes. A remote request may complete before a timeout. A multi-step workflow may create one resource and fail while linking another. Recovery begins by identifying the actual state, not by assuming the last returned error describes every effect. The planner should use operation identifiers, status queries, and recorded postconditions where supported. Blindly repeating a non-idempotent operation can turn an uncertain outcome into a definite duplicate.

Compensation is not the same as reversal. Deleting a newly created record may undo some state while leaving an email, audit event, charge, or downstream observation irreversible. A recovery plan should state which effects can be restored and which require disclosure or further action. This distinction constrains autonomous authority: a system may safely retry a read but need stronger authorization for an operation whose compensation is incomplete. A model’s confidence that it can fix a mistake later is not evidence that the environment supports reversal.

The plan should reserve resources for verification and recovery. Spending the entire budget on candidate generation can leave no capacity to inspect the final outcome. A deadline-aware controller can allocate a minimum final-check budget and stop exploration earlier. This is a constrained scheduling problem coupled to inference-time control in Chapter . Tool latency distributions matter: an operation with a short mean but a heavy tail can consume the recovery window. Report timeout and censored outcomes rather than treating them as if the agent had simply chosen to stop.

Fault injection can test recovery without inventing real failures in production. In a controlled environment, interrupt an operation after a known partial effect, drop a response, revoke permission between planning and execution, or replace a stored checkpoint with a stale one. Verify whether the agent reconstructs state, avoids duplicate effects, and preserves unresolved uncertainty. Keep these tests isolated and reversible. They diagnose mechanisms and do not estimate deployment incident frequencies unless the injected distribution is itself justified by operational data.

The evaluation record should contain the initial environment, interpreted goal, available tools, permissions, plan representation, observation policy, execution budget, and acceptance criterion. Baselines should include direct reactive control, a fixed decomposition, replanning without persistent reflection, and the proposed planning method. When a world model or verifier is added, hold the downstream policy fixed in a mechanistic ablation and also report a separately tuned system comparison. This separates component attribution from the practical performance of the complete integration.

Measure more than final success. Record invalid actions, violated preconditions, unnecessary operations, recovery success, corruption of initially correct artifacts, and the number of opportunities for irreversible effects. Use task-level paired comparisons and repeated runs where stochasticity is material. Preserve failures and censored runs in denominators. A planner that completes fewer tasks but avoids prohibited actions may satisfy a different operating objective from one that maximizes unconstrained success; the comparison must state that objective before ranking them.

Initial admission and finite termination require their own implementation conditions. Neither the operator names nor a positive goal verdict establish properties beyond the checker’s scope. Planning and self-correction improve agent behavior when they connect hypotheses to observed state and retain the evidence needed to revise them. Their failure modes are equally concrete: a wrong goal, an aliased belief, an invalid local contract, a misleading critic, a stale skill, or an unrecognized partial effect. Treating these as distinct mechanisms permits stronger analysis than attributing all outcomes to an undefined capacity for deliberation. It also connects planning to the rest of the system: context supplies the current evidence, memory supplies prior cases, the policy proposes actions, and execution determines what actually becomes true.

Consider a plan that reads a record at version seven, computes an update, and writes it after another actor has committed version eight. The read establishes the precondition only at observation time. If the write ignores the version, a locally well-formed plan can overwrite new information. An execution-time compare-and-swap condition changes the operation semantics: the write succeeds only if the version remains seven, otherwise the planner receives a conflict and must re-read or reconcile. This example shows why a correct textual deduction from a stale premise does not establish a valid external transition.

The same pattern appears with authorization. A permission observed during planning may be revoked before execution. A hard boundary checks the current authorization epoch, while the planner treats denial as new state information. Retrying the identical operation without refreshing that state is not self-correction. A learned policy can decide how to adapt after denial, but should not be allowed to reinterpret denial as permission because it believes the task is important. The separation of model inference and authoritative execution is what makes this behavior testable.

For multi-step plans, attach a state version or relevant precondition set to each consequential operation. A version mismatch does not always require discarding the entire plan: independent earlier conclusions may remain valid. The planner can maintain a dependency graph and invalidate only artifacts whose premises changed, provided that dependency relation is complete for the claimed reuse. Incomplete dependencies create the same kind of silent stale-state error as invalid KV reuse. Conservative full replanning costs more but supplies a useful reference baseline for evaluating selective invalidation.

A controlled test introduces concurrent updates at predetermined points while keeping the model and task fixed. Compare blind execution, full replanning after every change, and dependency-aware replanning. Measure lost updates, unauthorized attempts, useful work retained, observation cost, and complete task latency. These are proposed experiments; no result is presumed. The event schedule should be hidden from the agent but retained by the evaluator, and each run should start from a reproducible environment snapshot. Randomized schedules can test robustness after deterministic cases establish basic correctness.

This temporal view also improves self-correction evaluation. A revision that was correct when generated can become invalid before acceptance, while an apparent regression can reflect a changed task state rather than worse reasoning. Preserve the state against which each candidate and feedback item was judged. Without that association, a system can learn contradictory lessons from the same artifact or report a false improvement by comparing outcomes under different environments. State-indexed evidence is therefore a prerequisite for interpreting planning progress across long sessions, concurrent agents, and tool upgrades.

The 2026 Compaction Cliff study compares compression choices under task-dependent constraints rather than treating retained length as a sufficient quality measure . Its conditional results motivate the central distinction developed here: an input can fit a window while losing a decision-critical relation. The mathematical target is preservation of relevant information, with access, reasoning, and computational cost measured separately.

A context window is an admissible input length, whereas long-context intelligence is a property of a model interacting with a distribution of tasks. The difference becomes operational when an agent must combine an early instruction, a later correction, an external observation, and an unfinished commitment. A successful retrieval of an isolated sentence does not establish that the same model can reconcile those four objects. Conversely, an agent with a modest window may solve a long task by maintaining sufficient state outside that window. Input capacity, effective evidence use, and duration of operation therefore require different measurements.

The transformation includes serialization, retrieval, truncation, and any instruction or tool-description overhead. A model with token budget requires , but this inequality says nothing about whether contains the evidence necessary for a correct action. Define a task-dependent evidence set and an action loss . The relevant risk is

Here is the admitted input budget. If the serving interface constrains input and generated tokens jointly, an output reserve must first be subtracted from that joint limit. The distribution in this expectation must identify histories, decisions, environments, and evaluation times. Changing any of them can change the apparent effective context length without changing the architecture.

It is useful to distinguish a capacity failure from an accessibility failure. A capacity failure occurs when a chosen representation cannot fit a sufficient record into the available input. An accessibility failure occurs when a sufficient record is present but the model does not use it correctly. A third category, representation failure, occurs when information was transformed into an ambiguous or incorrect record before the model saw it. These categories imply different interventions: extend the budget, improve the model’s use of evidence, or repair the state-construction procedure. Treating them as one phenomenon encourages expensive remedies that miss the responsible subsystem.

The transformer construction makes every permitted earlier token potentially available through attention, but potential connectivity is not reliable semantic access . Position encodings, training distributions, intermediate representations, decoding, and instructions all mediate that access. A systems description should therefore specify the input length, the position of decisive evidence, the number of distracting or contradictory records, and the logical operations required to derive the action. The phrase supports a long context becomes scientifically informative only after those conditions are fixed.

This condition is demanding because the environment is partially observed and the action set may change when new tools become available. A task-oriented summary is usually an approximation to this condition rather than a demonstrated sufficient statistic.

Consider a repository task whose earlier history contains a requirement to preserve an undocumented compatibility behavior. A summary that retains the current implementation plan but omits that requirement may support the next edit and still fail a later regression check. The target variable in Eq. must then include that later check. If evaluation asks only for the next action, the compression can appear lossless even though it removes information necessary for task completion. Horizon and target definition are part of any claim about retained information.

An approximate decision bound can be stated without assuming optimal language modeling. Suppose two histories represented by the same induce future-trajectory laws differing by at most in total variation under every evaluated policy. For the same return functional taking values in , their expected returns differ by at most . If instead , the bound is . These follow from the range of a bounded function and the definition of total variation. The observation motivates evaluating behaviorally distinct histories that collapse to the same summary. It does not provide a practical certificate unless the required uniform bound can be estimated or established from environment structure.

The engineering consequence is to make discarded distinctions explicit. Preserve obligations, authorization, unresolved alternatives, evidence provenance, and invalidated assumptions as typed state rather than relying on a generic narrative summary. Exact sufficiency may be unattainable, but the system can identify which future decisions its representation is intended to support and which distinctions it knowingly loses.

Information availability and a fixed model’s competence must be separated when interpreting a full-history baseline. For a finite action space and bounded loss, define the Bayes risk under information by

If , a policy with access to can imitate every -measurable decision rule, so . An observed improvement after deleting context therefore concerns the evaluated model, assembly procedure, and resource constraint; it does not show that removing information improves the unrestricted optimal decision. Compression can reduce distraction or make a finite computation feasible while still discarding information that another policy could use. This distinction is essential when attributing gains to a 2026 editor rather than to a weaker full-history implementation.

Length is only one coordinate of task difficulty. A useful workload specification includes evidence distance, evidence density, distractor similarity, the number of required joins, contradiction depth, and the delay between observation and consequence. Evidence density is the fraction of input that contributes to a correct answer. Low density stresses selection; high density with many dependencies stresses integration. Two inputs of equal token length can therefore create different computational demands.

Lost in the Middle provides evidence that information placement can affect model performance in its tested retrieval and question-answering settings . RULER and LongBench broaden long-context evaluation through controlled and heterogeneous tasks . Their central methodological value here is to make context use observable under specified tasks. They do not establish a universal conversion from advertised token capacity to a reliable operating horizon. Synthetic retrieval, document question answering, and multi-step interactive execution expose overlapping but different failure modes.

The pinned RULER implementation makes several controls inspectable. In scripts/data/synthetic/niah.py, generate_input_output varies needle keys, values, queries, distractors, and insertion positions; generate_samples uses the selected tokenizer and reserves generated tokens and model-template overhead while fitting inputs. The standalone scripts/pred/call_api.py prediction path appends the stored answer prefix before dispatch. In scripts/eval/evaluate.py, run_evaluation_per_task applies the task metric and separately counts empty predictions . Preserve the exact rendered input, tokenizer, seed, target position, and generation reserve when comparing lengths. The inspected prediction helper retries exceptions without a finite retry limit, and the evaluator skips absent task files after printing a warning. A reproducible adaptation should impose a declared deadline, reconcile expected and completed task identifiers, and retain failed requests in its accounting. These are implementation obligations; this static benchmark does not itself certify session continuity or correct external effects.

To separate these effects, construct a family of tasks with fixed decisive records and systematically permute their positions while keeping total length constant. Next, increase distractor similarity without changing the decisive records. Finally, change the number of relations needed to connect the records. The resulting response surface records success as a function of length , evidence distance , join count , and distractor parameter . A length-only curve is a projection of this surface and can conceal strong interaction effects.

Repeated facts require special care. Repeating a constraint near the decision can improve accessibility while changing the workload’s redundancy. If a long-context method benefits from explicit reminders, that result should be distinguished from recovery of a unique distant fact. Likewise, a task that includes both a stale fact and a corrected fact tests temporal interpretation as well as retrieval. An answerer can retrieve both perfectly and still resolve their authority incorrectly. Position permutations must preserve timestamps and source roles or the experimental manipulation changes the intended semantics.

Compositional difficulty also interacts with output format. Choosing a cited answer from a small candidate set can be easier than synthesizing an executable action with multiple arguments. An agent must often retrieve an entity, infer its current state, select a tool, satisfy a schema, and respect an authorization boundary. Evaluation that terminates after entity retrieval measures only the first component. For expert comparison, the action-generation stage should be retained, and failures should be attributed to evidence access, reasoning, argument construction, or execution.

An informative negative control inserts irrelevant but lexically attractive records whose instructions conflict with the user task. The model should recognize these as data rather than authority. This extends context evaluation toward the security analysis in Chapter . Success under benign distractors does not imply robustness when retrieved content attempts to redefine the task or rewrite the memory policy.

Length generalization depends on more than the numerical range of a position encoding. Training establishes distributions over token positions, document boundaries, dependency lengths, and tasks. Increasing an inference limit changes the region in which those learned mechanisms operate. Rotary or recurrent positional constructions address parts of this problem, but an architectural ability to represent a position does not by itself demonstrate competent reasoning at that position .

For an agent, training must additionally expose the model to histories with interrupted plans, corrected observations, failed tool calls, and records that have become irrelevant. A long concatenation of independent documents is not equivalent to a coherent interaction trajectory. The latter contains dependencies between what the policy observed, what it attempted, what the environment changed, and what remains unresolved. Training data that omit these distinctions can reward answer extraction while failing to teach durable task-state maintenance.

Let describe training examples by length, dependency complexity, and interaction type, and let describe deployment. Reporting only a maximum training length suppresses shifts in the other coordinates. A model may encounter deployment histories within the trained length range but outside the trained distribution of corrections or tool-output redundancy. The appropriate claim is then distribution-specific performance, not unrestricted length generalization.

A defensible extension experiment holds architecture and total training compute fixed where feasible, varies the long-sequence curriculum, and evaluates both short and long tasks. The short-task control detects capability tradeoffs, while the long-task suite distinguishes retrieval from integration and interactive continuity. If extra long-sequence training also increases the token budget or improves data quality, the comparison must identify those additional factors. A recovery phase after agentic post-training has a real compute cost and should not disappear from the accounting boundary.

Contamination controls operate at the level of both documents and tasks. Removing exact benchmark documents does not rule out exposure to paraphrased questions, released solutions, or public environment traces. For interactive tasks, the environment schema and common solution trajectory can leak even when the surface instruction is novel. Separate held-out entities, templates, environment states, and required action compositions. Record which dimensions were held out and avoid claiming general transfer from a single split.

Implementation should preserve document and event boundaries through packing. If truncation removes the role or timestamp of a message, the remaining content can acquire a different interpretation. Tokenization and serialization are therefore part of the learning distribution. Chapter analyzes the stronger problem arising when training reconstructs a different context from the one used during rollout. Long sequences can be correctly packed in memory and still be conditionally wrong for learning.

Grouped-query attention changes ; changing the total query-head count without specifying key-value sharing is insufficient for memory accounting . Cache paging changes allocation behavior rather than the semantic amount of remembered evidence .

For dense attention, an incremental decode step reads a growing cache and performs attention against the visible prefix. A simplified traffic model is , with representing actual cache access, reuse, and implementation overhead. The bandwidth lower bound assumes an effective bandwidth and cannot predict observed latency without accounting for compute, synchronization, batching, and competing traffic.
