The interaction horizon introduces cumulative costs. If each tool turn contributes input tokens and the system repeatedly reconstructs the full history, the total input volume over turns scales as

This is an analytic count under equal-sized turns and no reusable prefix accounting. Prefix caching can reduce repeated computation, while billing rules may count tokens differently. The expression therefore diagnoses a growth pattern rather than an invoice. A bounded working context of size changes the repeated-input term toward but introduces storage, retrieval, editing, and error-recovery costs.

Long-context serving also creates capacity competition. A scheduler holding a large inactive session can reduce concurrency for short requests. Evicting that session’s cache saves device memory but may incur a costly prefill when it resumes. The correct objective depends on the workload mixture and service-level constraints: minimize mean cost, maximize throughput, or control tail latency. A policy optimized for average token throughput can be undesirable when a few latency-sensitive tool decisions gate an entire workflow.

Latency should be decomposed into queueing, context construction, prefill, generation, tool execution, and validation. These components are not independent. Large contexts can increase queueing through resource contention; additional retrieval can reduce prefill but add a network round trip; compression can reduce the next call yet increase retries after information loss. Report distributions over complete tasks and retain timeouts. Measuring only successful completions introduces survivorship bias into both latency and cost estimates.

The practical design question is consequently when additional retained context produces enough decision value to justify its full systems cost. That tradeoff depends on the probability that distant evidence becomes decisive, the cost of reacquiring it, and the consequences of forgetting it. Uniform retention and uniform eviction are both coarse approximations to this decision problem.

A proposed long-context evaluation should begin with matched information access. Full-history, retrieval, and summary systems should receive the same underlying evidence, tools, model version, and authorization. The comparison then varies only how evidence reaches the model. A second experiment can permit learned context control, but its training and search costs should be reported separately. Otherwise, architectural selection effects become entangled with an additional optimization budget.

Recent work makes these distinctions concrete. The Compaction Cliff classifies knowledge by type and applies separate operators for compaction, decomposition, and retrieval, retaining recognized constraints under type-specific rules . Its guarantees depend on constraint classification, applicable scope, feasible budgets, and verification; they are not unconditional preservation of every real safety requirement. Its behavioral retail comparison is not token-matched, and some reference labels are model-generated. Those qualifications prevent an observed advantage from being assigned solely to typing. The preprint was available before the cutoff even though its listed conference dates fall later.

The methodological conflict is useful. Uniform summarization assumes that one semantic compression objective is adequate across records, whereas typed retention treats some distinctions as constraints that should survive with stronger fidelity. The latter can preserve a rare prohibition even when a relevance score prefers repeated descriptive content. It can also fail if the classifier mistakes a declarative fact for ordinary background or assigns an inappropriate scope. A test of constraint preservation should therefore vary grammatical form and authority independently of content frequency.

Two 2026 surveys supply organizing lenses rather than independent experimental confirmation. The rate–distortion view groups several forms of context-derived compression under budget and downstream-utility tradeoffs . The October selective-memory survey distinguishes information participating in computation from stored information that can later be activated . These taxonomies help align accounting boundaries, but they do not prove that cache eviction, semantic forgetting, and text summarization have identical guarantees. Their state transitions and recovery mechanisms remain different.

An original deduction follows from combining these distinctions with the sufficiency criterion: fidelity should be allocated according to the loss of the distinction being removed, while activation cost should be charged when stored evidence becomes computation. This does not yield a universal scalar salience score. It yields a falsifiable comparison: preserve the same constraint set, vary non-constraint evidence and activation policy, and measure both justified action and full resource use. A method that wins only by silently relaxing the constraint set has changed the task.

Use at least three baselines: a full-history baseline within the admissible budget, a recency window, and a simple retrieval or structured-state baseline. The full-history baseline tests whether the proposed transformation removes harmful distraction or merely compensates for capacity. The recency baseline measures whether most tasks are effectively short. The simple structured baseline tests whether elaborate learned control is necessary. An oracle evidence condition is useful as a diagnostic ceiling, provided it is clearly labeled and never compared as an executable production method.

For each task, instrument the first decision at which a required historical distinction matters. Record whether the distinction exists in storage, appears in the model input, is interpreted correctly, and leads to the correct tool action. This decomposition prevents a retrieval miss from being mistaken for weak reasoning and prevents a correct answer with an invalid side effect from being counted as success. The same decomposition supports targeted ablations: preserve the record but perturb its timestamp, preserve its content but remove its source role, or preserve both while moving its position.

Uncertainty should reflect the unit of generalization. Repeated decoding seeds on the same task measure stochastic policy variation, not variation across task families. Use task-level resampling for task uncertainty, environment-level separation where tasks share state, and independent training seeds when comparing learned context policies. Task order matters whenever memory or a learned skill bank persists. A single favorable sequence can behave as an implicit curriculum and should not be treated as evidence of stable continual improvement.

Contamination testing should include withheld corrections and contradictory updates rather than only unseen questions. A system that remembers the original fact but fails to adopt an authoritative revision has failed a different requirement from one that never stored the fact. Include negative controls where an old record should be ignored and where no historical record is relevant. Without these controls, systems that overapply memory may appear strong on a benchmark constructed entirely from positive recall opportunities.

The proposed experiment is discriminating only if the result can falsify a mechanism. If a method claims to preserve decision-critical evidence, a loss of that evidence under matched storage and retrieval is directly informative. A small change in an aggregate score without an inspectable failure record may be insufficient to identify whether retention, attention, or action selection changed.

Consider an explicitly hypothetical decoder with 32 layers, 8 key-value heads, head dimension 128, and two-byte cached scalars. Equation gives 131072 bytes per cached token. A sequence of 32768 tokens therefore requires 4 GiB of raw keys and values, while 131072 tokens require 16 GiB. These are arithmetic consequences of the stated configuration, not measurements of a named model or service. They exclude every other allocation and do not establish how many sessions fit on a particular accelerator. Replication, quantization, cache paging, and attention implementation can change the actual residency.

Suppose a deployment must hold ten such long sequences concurrently. The raw cache term alone becomes 160 GiB before weights or workspace. Moving half the sessions to host memory reduces device residency, but a resumed session may need cache transfer or recomputation. A throughput analysis that treats those sessions as permanently active can differ sharply from a workload in which users pause for minutes between tool decisions. Concurrency is therefore a property of arrival and activity patterns, not merely a maximum batch-size argument.

Now consider two histories and that are identical except for a valid user correction: one permits publishing an artifact and the other permits only preparing a draft. A summary function that omits the correction maps both histories to the same state . Suppose the task requires a binary publish-or-hold action, the two histories are equally likely, and the correct actions differ. Any deterministic policy conditioned only on must be wrong for one history, giving error at least one half. Randomization cannot lower the average error because the optimal mixture still lacks the distinguishing bit. Unlimited additional reasoning on cannot recover an observation the representation discarded.

If the correction remains available in raw storage, retrieval can repair the failure, but only if the retrieval policy requests the right evidence before the consequential action. The memory system has then preserved capacity while the working-state policy has failed accessibility. If the correction was deleted from all retained evidence, retrieval cannot repair it. If the correction is present but labeled as an untrusted web instruction, its authority is misrepresented. These three cases can yield the same final wrong action, yet their engineering remedies are different.

This example also exposes a limitation of average semantic fidelity. The omitted correction can occupy a tiny fraction of a very long history while determining the entire action loss. A representation that preserves almost every token may be worse for the task than one that retains only a small structured set of obligations and evidence pointers. Token retention is not a monotone proxy for decision sufficiency. Conversely, a compact obligation list can fail when a later task needs an unforeseen detail, which is why retaining reversible access to raw history remains useful.

The proposed diagnostic is to create matched history pairs differing in one consequential fact and test whether a context policy preserves that distinction through length extension, compaction, interruption, and resumption. Positive results would support a specified invariance over the tested transformations. They would not prove that every unknown future distinction is preserved. This makes a carefully delimited behavioral claim possible without pretending that a generic summary is a sufficient statistic for all future tasks.

Long-context systems expose an important asymmetry: storing more evidence is straightforward to specify, whereas identifying what will matter later requires assumptions about future tasks. A larger window relaxes a resource constraint, but it does not remove the need for organization, authority, or temporal interpretation. At sufficiently long horizons, unfiltered history becomes a record of abandoned plans, obsolete facts, and adversarial content as well as useful evidence. More history can increase both opportunity and ambiguity.

The original synthesis of this chapter is that effective context should be evaluated as a controlled state representation. Its quality depends jointly on information preserved, the policy’s ability to use that information, and the operational cost of making it available. Equation supplies a precise idealization for predictive loss, while the control-state condition extends the concern to future action consequences. Neither equation turns present agents into certified sufficient-state estimators; both clarify which claims an experiment would need to support.

Several practical rules follow from that formulation. Preserve authoritative constraints independently of conversational salience. Retain references to raw evidence whenever summaries may be revised. Expose version and timestamp metadata at the decision point instead of expecting the model to infer them from prose. Measure complete-task cost rather than one-call context size. Treat cache state as an implementation of inference, not as a validated semantic memory. These are design deductions under explicit state and cost assumptions rather than reported superiority of a particular platform.

The limits of current evidence are substantial. Controlled context benchmarks are useful, but their target distributions need not match a changing enterprise workflow or a long scientific investigation. Public papers can establish gains under specific environments and budgets without establishing reliable indefinite operation. A context-management method may transfer across several tasks yet still depend on the same backbone, retriever, or evaluator. Independent reproduction and operational deployment answer additional questions.

For implementation, a useful boundary is to keep immutable interaction evidence, mutable task state, and the assembled model input distinct. This allows context construction to be inspected as a transformation rather than an invisible consequence of token overflow. It also permits counterfactual replay: reconstruct a prior decision with the original context, an edited context, or an oracle evidence set, while holding the environment snapshot fixed. Such replay is expensive, but it can reveal failure mechanisms that aggregate success rates conceal.

Chapter develops the editing policy that chooses the model’s working view. Chapter treats the event and session substrate that makes those choices recoverable. The resulting picture is an agent whose finite context is one deliberately managed component of a larger stateful system. Its generality remains an empirical question about task transfer, adaptation, and reliable execution under bounded resources.

The October 2026 transparent-compaction implementation preserves conversational prose while masking recoverable blocks and exposing delegated lookup; Context Language Models instead permit programmatic edits to the live context . These mechanisms alter different information and execution boundaries. Comparing them requires a transformation contract, downstream continuation loss, restoration cost, and an exact record of which view conditioned each action.

Context engineering is the construction of the actual conditional input on which a policy selects its next action. It includes the selection of instructions, evidence, tool descriptions, intermediate results, and unresolved commitments. Compaction is one intervention within that broader process. An agent can compact history while preserving raw storage, evict a cache without editing text, or edit its visible history without deleting a persistent record. These operations affect different state variables and should have different names in an implementation.

Let denote the append-only interaction evidence, the persistent memory, and the model’s working context. A context controller chooses an editing action before the task policy chooses an environment action :

Here is the remaining resource budget. The decomposition can be implemented by separate models, one model with distinct action types, or deterministic harness logic. It is a functional distinction, not a claim that a separate context model is always beneficial. Access to is not free: the total account must charge the controller’s scans, retrieval, model calls, and storage operations as well as the task policy’s input.

The context controller faces an unusual delayed-control problem. Removing a record can make the next request cheaper but create a failure many steps later. Its reward is mediated by another policy and by the environment. A controller trained only to reduce input size may learn aggressive deletion that looks efficient until a deferred constraint becomes decisive. Conversely, penalizing every retrieval call can encourage a policy to retain large amounts of irrelevant content. The objective must include task outcome and complete lifecycle cost.

A useful constrained formulation uses a total resource cost , a terminal success indicator , and an indicator that at least one unauthorized effect occurred. For fixed task and environment distributions, define

The thresholds are workload-specific requirements. They are not established constants, and success estimation must retain failures and timeouts. A Lagrangian objective can aid optimization, but it does not prove that the constraints hold after training. Authorization should generally be enforced outside a stochastic controller rather than represented only as a reward penalty.

The central design question is which distinctions the working view must preserve. A context assembled for code editing needs current files, interface constraints, test outcomes, and rejected hypotheses. A literature agent needs claims, supporting passages, conflicting evidence, and unresolved source identities. Applying the same generic summary template to both workloads can remove the information that makes their next actions valid. State fields should follow decision requirements, with prose used where a schema would erase necessary nuance.

Selection retains some records verbatim; abstraction constructs a new record that represents several old ones. These operations have different error modes. Selection can omit a decisive source while faithfully preserving everything selected. Abstraction can include the right sources but misstate their contents, merge incompatible claims, or remove a qualification. A practical pipeline should make the two stages separately inspectable instead of treating a single generated summary as an opaque transformation.
Suppose records have token costs , and is the task-dependent utility of retaining the records indexed by . A simple selection model is a budgeted set problem:

If is monotone submodular, marginal-gain heuristics have useful theoretical properties under suitable assumptions. Agent evidence does not generally satisfy those assumptions. Two individually useless records can jointly identify a contradiction, while one new correction can invalidate many older records. Utility may be complementary or nonmonotone. Using a greedy score can still be an engineering heuristic, but its approximation guarantees do not transfer without verifying the required structure.

Abstraction introduces a different optimization target. Let be a summary of records and let be a specified conditional distribution over future requests and targets given that source record. Define distortion through paired decision losses rather than textual similarity:

This is a proposed operational distortion measure. Both conditions receive the same request–target draw; a stochastic policy’s internal sampling is also included in the expectation. The controller observes and the current request, not the evaluation target . Distortion can be negative when abstraction removes distraction, and it depends on the evaluated policy. It is not a mathematical distance. Holding fixed prevents a change in the future-question distribution from being misreported as better preservation.

Preserving exact text is especially valuable for identifiers, numeric requirements, authorization, and claims requiring attribution. A summary may safely paraphrase a search strategy while retaining an exact test failure or contract clause as a quoted evidence object. The representation can combine concise state with evidence pointers rather than forcing every item into the same compression format. Token allocation should reflect the cost of a mistaken abstraction, not only the record’s length.

An implementation can maintain an immutable source layer, a typed decision-state layer, and a generated narrative layer. Each narrative assertion should link to one or more source objects or be marked as an inference. Contradictions remain separate objects until resolved by an explicit rule. This architecture makes it possible to regenerate a summary after a correction without pretending that the first summary was an authoritative replacement for the evidence.

ACM makes context management an explicit part of agent behavior through a summarization action and retrieval of earlier raw interaction history . Its distinction between a bounded active view and preserved external history is technically important. Offloaded text can remain intact while the working context becomes lossy. The agent still has to recognize when it needs an omitted detail, issue a suitable retrieval request, and interpret the returned record correctly. Storage reversibility and behavioral reversibility are different properties.

The paper’s mechanism can be understood as a state transition with a retained suffix, a compacted prefix, and access to raw evidence. The resulting policy is more flexible than mandatory truncation at a fixed threshold because it can choose when to summarize. That flexibility creates a larger action space and additional credit-assignment demands. The context-management decision can be correct locally but harmful to a later step, so evaluating only the immediate post-summary answer is insufficient.

Context Language Models go further by making the live context directly editable and studying serving support for such edits . Their reported FLOP accounting should not be equated with measured latency or service expenditure. The generalizable distinction is between a fixed set of harness editing operations and a model-controlled editing program. The latter expands expressivity but also expands the space of invalid or semantically damaging edits.

A conservative editing interface can represent operations as typed transformations: retain, summarize, externalize, restore, annotate, and invalidate. Each operation has preconditions and a provenance record. Invalidate should preserve the reason a fact became obsolete; it should not silently erase the record needed to understand a past decision. Restore should recover source roles and timestamps together with text. A raw paragraph returned without its original authority can change its meaning.

The proposed construction below is an implementation contract, not a reproduction of ACM’s code. Here summarizes with source identifiers and serializes the pinned records, summary, and recent events. No optimality of or semantic sufficiency of is assumed. An infeasible result requires replanning or a larger admissible budget, rather than deletion of a pinned obligation. The final length test is an explicit admissibility requirement: a raw-evidence selection bound alone does not constrain summary expansion or the cost of adding recent events. It is a conservative completion of the construction, not an assertion that the cited implementation already enforces this gate.

Let be the edit journal, the manifest linking the complete candidate view to its pinned records, selected sources, recent events, roles, timestamps, and transformation, and append a durable record. Persistence is conditional on admission:

The preservation test is only as strong as its validator. A deterministic check can confirm that an identifier or typed obligation survives, but it cannot generally establish semantic sufficiency of a prose summary. Structural preservation and budget admission remain useful invariants, not a complete proof that future decisions will remain correct. Returning as an installed view additionally requires successful manifest persistence; a failed journal write is an unresolved transition, not a completed edit.

The budget is residual capacity after fixed instructions, selected schemas, fixed serialization overhead, and any reserved output allowance. If pinned requirements exceed that residual, the feasible selection set is empty. Silently dropping a prohibition to make the request fit changes the task rather than solving the allocation problem. Replanning can reduce execution granularity, move validated control fields outside model-visible prose, or acquire a larger admissible input; it must preserve the dispatch monitor’s current authority. A tool or protocol revision can change schema overhead and thus invalidate an otherwise unchanged compaction schedule.

A fixed threshold triggers compaction when the current input exceeds a fraction of the window. This is easy to implement and creates predictable resource bounds, but it ignores semantic phase boundaries. Compressing immediately before a decisive action can discard evidence that would have been useful for verification. Compressing after a stable subtask finishes may be less risky because its outcome can be represented as a validated artifact. A trigger should consider both token pressure and the task’s transition structure.

For a fixed continuation policy and the same pre-edit history , let and denote potential continuation costs under editing and retaining the current view, respectively. Both costs include the transformation itself and subsequent repair work. A controller may compare

Choosing an edit when minimizes this local two-action cost only if the estimates are correct, both actions satisfy the outcome and authority constraints, and the horizon captures relevant consequences. Observational averages over previously edited and unedited tasks do not identify this contrast when selection differs. In practice, these estimates are uncertain. A trigger can include a margin that reflects uncertainty, or it can defer compaction until a task checkpoint establishes a stable state. Neither device eliminates the need to test delayed failures.

Reward shaping can help assign local feedback to context actions, but it can also change the optimized behavior. Penalizing context length rewards short inputs even if later repair is expensive. Rewarding successful retrieval can encourage unnecessary retrieval. A better diagnostic records downstream task outcome, semantic information loss, tool interactions, and cumulative cost separately. A scalar training objective may combine them, while the evaluation retains the separate quantities so tradeoffs remain visible.

Counterfactual continuation is particularly informative. Save the environment state before an edit and evaluate continuations with the original view, the edited view, and an edited view augmented with the omitted decisive record. If the third condition repairs a failure, the evidence supports a context-loss mechanism. If it does not, the failure may involve reasoning, environment stochasticity, or a changed action policy. Environment restoration must itself be validated; otherwise the counterfactual comparison changes more than the context.

Training introduces an additional requirement: each generated token must be associated with the context actually visible when it was produced. MemoryWalker identifies conditioning errors when edited rollouts are flattened into a final compressed trace or a full physical history . Chapter develops the corresponding likelihood contracts. The point for trigger design is that an edit is not only an inference-time event. It changes the data structure required to train correctly on the resulting trajectory.

Practical controllers should therefore emit an edit manifest containing the decision time, removed spans, replacement text, source identifiers, and view version. This manifest supports both failure analysis and correct rollout reconstruction. Recording only the final summary loses the temporal information needed to determine whether a token was trained under a future edit or under content that had already disappeared.

Text editing changes the input sequence, while cache reuse assumes particular computational dependencies remain valid. In a standard causal transformer, a cached hidden state for a later token can depend on earlier tokens through attention and residual computation. Deleting an earlier span does not generally leave later states unchanged, even if the surviving text is byte-identical. Reusing cached values therefore requires a justified dependency rule, not merely matching the visible suffix.

For a simple prefix-cache implementation, an edit at position invalidates the reusable prefix from that position onward. If is the new length, the re-prefill work depends on as well as newly generated tokens. A context policy that repeatedly edits early content can reduce token count while destroying reuse. This explains why a representation optimized only for shortness can be expensive under an actual serving architecture. The relevant objective includes both retained size and edit location.

PagedAttention addresses logical and physical allocation and sharing of cached blocks . It does not, by itself, establish that arbitrary semantic edits preserve the numerical validity of a cached block. A page allocator may retain bytes correctly while the model computation those bytes represent is no longer appropriate for the edited sequence. Allocation validity and inference validity must be checked separately.

CLM Suffix Cache Reuse is an explicit approximation: surviving suffix states retain dependencies on the pre-edit prefix . Its full-attention path re-rotates relocated keys for their new positions, while the studied hybrid path resumes pre-edit recurrent state instead of recomputing inserted content in linear-attention layers. Position adjustment does not remove stale content dependencies. Report this quality–compute tradeoff separately from exact prefix reuse and from measured end-to-end latency.

An edit-aware serving contract can attach a dependency fingerprint to every reusable region. The fingerprint identifies model version, tokenizer, position convention, attention mask, and relevant predecessor state. A reuse decision is valid only if the implementation’s equivalence conditions hold. Exact fingerprints may be expensive; conservative invalidation sacrifices reuse to preserve correctness. Approximate reuse is possible, but its approximation should be evaluated as a quality tradeoff rather than described as lossless without proof.

Measure context-control latency end to end. Include the editing model call, storage writes, cache invalidation, re-prefill, extra retrieval, and any retries after a damaged summary. Report warm and cold behavior separately. A policy that looks strong when every prompt receives a fresh prefill can perform differently in a service with extensive prefix reuse. The comparison must reflect the intended deployment instead of selecting the serving regime most favorable to one method.

Consider a task with three obligations: modify a parser, preserve a legacy behavior, and produce a reviewable patch without publishing it. The raw history includes a failed test, a revised hypothesis, and a user correction that narrows the authorized output. A token-oriented summarizer may retain the patch plan and the latest test output while dropping the legacy requirement and the authorization correction as old discussion. The resulting input is shorter but misrepresents the permitted output scope and success requirements in the model-visible view.

Represent the validated state as : goals , obligations , authority , evidence references , and unresolved hypotheses . A proposed compaction operator should preserve and exactly, preserve enough of to justify current conclusions, and mark unresolved hypotheses as unresolved. This is an application-specific contract. It does not claim that these five fields are sufficient for every task; it states which distinctions this parser workflow requires.

Suppose the original and compacted policies induce action distributions and at the next decision. For a bounded immediate loss , their expected losses differ by at most . If a validator can establish a bound on distribution change, that bound controls immediate risk under the stated loss. It does not automatically control the complete task, because a small action change can place the environment in a different region. Long-horizon guarantees require bounds on transition sensitivity or repeated coupling assumptions, which are rarely available for arbitrary tools.

For deterministic safety constraints, comparing distributions is unnecessary. Suppose every tool call passes the same monitor, whose allowed-action set is determined exclusively by the authoritative grant state and the current enforcement configuration. Holding those inputs fixed preserves the same syntactic boundary even when compaction changes the policy. Copying an old into a summary does not satisfy this condition after a grant is revoked; the monitor must consult current authority at dispatch, independently of the edited prose. Semantic correctness remains open: the agent can take an allowed but wrong action. This separation is valuable because it prevents summary quality from being responsible for all enforcement. Authority should survive in a typed control layer even when task evidence is compressed.

The corresponding experiment compares four views: full history, generic summary, typed-state summary, and typed state plus targeted raw retrieval. Keep the model, tools, and environment snapshot fixed. Randomize whether the legacy constraint appears early or late and whether the latest correction expands or narrows authority. Score patch correctness, publication behavior, retrieval use, and cost separately. This is a proposed experiment. No numerical outcomes are implied by the formulation.

A successful typed-state condition would support the mechanism that explicit obligations survive compression in this workload. It would not establish that a manually designed schema generalizes to unknown scientific or legal tasks. A failure would still be useful if it identifies a missing state field or an incorrect validation rule. The scientific objective is to expose which information transformations preserve behavior, rather than to award a generic summary the label of memory.

ContextPilot separates the editing toolset from the learning rule. Its tools include structured memory, notes, planning, and reversible context offload. Training uses snapshots at editing boundaries, masks previously optimized tokens, and allocates continuation sampling around consequential editing actions . Its action-level feedback addresses the fact that final task correctness is an imperfect label for every earlier edit. This does not make the feedback causal ground truth: continuation outcomes still depend on the downstream policy and environment. A comparison must separate the expanded toolset, supervised initialization, branch allocation, and advantage estimator rather than attributing their joint effect to one component.

CompactionRL jointly trains execution and summary generation with token-level normalization. Its cross-segment credit correction is approximate, not exact full-trajectory GAE . For segment with optimized tokens, discount and trace parameter , the method scales its locally computed advantages by the number of later optimized tokens:

This restores the terminal-reward discount distance when the shared reward is placed at each independently optimized segment end. It does not recursively propagate all later TD residuals into earlier segments. The authors trade that reconstruction for parallel segment processing; a reproduction must distinguish reward-distance correction from full-trajectory GAE. Their coding evaluation uses a specified 200-task SWE-bench Verified subset, rather than the full benchmark. Successful joint optimization does not establish preservation of arbitrary future constraints.

TRACE v2 evaluates candidate summaries through paired closed-loop continuations from the same AppWorld state while keeping the agent and proposer weights frozen . Its local verifier counts the union of blocked actions and canonicalized repeated tool calls over a fixed horizon; this does not detect every silent state corruption. Preferences between summaries reuse the same PRE continuations. The proposer receives the downstream system prompt, compressor input, and better–worse summary pairs, but not rollout traces or the verifier decomposition. Five candidate compression templates are then selected on development-set success in both repeated runs, not success in either run; the selected template is frozen for test evaluation. This separates boundary-local supervision, prompt selection, and held-out testing. The evidence remains concentrated in AppWorld, and restoration fidelity and verifier scope limit the causal interpretation.

PAIR likewise uses counterfactual continuations to identify damaging individual compressions and adapts sections of a structured prompt . It distinguishes repeated-run reliability from finding one successful attempt. Its offline continuation search and restored-state access are part of the adaptation cost. These requirements can be reasonable in an experimental environment while unavailable for an external business tool with irreversible side effects. TRACE and PAIR share research lineage, so their agreement is evidence of a developing mechanism rather than two independent replications.

These mechanisms expose a concrete disagreement with purely semantic compression objectives. A summary can retain entities and facts yet obscure whether an action already happened, whether a plan is obsolete, or whether the task is complete. In that case the failure is execution-state mislocalization, not necessarily absence of a fact. Evaluating summary similarity would miss the directional role of action-observation history. The appropriate response is to preserve validated progress and effect receipts, then test whether the agent stops, resumes, and avoids repeating completed work. This is a synthesis of the mechanisms above, not a new measured result.

ACM provides author-reported evidence that explicit context actions can improve its evaluated tasks while reducing peak active context . The same study also illustrates why resource metrics must remain separate: in its reported BrowseComp-Plus comparison, tool calls increase from 19.5 to 46.2 per episode. This observation does not negate a context benefit; it limits the inference that smaller context necessarily means lower total latency or expense. These results have not been independently reproduced for this monograph.

Comparing learned compaction with deterministic summarization requires matching more than model identity. A learned controller may have seen environment-specific trajectories, received a larger training budget, or benefited from a retriever tuned to the evaluation interface. An ablation that removes the controller but also removes access to raw history changes two mechanisms simultaneously. Preserve the same storage and retrieval interfaces while varying the decision policy if the claim concerns control rather than memory availability.

Author-reported improvements across several benchmarks can support broader relevance, but shared infrastructure creates dependence between results. The same backbone, tool wrapper, answer extraction, and evaluator may appear across tasks. A cross-domain average does not turn those results into independent replications. Report task-specific outcomes and explain which components are shared. If one task improves and another regresses, the average should not hide the mechanism-specific disagreement.

The key comparison axes are behavior preservation, resource accounting, reversibility, training consistency, and implementation transparency. Full-history methods preserve observations but can suffer distraction and expense. Summaries reduce active input but can lose qualifications. Retrieval retains scalable access but can miss implicit relevance. Editable contexts increase flexibility but complicate cache and rollout semantics. These are structural tradeoffs, not a ranking without workload assumptions.

Evidence should also identify what remains unavailable. If a paper describes prompts but releases no execution adapter, code-level reproduction is incomplete. If code exists but requires a private checkpoint or undisclosed environment, the visible repository does not close that gap. A reproducibility claim should identify model weights, data, tool fixtures, edit policy, and evaluation version. Successful compilation of a harness is not successful reproduction of its scientific results.

The practical implication is to choose the simplest context-control mechanism that satisfies measured task and authority constraints. A sophisticated learned editor can be appropriate when decision value changes rapidly and enough training feedback exists. A deterministic structured state can be preferable when obligations are explicit and failures are costly. The evidence needed to choose between them is a matched workload study, not the elegance of the editing interface.

An October 2026 alternative is transparent-compact for the Pi coding agent. The inspected paper evaluates version 0.8.0, retaining user messages and assistant prose verbatim while masking tool outputs and reasoning, explicitly marking removed material, and providing delegated recovery . Its recovery action is context_lookup, with bounded fallback access. The guarantees are budget-limited: when retained prose reaches the configured cap, truncation begins. It therefore does not establish indefinite verbatim memory. Its next-turn probes concern commitments and planted facts with file and shell tools removed to isolate conversational memory. They do not establish complete software-engineering task success.

This method exposes a different comparison axis from learned abstraction. It preserves what was said while declining to treat that prose as verified truth. A retained assistant claim can still be wrong, and a removed tool result can require recovery before the claim is reused. The working view gains transparency about missing evidence at the cost of carrying more conversational text. Whether that tradeoff improves a task depends on the importance of exact commitments, the recoverability of observations, and the model’s tendency to act confidently on an ambiguous summary.

The pinned CLM implementation supplies a concrete interface boundary. In clm/clm_harness/context_env/env.py, ContextEnv._apply_edit round-trips candidate messages through parse_back, counts tokens, and invokes edit_gate.may_grow before replacement . The gate constrains growth; a shrinking edit that remains over budget can still be accepted with a warning, so this helper alone is not an absolute budget-admission guard. In clm/clm_harness/context_utils/context_string.py, parse_back restores the protected prefix but maps every editable non-assistant role to user text and does not reconstruct structured tool calls. Legal serialization therefore does not preserve all original role and effect provenance. Evaluate those changes separately from semantic commitment preservation and from the stricter proposed admission contract in Eq. .

Context transformations should be recoverable operations. Persist the source view and its edit manifest before replacing the active context. Commit the replacement only after structural validation, and retain a rollback reference until the affected task stage has been verified. This does not require keeping every cache allocation forever; it requires retaining enough evidence and metadata to reconstruct the decision input. Storage retention and privacy constraints still apply.

Use separate error classes for failed summarization, invalid serialization, missing raw evidence, retrieval failure, and an edited view that violates a pinned obligation. A generic context error obscures whether the model, controller, or storage layer is responsible. Recovery can then be targeted: restore the prior view, fetch an omitted record, regenerate an abstraction, or stop before a consequential tool effect. Blindly retrying the same damaged summary can amplify the failure.

Concurrent editing requires ownership. If a worker updates a plan while a controller compacts an older version, a last-write-wins replacement can erase legitimate progress. An optimistic commit should compare the base view version with the current version and reject or merge a stale edit. Semantic merges deserve special treatment: two summaries can each be locally valid while their union contains contradictory commitments. A storage-level conflict resolution rule cannot determine which commitment the user currently authorizes.

Human-readable state remains useful for audit, but readability should not replace machine-checkable boundaries. Identifiers, timestamps, tool-effect receipts, authority, and completion predicates can be represented in typed fields. Generated prose can explain those fields without becoming their sole source of truth. The boundary between recorded fact and model inference should survive every compaction. This reduces the chance that repeated summaries gradually promote a tentative hypothesis into an asserted observation.

The implementation path is incremental. First instrument the existing context assembly. Then introduce explicit source references and pinned obligations. Next add reversible offload with deterministic triggers. Only after those controls are measurable should a learned editing policy be compared under matched budgets. This sequence is a systems deduction about observability and attribution, not a claim that one particular product follows it or that it guarantees success.

The strongest outcome of context engineering is not a permanently small prompt. It is a working view whose contents, omissions, cost, and authority are deliberate and inspectable. Such a view supports the policy’s current decisions while preserving a path back to evidence when assumptions change. Durable sessions in Chapter provide the substrate for that path; persistent memory in Chapter determines which evidence and abstractions remain useful across tasks.

The 2026 ACM implementation exposes a consequential boundary between its live conversation, retained raw history, and checkpoint interface . Continuity therefore depends on what a snapshot actually restores, rather than on the existence of a session identifier. That boundary connects model context directly to event ordering, external-effect reconciliation, concurrency, and retention semantics.

A session is a bounded continuity relationship among an actor, an objective, a sequence of observations, and the authority under which actions occur. It is not identical to one model request, one browser tab, or one transcript. A task can span several model calls and tool processes; one user session can contain several tasks; a durable agent can serve many sessions while maintaining selected cross-session memory. Conflating these identities makes it difficult to determine what should survive interruption and what information may legitimately transfer to a new interaction.

Use separate identifiers for tenant, user or principal, session, task, run, model call, and external effect. A run is a particular attempt to advance a task under a chosen configuration. Retrying a run does not create a new user objective, and creating a new session does not automatically revoke or inherit every earlier authorization. These relationships should be explicit data rather than inferred from a conversational summary. Otherwise, a model may treat an old permission as current merely because both appear in the same retrieved context.
A useful state decomposition is

where contains identities and scope, the goal and completion predicate, authorization, progress and pending work, evidence and effect receipts, and version references. The decomposition is a proposed systems specification. It does not claim that a tuple of these fields is a universally sufficient control state. Its purpose is to prevent model-visible history from being the only place in which operational commitments exist.

Session termination also needs a definition. A session can be paused, abandoned, completed, or closed for retention purposes. Those states have different consequences. Pausing should preserve pending work without implying that an external operation has been canceled. Completing a task should identify which success predicates were checked. Closing a session may remove active context while retaining legally or operationally required effect records. Memory consolidation can occur after closure, but only under the applicable retention and sharing policy.

Managed agent documentation and persistence frameworks expose concrete session and checkpoint mechanisms . These interfaces support implementation, but they do not establish the semantic correctness of a resumed task. A checkpoint can faithfully restore an obsolete plan. A session service can preserve every message while allowing a stale authorization to influence a new run. The application must define which state is authoritative and which transformations are permitted at each boundary.

An event record states that a particular observation or transition was recorded under specified conditions. It should distinguish a requested action from a completed effect, and a model’s prediction from an environment observation. A proposed minimal envelope includes an event identifier, causal parents, producer, observed time, effective time where known, payload type, schema version, and integrity metadata. Sensitive payloads can be stored separately behind access controls while the envelope retains a reference and retention status.

The distinction between observed and effective time is essential for corrections. A user can report today that a preference changed last week. A system can discover a failed external operation after it previously recorded a timeout. Ordering by ingestion time alone does not establish which belief is currently valid. The event log should preserve both when information entered the system and what interval it describes. A query for the latest known fact and a query for what the agent knew at a past decision then become different operations.

Let denote a causal dependency. A tool result depends on its invocation, and a summary depends on the source events it abstracts. Causal order need not coincide with a single globally synchronized clock. Lamport’s treatment of event ordering supplies the foundational distinction between causal precedence and a compatible total ordering . For agent logs, the practical consequence is to retain causal links rather than assuming that wall-clock sorting reconstructs the decision process.

Typed events enable different validation rules. A model proposal can be accepted as a proposal without being accepted as a fact. A tool receipt can require a validated tool identity and matching invocation identifier. A completion event can require specific tests. An authorization event can require an authorized principal and a scope. If all four are serialized as untyped text, later summarization can accidentally promote the first into the last. Data typing reduces this risk but cannot determine whether the content of a tool observation is itself truthful.

An append-only evidence log does not imply indefinite retention of all raw payloads. Deletion, redaction, and access revocation can be represented by policy-controlled transformations while preserving the fact that an earlier decision referenced an object that is no longer accessible. The system should avoid claiming that a deleted payload remains reconstructible if its retention policy intentionally removes it. Auditability and privacy create a real design tradeoff; an implementation must state which forms of evidence survive.

The resulting event history is different from a polished narrative. It can contain conflicting reports, partial failures, and superseded plans. Those are necessary evidence for diagnosing why the agent acted as it did. A model-facing summary is a derived view of that history, with its own version and provenance, rather than a replacement for the record of events.
Define a reducer that constructs application state from a prior state and an event under schema version :

If is deterministic and all inputs are retained, replay can reconstruct the same application state. The assumptions matter. A reducer that silently consults the current clock, a mutable external service, or a newly upgraded language model is not deterministic under the recorded event stream. Nondeterministic results must be materialized as events if replay is expected to reproduce their consequences.

A checkpoint is a persisted state snapshot at a known event boundary. It can reduce replay cost from processing the complete history to processing the suffix after that boundary. Its identity should include the reducer version, event position or causal frontier, relevant schema versions, and references to external artifacts. A checkpoint that stores only the visible conversation can omit pending tool operations, unpublished artifacts, and reservations on a resource budget. Restoring that conversation may reproduce the model input while failing to restore the actual task.

There are at least three replay objectives. State replay reconstructs the recorded application state. Decision replay reconstructs the exact model input used for a past action and, where possible, its sampled output. Environment replay reexecutes actions against an equivalent environment snapshot. State replay does not imply decision replay if tokenization or context assembly changed. Decision replay does not imply environment replay if tools read changing data or produce irreversible effects. Evaluation should identify which objective it achieved.

A proposed checkpoint protocol writes an event frontier, state snapshot, artifact manifest, and integrity digest as one committed checkpoint object. An interrupted write should remain uncommitted rather than becoming an apparently valid partial snapshot. Restore verifies that all required objects exist and satisfy their recorded schemas. Missing optional caches can be recomputed; missing effect receipts or authority records may require stopping or external reconciliation. The distinction should be encoded instead of handled through a generic best-effort restore.

Checkpoint frequency trades storage and synchronization work against recovery time. If failures occur with a workload-dependent rate, a more frequent checkpoint can reduce lost computation but increase steady-state overhead. Language-agent workloads complicate this tradeoff because expensive steps are not uniform: one model call may be cheap while one external operation changes the world. A checkpoint before a consequential effect can be more valuable than one after a fixed number of tokens. Recovery cost should therefore be measured in both computation and semantic work lost.

LangGraph distinguishes checkpoints at super-step boundaries from per-task pending writes. Its documented durability modes also differ: synchronous mode completes persistence before the next step, asynchronous mode overlaps it with execution, and exit mode delays persistence until graph exit. An in-memory saver does not survive process restart. Moreover, replay from an earlier checkpoint reexecutes subsequent nodes, including model calls and API requests . These are distinct recovery contracts, not interchangeable settings. They do not make an external effect atomic with checkpoint storage. The application must state the selected backend, durability mode, replay frontier, and treatment of side effects.

A concrete distinction appears in ACM’s inspected HistoryManager. Its live message list is separate from an append-only raw mirror; compress_range removes a half-open slice only from the live list. However, snapshot returns the live messages, and load_snapshot initializes both lists from that snapshot. A different constructor, from_saved_history, accepts a separate raw history . Therefore, using the snapshot path alone after compression need not preserve the original raw archive. This is a source-level contract difference, not a measured failure in the paper’s experiments. A durable wrapper should persist both views when its recovery guarantee includes original evidence. Testing only that the live conversation restores would miss the archive distinction.

The difficult interruption occurs between an external effect and recording its receipt. Suppose an agent submits a transaction, the remote service commits it, and the network response is lost. The local system observes a timeout. Retrying can duplicate the effect; assuming success can advance a task whose operation actually failed. A session transcript containing tool timed out does not distinguish these worlds. This is an information problem before it is a language-model problem.

Represent an effect by an operation identifier , a payload digest , a target resource, and a state from a declared effect state machine. A useful application-level sequence is proposed, authorized, dispatched, confirmed, and reconciled. Unknown is a legitimate state after a timeout. It should not be silently mapped to failure. If the remote service supports a stable idempotency key and records the corresponding result, retries with the same key can retrieve or complete the same logical operation under that service’s contract. Without such support, exactly-once external execution cannot be inferred from local retries.

The ambiguity admits a minimal impossibility witness. Let be a world in which the first attempt did not commit and one in which it committed but its receipt was lost. Assume that both produce the same local observation and that an unkeyed retry commits once in either world. Let indicate a duplicate effect and an omitted required effect. If the recovery policy retries with probability , then

Omission here means failing to realize the required effect under a policy that terminates after this recovery choice. No policy based solely on the indistinguishable local record can guarantee both completion and absence of duplication. Indefinite abstention avoids a new effect but does not establish completion. A status query, a service-enforced operation key, or additional external evidence changes the information structure and can break the witness. This is an analytical construction, not an observed failure rate; its bound must not be applied to services whose retry contract differs.

Here durably records the intent and durably marks possible dispatch, changing to before the call. The local branch selection and marker transition assume a serialized dispatcher for each key or an equivalent atomic, fenced claim; separate lookup and unconditional writes do not enforce that assumption. The lookup in is evaluated only when returns an acknowledged journal; otherwise it returns . Terminal replay and unresolved reconciliation never call . In particular, current dispatch authority is necessary for a new effect but does not make an unresolved retry safe. A service-enforced retry contract can justify a different explicitly declared recovery branch; it is not assumed here. These maps specify application obligations, not an atomic transaction across the journal and remote service. Authority must be current at dispatch, even when no conversational state changed. Service-enforced key scope, retention time and payload-conflict behavior bound the idempotency guarantee; a key cached locally cannot impose that guarantee on the remote endpoint. The reconciliation path may query the remote service, inspect a resource version, or request a human decision when the outcome cannot be determined safely. It should not ask the model to guess what probably happened. A model can assist in interpreting receipts, but the effect state must remain tied to evidence.

Linearizability supplies a precise correctness condition for concurrent objects whose operations appear to take effect at a point between invocation and response . It does not automatically extend across unrelated services or provide an application with a global transaction. A local database can atomically record an intent while an external email, payment, or deployment remains outside that transaction. Calling the local workflow durable does not make the combined operation atomic.

Compensation is another distinct mechanism. A compensating action attempts to restore an acceptable business state after an effect has happened. It need not restore the original world exactly: a sent message cannot be unsent from every recipient’s memory. The agent’s plan should therefore distinguish reversible local edits, remotely idempotent operations, and effects requiring compensation or manual resolution. Session recovery should preserve those distinctions through summarization.

This analysis explains why successful restart tests can be misleading. If tests interrupt only before a tool call or after its confirmed receipt, they miss the ambiguous interval. Fault injection should include the boundary after remote commit but before local acknowledgment. That experiment directly tests whether the implementation’s effect model matches the guarantee claimed for long-running execution.
The loss point in Figure separates remote commitment from local knowledge; a missing receipt cannot establish absence of the effect.

Parallel workers can advance the same objective while holding different views of its state. One worker may discover a requirement while another modifies the artifact that requirement constrains. If both publish free-form summaries into a shared record, the last writer can erase the first worker’s evidence. A shared session therefore needs concurrency semantics, not merely a shared context window.

An optimistic transaction can read state version , compute a proposal, and commit only if the relevant base version remains unchanged. This prevents a stale proposal from silently overwriting intervening updates. The relevant version need not be the entire session: an artifact, plan node, or authority record can have its own version. Finer granularity improves concurrency but requires an accurate dependency set. If a worker reads an unrecorded constraint, the commit validator cannot know that its proposal became stale.

For a precise local commit rule, let be the recorded read set, the version read for object , and its current version. Let be the proposed update and a declared invariant check. A candidate can commit to the local transaction only if

This prevents stale-read acceptance only when contains every relevant dependency and validation is atomic with the local write. It does not certify the semantic truth of the read values. A remote dispatcher additionally needs a service-recognized fencing or version condition if another worker can supersede ownership between local validation and the effect. Merely placing a monotonically increasing token in a prompt does not fence an old worker.

Not every concurrent write is a conflict. Appending independent observations can be safe when each retains provenance and source identity. Replacing a shared completion predicate or deleting a task obligation is more sensitive. Commutativity should be established for the operation’s semantics rather than guessed from data format. Two JSON patches that touch different fields can still conflict if one changes the meaning of the other. For example, changing a tool target while another update broadens a permission can create an unintended combination.

Forking a session creates a branch of reasoning and action history. The branch should record its common ancestor and any inherited authority. A branch used for simulation should not be mistaken for a branch whose actions affected the real environment. Merging branches requires comparing effects and evidence, not concatenating their final narratives. If two workers both report that a document was published, the merger must inspect operation identifiers to determine whether there was one shared effect, two effects, or merely two plans.

Authority also needs version-aware propagation. A user correction that narrows scope should invalidate pending proposals whose admissibility depended on the older scope. Canceling those workers does not prove that in-flight effects were prevented. The system must distinguish cancellation of local computation from revocation enforced at the effect boundary. An authoritative check immediately before dispatch is stronger than a permission check performed only when the worker started.

A proposed test uses two workers with controlled scheduling: one receives a correction, the other attempts a previously permitted action. Vary the point at which the correction becomes visible and inspect whether the monitor, context assembler, and effect dispatcher use the same authority version. This exposes races that ordinary task-success benchmarks rarely exercise. No empirical outcome is implied by the test design; its value is the explicit causal sequence it makes observable.

Durability and retention answer different questions. Durability concerns surviving failures under a storage contract; retention concerns how long information should remain available and to whom. An agent can be durable while enforcing short retention, or retain data indefinitely while providing weak recovery guarantees. The design should state both instead of using persistent as a substitute for either.

A retention model should distinguish raw event payloads, derived summaries, embeddings, caches, effect receipts, and learned parameters. Deleting a source document does not necessarily delete the summary or embedding derived from it. Conversely, invalidating a derived record can prevent future use without physically erasing all copies. A truthful deletion claim must identify its scope and verification boundary. Cross-service backups and model-training artifacts require different mechanisms from a local database deletion.

Let denote the set of derived objects depending on source object . A deletion or access-revocation event can traverse this dependency relation to invalidate downstream objects. The graph need not imply that each derivative can be perfectly unlearned from a model; it identifies objects for which the application has provenance. If provenance was not recorded, the system may not know which summaries contain the deleted fact. This is a concrete operational cost of treating generated summaries as untraceable text.

Access checks should occur when evidence is retrieved and again when it is exposed to a model or another agent. A cached result may have been authorized when created but unauthorized when reused. Partitioning by tenant and project reduces accidental mixing, but semantic records can still reveal information across boundaries if extraction merged facts from multiple principals. The memory writer must preserve ownership or refuse a merge that destroys the ability to enforce access.

Past-decision audit creates a difficult case. An organization may need to explain why an agent acted while also respecting deletion of the underlying sensitive content. A record can preserve that a decision used an object with a given identifier and policy state without retaining the full payload. Such an audit supports a narrower claim than exact reconstruction. The distinction should be reflected in the recovery interface: a deleted evidence object should produce an explicit unavailable state, not a fabricated reconstruction.

Session summaries should therefore carry retention and provenance metadata alongside their semantic content. Consolidation into cross-session memory is a new use of information, not an automatic entitlement granted by the existence of a transcript. The application must decide whether the information belongs to the user, the project, a shared team, or a short-lived task. Chapter analyzes how those choices interact with semantic and episodic memory formation.

A proposed session evaluation begins with a set of invariants rather than a single completion score. Examples include preserving the current goal, retaining unresolved obligations, keeping authority current, avoiding duplicate external effects, and making every confirmed effect traceable to an authorized intent. Each invariant should identify the component responsible for enforcement and the evidence required to check it. An invariant that depends entirely on a model judge should be labeled accordingly.

Create interruption points before and after each event append, checkpoint commit, model response, tool dispatch, and effect receipt. Inject failures that lose local process memory, delay messages, duplicate deliveries, and reorder independent observations. Use deterministic tool fixtures where the objective is to isolate session mechanics. Then repeat selected cases against realistic external services or environment snapshots to test whether fixture assumptions hold. Both stages matter: the first improves diagnosis, while the second tests external validity.

A current managed-runtime boundary makes this distinction testable. OpenAI’s Agents API documentation separates live events from saved items: reconnecting restores saved work rather than replaying every missed event. It also warns that an idle session or a completed turn does not prove every tool succeeded. Required input is read from the current session, not reconstructed solely from historical items . A reconnect test should therefore reconcile item identifiers, current pending requests and effect evidence separately; retransmitting a prior action because a stream ended is not a valid recovery rule.

Metrics should separate restoration correctness, resumed-task success, duplicated effects, lost obligations, reconciliation frequency, and recovery latency. A fast recovery that repeats an irreversible action is not operationally successful. A correct recovery that waits for external reconciliation may be slower but necessary. Report the rate of indeterminate outcomes rather than removing them from the denominator. This prevents an implementation from appearing reliable by declining to classify its hardest failures.

The baseline cohort can include restart from the initial task, restore from a conversation-only checkpoint, restore from typed state plus events, and restore with effect reconciliation. Hold the policy and tools fixed where possible. The comparison asks which information and contracts are required for continuity. It should not be confounded by giving one baseline a stronger model or more generous retries. State exactly which external effects are mockable and which cannot be rolled back.

For concurrency, use a schedule matrix that forces stale reads, conflicting updates, and mid-flight authority changes. Verify that optimistic conflicts are detected and that accepted merges preserve the intended invariants. Storage-level correctness is necessary but insufficient: the semantic content of a memory update can be wrong even when its transaction commits correctly. Combine deterministic checks on identifiers and versions with targeted semantic judgments whose disagreement is reported.

These experiments are proposed and have not been run here. Existing persistence interfaces establish that checkpoints and durable execution can be implemented; they do not settle the workload-specific question of what must be restored. The scientific contribution of a session study is strongest when it connects a particular invariant, an injected failure, and an observed recovery mechanism. An average success score without that chain is weak evidence for durable agent behavior.

The following continuity contract is an original synthesis of the state and effect distinctions above. A resumed run should identify its session and task, load a validated event frontier, restore the authoritative goal and permissions, reconstruct the model-visible state through a versioned transformation, reconcile pending effects, and only then choose a new action. This ordering prevents the policy from treating uncertainty about external effects as if it were ordinary conversational ambiguity.

The contract does not require byte-identical future generation. A stochastic model can choose a different valid action after resumption. What should remain invariant is the set of obligations and the evidence about what has already happened. Reproducible sampling can help debugging, but operational continuity is not equivalent to deterministic decoding. A system that produces the same text while repeating an external action has reproduced the wrong aspect of the run.

Similarly, a session can migrate to a different model while retaining application continuity. That migration changes the policy interpreting the restored state and can alter how summaries, skills, or tool descriptions influence behavior. Version references make the change inspectable but do not prove compatibility. A migration gate should test representative obligations, stale-memory handling, and effect recovery under the new model. Chapter analyzes this as a context-memory-policy compatibility problem.

For implementation, keep three stores logically distinct even if they share a database: immutable or policy-governed evidence, mutable task state, and derived model inputs. Evidence supports audit and reconstruction. Task state supports coordination and recovery. Derived inputs support efficient inference. Collapsing them into a single transcript makes every summarization operation responsible for persistence, authority, and learning provenance simultaneously. Separating the contracts makes failures attributable and allows different retention policies.

There is no implication that every agent application needs the strongest distributed guarantee. A read-only literature assistant can tolerate some duplicated searches, while a system dispatching externally consequential operations needs a more explicit effect model. The appropriate guarantee follows from the workload’s failure costs and authority boundaries. The important scientific requirement is to state that guarantee precisely and test the intervals in which it could fail.

Durable state supplies continuity of evidence and obligations; it does not supply correct beliefs by itself. A faithfully restored session can still contain a mistaken inference or an obsolete semantic memory. The next chapter examines how memories are admitted, revised, and used, while Chapter extends the operational analysis to deployment monitoring and rollback. Together these distinctions keep recovery claims bounded by the state that is actually preserved.

RecMem consolidates through recurrence-sensitive write stages, whereas October’s Hy-Memory learns a memory writer from attributed feedback . InMind shows why stored or directly recallable information must still be tested for appropriate indirect influence . The comparison unit is consequently the complete write–represent–retrieve–use lifecycle, including validity, delayed feedback, and the cost of maintenance.

Agent memory is a collection of mechanisms for preserving, transforming, locating, and applying information across decisions. Working memory describes the task-relevant information currently available for control. Episodic memory preserves contextualized experience, including what was attempted, observed, and concluded in a particular situation. Semantic memory represents more reusable propositions or abstractions. These are functional distinctions. A vector database can store episodes or semantic statements, and one text document can contain both. The storage technology does not determine the memory function.

Biological terminology can motivate questions about consolidation, salience, interference, and forgetting, but it does not establish a shared implementation. A transformer context is not a demonstrated model of human working memory, and a graph of extracted facts is not a biological semantic system. Parametric knowledge, key-value caches, external records, and application state have different update and access mechanisms. The memory surveys provide useful taxonomies of forms, functions, and dynamics while also revealing how heterogeneous the underlying mechanisms are .
Represent a memory object as

where is content, its functional type, provenance, valid time, observation time, confidence or status, ownership and access scope, and its version. This schema is proposed synthesis. It is deliberately richer than an embedding and text pair because future decisions can depend on whether a record is a direct observation, a tentative inference, or an obsolete preference. Embedding proximity alone does not supply those distinctions.

Working context should contain selected memory objects and the metadata needed to interpret them. A persistent store can retain a much larger set, but persistence does not ensure that the right item is retrieved or used. A useful evaluation separates admission, retention, retrieval, interpretation, and action. A failure at the final action can originate in any earlier stage. Treating all failures as forgetting obscures whether the information was absent, inaccessible, misclassified, or correctly retrieved but improperly applied.

Three changes should also remain separate: adding an external record, updating a reusable procedure, and changing model parameters. All can alter future behavior, but only the third changes the parameterized policy directly. A memory method around a frozen model can improve task outcomes without demonstrating continual weight learning. This distinction becomes important when a product or paper uses learning to describe a growing external store. The mechanism should be identified before its generality or long-term stability is assessed.
