The versioning policy permits backwards-compatible changes while a revision is current, so a dated specification URL alone does not freeze every document; the inspected schema commit is recorded separately. Earlier handshake-based revisions remain historically important, but their session and initialization assumptions must not be presented as the current core protocol. A2A’s task lifecycle is anchored to the v1.0.1 repository snapshot ; ancillary documentation using a moving latest URL remains a reproducibility limitation unless archived or pinned independently.

The application must map protocol identities to its own semantic identities. A JSON-RPC request identifier correlates a request and response. It is not automatically a durable task identifier, a user session, or an idempotency key for an external effect. Similarly, a remote agent’s declared name is not proof of its authority. Confusing these roles can produce duplicate work, cross-session state mixing, or misplaced trust while every message still validates against a schema.

For technical comparison, define interoperability at several levels: transport connectivity, message-schema compatibility, feature negotiation, semantic agreement about state transitions, authority propagation, and reliable recovery. Passing a connectivity test establishes only the first levels. A useful conformance report should identify which levels were exercised and which remain assumptions. The analysis below separates the current normative message facts from the systems deductions that follow when those messages carry long-running agent work.
Figure distinguishes request correlation, task lifecycle, and conversational context; none of these identifiers establishes current dispatch authority.

Protocol identifiers bind different objects. MCP RPC identifiers correlate individual exchanges; an optional Tasks-extension handle can relate requests to durable work. A2A context identifiers group interactions, while task identifiers bind units of work. A terminal task is not restarted; a later follow-up can create a new task in the same context. Returned artifacts still need local validation. No automatic cross-protocol identity or authority mapping is implied.

MCP 2026-07-28 uses per-request version and capability metadata, without a negotiation handshake. The server accepts or rejects each request independently. Servers implement server/discover; clients may call it to obtain supported versions, capabilities, and identity, but may also send another request directly and handle an unsupported-version error . This is the current behavior, not a renamed form of the legacy initialization sequence.

The base protocol requires the protocol-version and client-capabilities fields in request _meta; client identity is recommended but not universally required . The tool page’s prefatory example note groups identity with required metadata, whereas the base requirements and RequestMetaObject make it optional. Requiredness here follows those explicit base and schema definitions . A discovery request can be described as a typed record without conflating its wire encoding with its semantic identities. Let , and be the admissible RPC versions, correlation identifiers, methods, and parameter records. A constructed request is

The first four coordinates encode the jsonrpc, id, method, and params fields. The constant denotes JSON-RPC 2.0, an arbitrary request-correlation identifier, and the server/discover method. Inside the parameter record, encodes _meta; is the 2026-07-28 revision carried by io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion, and is the capability-declaration map carried by io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities. The empty map declares no client capabilities. These coordinates do not identify a durable task, conversational session, or external-effect key.

Equation is a constructed schema-level record, not a trace from a tested server or a complete JSON serialization. On Streamable HTTP, the declared version is also represented in the protocol-version header under the transport’s rules. A mismatch must be treated according to that binding rather than silently guessing which version the peer intended.

The same revision makes result interpretation explicit through resultType. Core values distinguish complete from input_required; a value unrecognized by both the core and agreed extensions is invalid, while an absent field from an earlier server is treated as complete for compatibility . An input-required result is neither a completed tool effect nor a generic transport error. It can carry input requests, opaque continuation state, or both; continuation state alone need not mean that a user form is missing. A resubmission follows that continuation contract, uses a new RPC correlation identifier, and preserves the application operation identity where applicable. The continuation token is not itself a grant or proof of effect completion. This spelling and message role also differ from A2A’s interrupted task state: translating between the protocols requires a semantic mapping, not replacement of one status string by another.

An unsupported-version response lists supported versions, allowing the client to retry with a mutually supported choice or surface incompatibility . The retry should preserve the application operation’s identity while respecting that a protocol retry and an effect retry are different concepts. A rejected version normally precedes application execution, but clients should not generalize that ordering to arbitrary transport failures or tool timeouts.

Self-contained requests reduce reliance on connection-local negotiation state. They do not mean that the server cannot maintain application data. Persistent state must be referenced explicitly rather than inferred from a shared socket or process. This supports multiplexing unrelated tasks while making the application responsible for its own session and authorization identifiers. Reusing a connection does not create a shared conversational memory contract.

Legacy revisions through 2025-11-25 establish a session through initialization. A dual-era implementation can support both modern and legacy behavior, using the transport-specific fallback rules . A recognized modern error should not be mistaken for evidence that the peer is legacy. An indiscriminate fallback can hide a real version or capability error and accidentally select weaker semantics. Compatibility testing should therefore exercise explicit modern rejection, genuine legacy behavior, and a peer supporting both eras.

MCP exposes several kinds of objects whose roles should remain separate. Tools are invocable capabilities with schemas; resources expose addressable context; prompts provide reusable interaction templates . A host decides how those objects enter the model’s working view. The protocol does not specify a universal context-selection, memory-consolidation, or reasoning policy. A shared transport therefore does not make every object an instruction or every server a memory system.

The current tool interface separates listing from invocation through tools/list and tools/call. Available tools can depend on request authorization, and descriptions and schemas guide the caller . The host still needs grounding, argument validation, and an authority check before effects. A tool annotation is not a substitute for an enforced permission boundary. Chapter analyzes these application-level contracts.

Resources have URI identities and can be listed, read, or described through templates . A resource URI is a reference in the server’s namespace, not necessarily a local filesystem path accessible to the client. The host should preserve the server and version context when storing or citing retrieved content. If a resource later changes, a previous citation requires a content snapshot or version reference to remain reproducible. A stable URI alone does not imply immutable evidence.

A skill is procedural knowledge packaged for selective use, as developed in Chapter . It may be delivered through a protocol extension or represented using resources, prompts, and tools, but those representations do not collapse its meaning into the underlying primitive. The Agent Skills specification concerns the skill artifact; MCP concerns exchange and invocation; the model policy decides applicability. A skill can instruct the use of a tool without having authority to grant access to it .

This separation has a concrete security consequence. A retrieved resource can contain adversarial text that asks the agent to change its goal. The host should label it as untrusted evidence rather than promote it to a privileged instruction. A prompt template can be selected by an authorized user while still containing external fields that require careful interpolation. A tool result can contain both structured data and explanatory prose with different trust properties. These distinctions must survive serialization and compaction.

The proposed implementation stores a typed provenance envelope for every imported object: server identity, object kind, object identifier, schema or content version, access scope, and insertion role. A context assembler then decides what is visible without losing those labels. This is an application design, not a protocol guarantee. It makes cross-layer errors observable when the same bytes are later retrieved as memory or passed to another agent.

The 2026-07-28 Streamable HTTP binding changed earlier behavior by removing the GET stream endpoint and protocol-level sessions . A description of the old transport that assumes those features remain current is technically wrong. Streaming and long-lived work must be interpreted through the current binding and per-request declared features rather than inherited from a historical tutorial. Transport connections remain implementation resources, not semantic user sessions.

The base protocol’s statelessness means that requests carry the information required to interpret them, with longer-lived application state referenced explicitly . A server can still operate on a database, a file collection, or an ongoing job. The critical rule is that the server should not infer user or task continuity from connection reuse. A reconnect should not require the client to recreate an implicit conversational state hidden inside the old transport.

The Tasks extension supports long-running operations through explicit durable handles and subsequent status or result access . Extension support is not assumed for every core endpoint. The returned task includes a retention lifetime and polling interval; a durable handle is not a promise of indefinite result availability. Cancellation is cooperative and can still end in a different terminal state . The client must distinguish a synchronous complete result from a durable pending operation and preserve the handle in its task state. Dropping the handle during compaction can make the agent lose track of work that continues remotely. Creating a new call in response can duplicate the operation rather than resume it.

A proposed application state machine records pending, awaiting input, completed, failed, canceled, and outcome-unknown states as appropriate to the negotiated feature. The exact protocol states should follow the cited extension; the application can refine them to track external effects. Cancellation of a request, cancellation of remote work, and compensation of an already committed effect are distinct operations. A successful cancel response should be interpreted within the remote service’s stated semantics.

Progress notifications are useful for liveness monitoring but do not prove successful task completion. A stream can stop because the network failed while the remote work continues. A host should retain explicit operation identifiers and use a status or reconciliation path when available. The same reasoning applies to retries after a timeout: a self-contained request improves routing and interpretation, but does not by itself make the requested effect idempotent.

The engineering benefit of the modern boundary is that session meaning becomes explicit. The cost is that applications cannot rely on an old initialization handshake to carry hidden task continuity. Durable agent state must record handles, versions, authority, and receipts independently of the socket. This aligns the protocol layer with the session contracts in Chapter and makes failure recovery a testable application responsibility.

MCP’s HTTP authorization specification distinguishes client, protected resource server, resource owner, and authorization server roles. Authorization is optional at the protocol-implementation level; HTTP implementations that support it SHOULD conform to the cited framework, while stdio implementations SHOULD instead obtain credentials from their environment . A server being reachable does not imply that every capability is authorized, and a client being authenticated does not imply that every requested effect is within the user’s task scope.

The current specification uses protected-resource and authorization-server discovery mechanisms and defined registration options . These are protocol and credential contracts, not a complete application policy. An access token can permit a broad API scope while the current user request authorizes only a narrow task. A local monitor may need to enforce the narrower boundary even when the remote service accepts the credential.

The protocol’s client and server information fields are self-reported metadata rather than cryptographic proof of identity . Applications should not treat a familiar display name or version string as authorization evidence. Trust should derive from the configured endpoint, transport authentication, credential validation, and applicable policy. This is particularly important for discovery catalogs that combine many servers with similar tool names.

Delegation adds another question: whose authority is being exercised? A host can authenticate to a tool server using its own credential while acting on behalf of a user. A remote agent can request a capability that the original user never intended to delegate. The application should preserve the principal and scope through each hop, avoiding silent expansion when a worker or skill is loaded. Protocol compatibility makes the message exchange possible; it does not decide the appropriate delegation policy.

Credential exposure should not be treated as ordinary memory. The model generally needs a capability reference and allowed scope, not a plaintext token in its context. If a token or secret enters a tool result, subsequent summaries and indexes can spread it beyond its intended lifetime. A secure wrapper can keep credentials outside the model-visible evidence packet while recording which credential scope admitted an effect. The exact storage and redaction mechanism remains application-specific.

A proposed authorization test matrix includes correct credentials with excessive task scope, stale authorization after a user correction, catalog changes under different principals, and a reconnect that interleaves unrelated users. Measure both unauthorized acceptance and false rejection of legitimate work. A system that blocks every call is not a useful agent, while one that completes every task with broad credentials has not demonstrated least-privilege operation.

A2A allows a remote agent to respond with a self-contained message or initiate stateful work represented as a task. Its lifecycle distinguishes interrupted states, such as input-required or auth-required, from terminal outcomes. A context identifier can group multiple interactions, while a task identifier refers to a particular unit of work . These identifiers should not be mapped automatically to the model’s active context window or to one transport connection.

Terminal tasks do not restart. A refinement creates new work within the related context and can reference the earlier task . Consequently, client artifact acceptance and mutation lineage must survive beyond the producing task’s terminal status. Reusing the old task identifier as a mutable revision slot would obscure which input produced which artifact. Continuity belongs to the explicit context and client-managed lineage, while terminal task identity preserves the completed unit of work.

A2A v1.0.1 also distinguishes idempotency by operation. Reads are naturally idempotent, message submission MAY use the message identifier for duplicate detection, and task cancellation is idempotent . Thus a repeated message identifier is not a universal delivery guarantee, and idempotent cancellation does not establish rollback of a previously committed effect. The client must record which remote deduplication contract was actually promised.

Discovery uses an Agent Card describing offered capabilities, endpoints, input and output modes, and security-related information . The card supports selection of a suitable remote agent; it does not prove the agent’s competence. A skill description in the card is an advertised capability, not necessarily a portable executable skill package. The caller still needs task validation, evidence handling, and a policy for trusting returned artifacts.

Delegating a task differs from invoking a narrow tool because the remote agent can choose internal methods and produce intermediate work. The caller may observe only status and artifacts rather than every internal action. This can be useful for modularity and privacy, but it changes verification. A completed task state is a protocol statement from the remote service, not independent proof that the original user’s success predicate was met.

Artifacts should preserve provenance, version, and a relation to the task. A document returned by a remote researcher can contain supported claims, unsupported synthesis, or stale citations. An execution artifact can be syntactically valid while violating a local constraint unknown to the remote agent. The delegation request should therefore include the relevant obligations and authority, and the caller should validate the artifact against them before publication or further effects.

Parallel follow-ups create a state-ownership problem. Several tasks can share a context identifier while working on different branches of an objective. A late artifact from one branch should not silently overwrite a newer accepted artifact from another. The application needs version and acceptance rules beyond the protocol’s ability to transport updates. Similarly, a request for more information should suspend or qualify dependent work rather than being ignored while the caller assumes progress.

A proposed delegation contract contains goal, completion predicate, budget, permitted effects, evidence requirements, and expected artifact schema. It allows the remote agent flexibility within those constraints. A callback or streaming update can report progress, while final acceptance remains a separate local decision. This distinguishes negotiated autonomy from unrestricted trust and connects protocol design to the orchestration analysis in Chapter .

Artifact transfer needs an explicit trust boundary. An A2A artifact identifier belongs to the producing task’s namespace; an MCP resource identifier belongs to the serving endpoint’s namespace. Resolving one into the other is an application mapping, not an equality implied by the identifier strings. A content digest can detect a changed payload but cannot establish the producer’s authority or the truth of its claims. Preserve the producing task, source version, content type, and verification status when constructing the resource representation. The consumer should distinguish an agent’s inference from evidence that the remote agent actually observed. Otherwise a technically correct transfer can launder a speculative conclusion into an apparently authoritative tool result.

An interrupted task also needs a scope-preserving continuation rule. Suppose a remote agent requests authorization for one operation and later resumes with changed arguments. Reusing the earlier approval solely because the task identifier is unchanged can authorize a different effect. A proposed application contract binds a grant to the relevant argument digest, resource scope, authority epoch, and expiry; a changed material precondition requires revalidation. This is an authority requirement derived from the execution model, not a claim that every A2A implementation enforces that binding. Protocol progress and user authorization are separate state machines, even when one user interface displays them together.

Consider a constructed workflow in which a coordinator delegates a research task to a remote agent and later uses a tool server to retrieve a source record. The A2A request identifies the objective, current constraints, and expected evidence artifact. The remote service returns a task handle or a direct message according to its supported interaction. The coordinator records the handle in durable task state rather than relying on an open stream to remember it.

When evidence requires a tool server, the coordinator’s MCP client sends a request carrying the current protocol version and client capabilities. It may first use discovery, then list the authorized tools and obtain the selected schema. Before invoking the tool, the host validates arguments and task authority. The server’s response becomes a typed observation with server and resource identity. It does not become a new user instruction merely because it was returned through a trusted transport.

Suppose the research task returns a completed artifact while one cited resource has changed. The coordinator should validate the cited version or preserve the captured passage, then decide whether the artifact satisfies the requested evidence standard. If the artifact proposes publication but the delegation allowed only preparation, local authority remains binding. A2A task completion and MCP tool success do not jointly imply permission to publish.

Now interrupt the network after a tool operation may have committed but before the coordinator receives the result. Reconnecting with the correct protocol metadata does not resolve the effect. The application needs an explicit operation identifier, remote status query, or reconciliation procedure. If no such mechanism exists, it should retain an outcome-unknown state. Reissuing the same semantic request with a new JSON-RPC identifier can duplicate work unless the tool supplies an independent idempotency contract.

This trace is original synthesis, not a tested integration or a claim that every SDK implements these steps. It identifies the records a correct implementation would need: delegation identifier, task/context relation, protocol versions, catalog/schema digest, authorization version, effect identifier, response receipt, and artifact acceptance decision. These records support causal diagnosis if the final output is wrong.

The most informative interoperability experiment would replay this workflow with independent client and server implementations, controlled delays, credential changes, and a mixed modern/legacy MCP environment. A successful result would support the tested semantic contract, not merely that two programs exchanged JSON. A failed result should identify whether the mismatch concerned version negotiation, capability declaration, effect semantics, or the meaning of task completion.

The normative implementation anchor is the versioned TypeScript schema. At the inspected July 28 commit, RequestMetaObject requires the protocol-version and client-capabilities members while declaring client information optional. DiscoverRequest fixes the discovery method, and CallToolRequest binds the tool-call method to its parameter structure . These definitions are stronger implementation references than copying an old SDK example and assuming it speaks the current protocol. They describe message shape; they are not an executed conformance test of any client library.

A concrete negative test removes only the capabilities member from the illustrative request while preserving valid JSON and a recognized version. A second test keeps the capabilities member but changes the HTTP version header so it disagrees with the body. A third requests an unsupported protocol version while keeping body and header equal. These cases should not collapse into one generic retry: malformed metadata, inconsistent transport declaration, and unsupported version are different failures. Their distinction matters because only some errors justify selecting a different protocol version.

An application can generate clients from schema definitions and still mishandle those outcomes. It might cache a successful discovery response under one credential and reuse the catalog under another. It might regard an optional identity string as a trusted principal. It might strip required metadata when forwarding a request to a worker. These are integration failures above the type definition. Test the complete forwarding path with different principals and concurrent tasks rather than validating only an isolated client serializer.

For long-running operations, retain two kinds of correlation. The protocol request identifier tracks a particular exchange, while an explicit application or extension handle tracks durable work. After a reconnect, a new exchange can refer to the same durable task. If the implementation uses request identity as the only operation identity, it can either duplicate work on retry or incorrectly suppress a legitimate new request. A reference fixture should model both identities and assert which one is stable across network retries.

The same distinction supports audit of delegated research. The coordinator can record that a remote task completed and that an artifact was received, while separately recording whether the artifact passed evidence validation. This avoids turning transport success into scientific acceptance. It also allows the coordinator to reject one artifact without falsely marking the remote operation as never completed. Protocol state, task state, and epistemic status remain separate even when the user interface displays one compact progress indicator.

Protocol evaluation should separate schema conformance from application correctness. Conformance tests can validate required metadata, unsupported versions, capability errors, pagination, and response correlation. They can inspect whether the current modern request model is implemented rather than a historical initialization flow. They cannot establish that an agent’s chosen action is useful or that a returned research artifact is scientifically sound.

Use a version matrix with modern-only, legacy-only, and dual-era MCP peers. Include missing required metadata, declared but unsupported capabilities, an unknown version, and a recognized modern rejection. Test whether fallback follows the binding’s rules instead of treating every error as a reason to initialize a legacy session. Preserve exact specification and SDK revisions in the result. A package release number alone is insufficient when examples or generated schemas change independently.

For A2A, test direct messages, stateful tasks, interrupted work, terminal outcomes, and artifact updates. Include delayed and duplicated updates, failed streams, and concurrent follow-ups. Check that the application preserves task ownership and does not interpret a progress event as completion. Independently verify a sample of final artifacts against the requested predicate. Protocol-level terminal status and task-level validity should remain separate metrics.

Performance accounting includes discovery, schema transfer, serialization, credential flows, network latency, polling or streaming overhead, model decisions, and remote work. Compare warm and cold operation, and identify which metadata is cacheable under which principal. A cached catalog can reduce overhead while becoming stale after a permission or tool change. Latency gains should therefore be reported alongside freshness and correctness behavior.

The official MCP architecture documentation identifies an additional current-version change: sampling and some prior utilities are deprecated in the 2026-07-28 era, and change notifications are delivered through opt-in subscriptions . Implementations and surveys should not infer present support from an older tutorial. Deprecation also differs from immediate removal; the exact feature lifecycle must be checked before asserting that a capability is unavailable.

No runtime conformance or cross-protocol benchmark has been executed for this chapter. The normative facts come from official specifications inspected at the cutoff; the execution trace, failure analysis, and test design are explicitly deductions and proposals. The main technical conclusion is bounded: interoperable messages make component composition possible, while durable state, authority, evidence quality, and verified outcomes remain contracts of the complete agent system. Those contracts determine whether interoperability improves reliable autonomy.

Harness and RRSI make a current experimental boundary explicit: a frozen backbone can be surrounded by a changing execution procedure, and the resulting gains belong to the configured system rather than automatically to the checkpoint . Harness adds inference and model-based selection whose cost and evaluator dependence matter; RRSI limits repeated selection against a finite evolve set. These 2026 cases motivate the central question here: which state transitions changed, what evidence selected them, and can the claimed benefit survive independent tasks and runtime failures?

A model supplies a conditional distribution over candidate actions. A harness decides which observations enter that conditional distribution, which candidates become executable operations, how their effects are recorded, and what happens when execution stops unexpectedly. Consequently, harness behavior changes the effective policy even when model parameters remain fixed. An evaluation that reports only a model identifier omits part of the system being evaluated. Conversely, an improved harness does not demonstrate that the underlying model learned a new capability.

The engineering objective is controlled progress under incomplete observations and partial failures. Reliability requires separating three claims: the agent selected a sensible action, the runtime executed the intended operation, and the operation produced a state satisfying the task. A successful transport response proves none of the other two. This chapter derives an execution contract, examines its failure windows, and connects implementation choices to experiments. The discussion extends the state-consistency analysis of Chapter and the interface constraints of Chapter .

Let denote the recorded interaction history, the constructed model context, persistent memory, and environment state. A harness configuration includes a context constructor , action parser , scheduler, authorization checks, and stopping policy. Let be the recorded execution state, defined in the next section. Let be the countable set of stopped output records and the dispatch-action space augmented with a no-effect rejection outcome. Assume termination for this single-call model; otherwise nontermination needs its own mass as in Chapter . For and , the induced distribution is

Here is the normalized stopped law of the actual decoder, uses only the declared policy-visible projection, and is the parser/enforcement kernel under current authority epoch . Its output is a dispatched action or a no-effect outcome; dispatch is not remote commitment. It can reject malformed output or substitute a deterministic fallback. A request for model repair is instead a transition to another inference call, not a free operation inside this single-call expression. Its likelihood, latency and cost belong to the subsequent trajectory. This distinction prevents a repair-enabled harness from being analyzed as though it executed only the final valid response. A parser that silently normalizes an ambiguous filename makes a policy decision; it is not merely formatting infrastructure.

This decomposition explains why two products using the same checkpoint can differ substantially. They may expose different tools, truncate different observations, retry at different boundaries, or terminate after different evidence. The code-as-harness survey organizes these mechanisms through interfaces, execution feedback, memory, and coordination . Its taxonomy is useful architectural synthesis, but does not establish that every additional mechanism improves performance. Additional machinery can increase failure opportunities and conceal the origin of a gain.

A clean causal comparison specifies the treatment as a configuration change. Suppose the treatment adds a planning file and a summarization tool. Its measured effect combines extra inference, altered context, persistent state, and a new action interface. Attributing the result to planning requires controls that preserve the other differences. One control allocates the same additional model calls to independent attempts; another retains the file interface but disables learned updates; a third supplies an oracle summary to estimate headroom. None is sufficient alone because the treatment can interact with task length and tool latency.

Harness adaptation creates a second policy. RRSI searches over harness changes while holding backbone weights fixed and constrains proposal and selection behavior . The important lesson is not a universal numerical gain, but that repeated selection against a finite evolve set can optimize quirks rather than transferable procedures. A runtime should therefore record the complete harness identity alongside the model and memory version. Reconstructing a trajectory with a later parser or prompt can change its interpretation even when every raw message is preserved.

For implementation, define the smallest state transition with an externally meaningful outcome. Avoid making an entire conversational turn the only transaction boundary: it can contain multiple tool effects and multiple opportunities for interruption. Also avoid recording every generated token as a committed action. Token streams are provisional inference products; an executable operation begins only after parsing, authorization, and allocation of a stable identity.
An execution record needs more than messages. A useful state is

where is an operation journal, authorization state, the compatibility tuple, and the remaining budget. The environment is observed through versioned evidence rather than assumed to be fully contained in . An email service, remote repository, or browser session can change independently. Storing an observation is not locking the corresponding external object.

The journal distinguishes intent, dispatch, observation, and reconciliation. An intent says what the application authorized. Dispatch records that a request crossed a boundary. Observation records the response or the absence of one. Reconciliation establishes what external state now exists. These states must remain distinct because a timeout after dispatch is observational uncertainty, not proof of failure. Retrying an uncertain operation without examining its effect can duplicate it.

Three invariants make this distinction operational. First, every effectful request refers to an authorized intent whose argument hash and policy epoch match the request. Second, every committed result identifies the exact intent and the evidence used to accept it. Third, resumption does not infer completion from an optimistic natural-language summary. It consults the journal and, when necessary, the authoritative service. A summary may help the model reason about the result, but it cannot replace the result record.

Typed states also prevent a subtle category error: task completion and runtime completion are different predicates. Let mean the user task is satisfied, mean required checks passed, and mean no operation remains unresolved. A defensible terminal condition is under the declared specification. A model-generated done token establishes only that the inference process proposed termination. A quality gate may still misclassify the output, so even this terminal condition is relative to the validators’ coverage.

Application frameworks expose parts of these distinctions. The inspected LangGraph persistence documentation separates thread checkpoints from cross-thread stores . That distinction should not be collapsed into a claim that a checkpoint already implements semantic memory. Checkpoints support restoration of declared graph state. Cross-thread stores retain application records. Neither feature independently establishes truth, relevance, authorization, or successful external-effect recovery.

The practical design choice is to make semantic commitments inspectable. A tool receipt should include object identifiers, version or timestamp, effective principal, argument digest, and verification status. Where a remote service exposes no stable receipt, record that limitation explicitly. It may justify requiring review before a consequential retry. The runtime must not manufacture transactional guarantees that the connected service does not provide.

Consider a request to create an external issue. A crash can occur before intent persistence, after persistence but before dispatch, after remote creation but before response receipt, or after receipt but before local commitment. These windows require different recovery actions. Before dispatch, replay can safely issue the request. After uncertain dispatch, recovery must first determine whether the remote creation occurred. After a committed receipt, replay should return the recorded outcome rather than create a second object.

An idempotency key helps only if the remote service gives it the required semantics. Reusing an application-generated string does not by itself make an API idempotent. The service must scope the key appropriately, retain its association long enough, reject incompatible reuse, and return a stable result. A short retention period can make an old replay unsafe. Idempotency may also apply only to one endpoint, leaving downstream notifications or billing outside the guarantee.

These relations specify required ordering and evidence semantics; they do not prove that a particular runtime or remote service implements them. Persisting a dispatch marker before calling introduces a conservative ambiguity: the marker may exist even if the request never left the process. Marking it after the call introduces the opposite ambiguity: an effect can exist without a marker. No local ordering removes both without cooperation from the remote system. This is the fundamental reason a journal cannot alone provide exactly-once external effects.

Compensation is a separate operation. Closing an erroneously created issue does not erase notifications already sent. Reverting a file does not retract information copied by another process. A compensating operation can restore an application invariant while leaving residual effects. Therefore recovery reports should distinguish restored local state, reconciled external state, and irrecoverable consequences. This classification supports meaningful incident analysis and prevents rollback metrics from becoming cosmetic.

Fault-injection experiments should target these exact windows. Kill the worker after remote acceptance but before local receipt persistence; interrupt between verification and commit; corrupt one journal entry; delay a response beyond the retry threshold. Compare stateless retry, checkpoint replay, and journal-based reconciliation under identical fixtures. Measure duplicate effects, unresolved operations, recovery latency, and task completion. These are proposed experiments; no failure rate is inferred from the protocol’s appearance.

Context management determines which parts of execution state the policy can use. A journal may be complete while omits the operation that explains a pending effect. Conversely, a summary may assert completion that the journal never committed. The harness therefore needs a projection contract between authoritative state and model-visible state. For a projection claiming effect-aware planning, the relevant unresolved operations and active constraints need a usable representation. Exact authority and sensitive effect evidence can remain privileged, with a policy-safe status projection; copying every grant or credential into the prompt is unnecessary.

A projection can be tested against invariants without requiring an exact semantic equivalence oracle. For example, inject a pending-operation record and verify that the constructed context includes its stable identifier and uncertainty state. Insert a revoked capability and check that the tool registry removes it regardless of whether the model remembers an earlier grant. These checks establish structural properties. Whether a compressed explanation preserves every decision-relevant fact remains a behavioral question and requires task-level evaluation.

Agentic Context Management supplies model-directed offloading and retrieval mechanisms . Its live-run raw mirror can preserve access to discarded content, but archival retention does not guarantee that the agent retrieves the right item at the right time. Its reported benefits also depend on a capable backbone and reimplemented baselines. This distinction matters for runtime design: storing raw history is a recovery affordance; selecting useful context is an additional policy with cost, latency, and failure modes. The snapshot-only restore path discussed in Chapter does not preserve a previously separate raw archive by itself .

An execution scheduler can reserve a protected context region for authoritative status and separately allocate a discretionary region for retrieved evidence. Protection should mean application-controlled serialization, not merely an instruction asking the model to respect a textual heading. The trusted region should be generated from current state on every call. If a retrieved document can overwrite it through string concatenation or malformed role boundaries, the separation is nominal rather than enforced.

The resource constraint couples context and scheduling. Long tool outputs increase prefill cost and may delay other sessions. An aggressive truncation policy improves throughput but can remove the evidence needed for reconciliation. A token budget should therefore distinguish required status tokens, candidate evidence tokens, and speculative reasoning allocations. When the budget cannot accommodate required state, the runtime should reduce work, retrieve narrower evidence, or request a bounded continuation. Silent removal of constraints is not a legitimate optimization.

Evaluate these choices with task-length and output-size strata. Average success can hide a regime where compaction helps short tasks but fails after the first interruption. Include a baseline that keeps authoritative status fixed while varying only discretionary history. This separates failures of the projection contract from failures of the model to interpret otherwise available evidence. Report the cost of reconstructing omitted evidence, not only the reduction in visible prompt length.

A runtime executes under several budgets that are not interchangeable. Tokens constrain inference volume; wall-clock deadlines constrain responsiveness; tool quotas constrain access; monetary limits combine model and service costs; risk budgets constrain permitted effects. Converting all of them into one scalar can obscure hard requirements. A cheap operation may still be unauthorized, and a low-token plan may wait indefinitely on a remote tool.

Represent remaining resources by a vector and each candidate action by a distribution of costs. Admission requires hard constraints to hold before expected utility is considered. For a deadline , current elapsed time , nonnegative uncertain duration , and tolerated miss probability , a chance constraint is meaningful only when the duration model is calibrated for the workload. A mean-latency estimate does not establish a tail guarantee. Timeouts truncate observations and can bias the estimated distribution if treated as ordinary successful durations.
A hard budget also needs reservations under concurrency. For a scalar budget , let be settled spend, outstanding operations and the reserved upper cost of operation . Require

Admission checks the invariant and reserves before dispatch in one linearizable budget-ledger transition. Settlement must use the same ledger and atomically add to settled spend while removing from outstanding reservations, with . It is idempotent under the logical-operation key: a repeated settlement returns the recorded result without charging or releasing again. Admission, settlement and release share one serialization order. Releasing a reservation before recording its charge would let another admission consume the apparent balance and invalidate the bound. Under these assumptions, each ledger transition preserves the invariant by induction. Vector budgets use componentwise inequalities. This guarantee requires valid cost bounds and linearizable, crash-consistent accounting; an expected-cost estimate or atomic reservation alone is insufficient. Cancellation does not release a reservation until the remaining charge or effect is bounded. An unbounded remote billing path cannot be turned into a hard cap by local accounting alone.

Cancellation propagates through an ownership tree. A parent may cancel its own inference yet leave a remote command, browser navigation, or delegated worker running. The runtime needs a record of outstanding operations, cancellation support for each tool, and a reconciliation strategy for tools that cannot stop. Returning control to the user does not prove that background effects have ceased. This distinction is particularly important when a later instruction changes authorization while an earlier operation remains in flight.

Backpressure prevents an overloaded system from amplifying its own failures. If a tool slows down, retries can increase offered load and make recovery less likely. A retry policy should distinguish transport failure, rate limiting, invalid arguments, and uncertain completion. Backoff addresses congestion; it does not repair a malformed request. A circuit breaker prevents repeated calls to a failing dependency but must preserve evidence about abandoned work. Otherwise the agent may reinterpret a dependency outage as evidence that a fact or object does not exist.

The scheduling objective must also include fairness. A single long-running agent can occupy scarce browser sessions or large KV allocations while shorter requests wait. Preemption can improve fairness but increases checkpoint and reconstruction cost. The appropriate policy depends on whether progress is checkpointable and whether external operations can be safely suspended. A runtime should expose these workload properties rather than apply one universal quantum to every tool.

Benchmark admission and cancellation under open-loop arrival processes, not only fixed concurrency. Fixed concurrency reduces offered load when latency rises and can conceal instability. Report queueing delay separately from execution time, and include rejected or cancelled work in the relevant denominator. Tail latency, budget overshoot, orphaned operations, and completed useful work collectively describe whether the scheduler preserves service objectives under stress.
Figure isolates the mechanism and its stated information boundaries.

A hard-budget invariant accounts for settled spend and bounded outstanding commitments. Admission reserves an upper cost before dispatch. Keyed idempotent settlement atomically records the actual charge and releases only the unused reservation in the same linearizable ledger used for admission. Unresolved operations retain commitments until remaining charges are bounded; cancellation alone does not release them.

An inspectable harness exposes action parsing, context construction, tool dispatch, state persistence, stopping, and error recovery as separable modules. Code location alone is insufficient: a module can delegate essential behavior to a proprietary endpoint. The implementation record should identify the local revision, external service version where available, configuration, and which semantics remain opaque. This is the minimum needed to connect an algorithm to an identifiable execution path.

The OpenAI Agents SDK documentation describes an application-owned deployment path, whereas a managed agent service supplies a different runtime boundary . A thin SDK wrapper does not transfer ownership of application storage, tool semantics, or approvals to the provider. Conversely, a hosted runtime may maintain session state without exposing the underlying scheduler. These are role differences, not evidence that one architecture is universally more reliable. Chapter compares their consequences without importing product priority rankings.

Harness2 illustrates adaptation of execution and improvement harnesses using behavioral comparisons and experience reuse . Without ground-truth task verifiers, such feedback remains vulnerable to shared model biases and execution variance. More editor sessions can improve the search over changes while also increasing cost and selection opportunities. A runtime supporting this mechanism needs candidate isolation, a record of rejected changes, and a rollback boundary that includes prompts, tools, and memory interpretation.

The current Harness2 source distinguishes logical stage accounting from all invocation costs. Its core/ledger.py checks rollout and improvement-stage identities and for recursion budget , rejects duplicate stage labels, and separately records retry attempts. Selection and reflection are outside this ledger’s stated counting boundary . These are source-level count identities, not measurements of runtime or total expense. A complete cost comparison must join those stages with selection, reflection and failed invocations. The ledger is an adaptation-budget record, not a transactional journal proving remote-effect recovery.

An implementation audit should begin with one complete request, not an abstract class diagram. Trace the request from input serialization to terminal artifact, identify every mutable dependency, and enumerate where errors are caught or suppressed. A broad exception handler that returns a plausible textual tool result can turn infrastructure failure into misleading model evidence. A successful deserialization test will not expose that defect; an injected dependency outage will.

The strongest verification combines local contract checks with end-to-end behavioral experiments. Contract tests can establish that duplicate operation identifiers are rejected or that schema changes invalidate cached decisions. They cannot establish that a proposed patch satisfies an underspecified user task. Behavioral tests can estimate task reliability but may miss rare transactional windows. The two forms of evidence answer different questions and should remain separately reported.

The practical implication is a narrow but consequential design principle: authoritative execution state should be machine-checkable, recoverable, and distinct from model narration. The model remains essential for interpreting uncertain tasks and choosing useful actions. The runtime supplies the boundaries within which those choices can be evaluated and acted upon. Reliability emerges from their interaction; neither a fluent agent nor a durable database independently establishes it.

Consider a repository-maintenance agent asked to update a dependency, run tests, and prepare a reviewable change. Its environment has four independently mutable surfaces: the checkout, dependency registry, test infrastructure, and remote review service. The task is deliberately narrower than autonomous deployment. The relevant success predicate requires the intended version change, passing required tests under the declared environment, and a review artifact referring to the verified revision. A passing local command is not sufficient if the remote artifact contains another commit.

Start by assigning an immutable task identifier and recording the initial repository commit. The package resolution step produces a lockfile whose content depends on registry state as well as the requested version. Therefore the transition record must include the resolved artifact identity, not only the human-readable version string. A registry can republish metadata or a moving tag can resolve differently. Replaying the same command later may produce different bytes even when the agent’s prompt is unchanged. Reproducibility requires controlling this dependency or recording that it remains uncontrolled.

Next, the agent edits files in a workspace branch. The harness can checkpoint a filesystem snapshot before execution, but the snapshot does not capture every external dependency. A test can consult network services, local caches, or environment variables. The verification record should bind the resulting verdict to the workspace digest, test selection, dependency manifest, and relevant environment identity. If the model changes a source file after tests finish, the prior verdict becomes stale. The runtime can enforce this mechanically by invalidating verdicts whose dependency digests no longer match the current artifact.

This binding can be expressed as an acceptance rule. Let be the proposed artifact, its digest, a verifier configuration, and a recorded test outcome. The gate accepts only if was produced for and the required checks passed. The rule establishes correspondence between artifact and evidence; it does not establish completeness of the tests. An independent specification defect remains possible. The separation is useful because it prevents a simple engineering mismatch from being obscured by philosophical uncertainty about correctness.

Now introduce a crash after the remote review service creates the artifact but before the harness stores its identifier. Replaying the create request can produce duplicates. If the service supports an idempotency key, recovery uses the original key. If it does not, the agent can query for an artifact marked with the task identifier and expected commit digest. That query may return zero, one, or several matches. Zero results are not conclusive under eventual consistency. Several results require reconciliation rather than arbitrary selection. A bounded waiting policy and an unresolved status are more accurate than asserting that the operation failed.

The cost of naive retries can be analyzed without inventing a measurement. Conditional on one dispatch, let be the event that the request takes effect but its acknowledgment is lost, and let mean recovery retries without reconciliation. For and , the chain rule gives . No independence assumption is needed with this conditional definition of . If , the joint event has probability zero without defining . Under the one-retry model this is a duplicate opportunity. The actual duplicate probability also depends on remote deduplication and whether the operation is intrinsically idempotent. This expression is not an estimate of any product. It identifies two distinct intervention targets: reduce acknowledgment ambiguity or eliminate blind retries. Improving model reasoning alone need not reduce either one.

Suppose authorization changes while the task is interrupted. The original grant allowed preparation of a review artifact, but the operator later revokes remote write access. Restoring the old checkpoint must not restore the old grant as if it were still current. Recovery loads execution progress from the checkpoint and authorization from the authoritative policy service. The resumed model may still see a historical permission statement in ; the tool boundary must reject a newly attempted write under the current epoch. This example shows why replay fidelity and present authorization can legitimately diverge.

Deletion introduces another dependency. If a user requests removal of sensitive task material, deleting the current context does not remove journal payloads, filesystem checkpoints, test logs, remote artifacts, or indexing copies. A retention service needs a dependency inventory and a distinction between records required for audit and content permitted for reuse. Where legal or operational retention prevents immediate physical deletion, the system should record the constraint and prevent subsequent model retrieval. It should not describe a tombstone as completed physical erasure. Chapter examines the authority and governance implications.

A controlled evaluation of this workflow uses deterministic repository fixtures and instrumented remote-service simulators. Each fixture specifies the allowed edits, required checks, and permitted remote effects. Failures are injected at journal, network, verifier, and artifact-publication boundaries. The primary unit is a task instance with its complete failure schedule, not an individual model call. Paired schedules allow comparison of recovery strategies without confounding one strategy with easier failures. Model sampling remains a separate repeated-run factor, and uncertainty should preserve clustering by fixture.

Report artifact correctness, stale-verdict acceptance, duplicate creations, authorization violations, unresolved outcomes, and complete execution cost. A runtime can achieve fewer duplicates by refusing all remote work, so benign completion must be reported alongside containment. It can achieve low mean latency by abandoning difficult recoveries, so abandoned and timed-out runs remain visible. These paired metrics force the experiment to evaluate the desired tradeoff rather than reward a degenerate implementation. The worked example yields no universal winner, but it supplies a precise testable distinction between durable progress and merely persistent conversation.

October 2026 LatComm replaces repeated text transfer with a reusable learned packet between frozen language models . It makes coordination a representation-compatibility problem as well as a scheduling problem: a receiver must interpret what another model encoded, under a finite communication budget. This is evidence from bounded question-answering experiments, not a demonstration that arbitrary autonomous teams share a sufficient state. The chapter therefore begins with task dependencies and proceeds to evidence contracts, latent channels, concurrent memory, and causal team evaluation.

Delegation changes the distribution of computation across contexts, models, tools, and execution times. It does not create additional evidence merely by creating additional agents. A team can improve coverage through parallel exploration, specialist interfaces, and independent checking, yet it can also multiply a shared misconception. The relevant research question is therefore conditional: which decomposition preserves the information required for the task, and when does the resulting gain exceed communication, coordination, and verification costs?

This chapter treats a team as a distributed decision system with explicit ownership and mutable state. The discussion separates parallel sampling from communication, role assignment from capability diversity, and workflow topology from actual execution semantics. AutoGen and MetaGPT provide influential examples of conversational and role-organized coordination . Their architectural patterns motivate comparisons; they do not license treating every multi-agent deployment as a stronger policy.

A task decomposition is a directed graph whose nodes represent work products and whose edges represent prerequisites. A node should specify a deliverable, evidence requirements, permitted tools, budget, and acceptance condition. Research the topic is too underspecified to support reliable integration. Identify contradictory primary results under the declared cutoff, returning source identity, claim, experimental population, and limitation defines an auditable information product. The distinction matters because integration quality depends on what the delegate was asked to preserve.
Let be an acyclic work graph, the execution time of node , and the worker limit. Ignoring communication and scheduling overhead, the makespan satisfies

where is the set of dependency paths. The first term is a work bound; the second is the critical-path bound. Adding workers cannot overcome a serial evidence dependency. Communication, verifier queues, tool contention, and failed retries increase observed makespan above this idealized lower bound.

The graph itself may be uncertain. A search task can reveal a missing prerequisite, invalidate a planned branch, or require another tool. Dynamic orchestration therefore operates over both task actions and graph-editing actions. A manager that repeatedly replans can spend more time maintaining the graph than the workers spend executing it. Graph-edit operations should have budgets and stopping rules, particularly when a model is rewarded for producing elaborate plans rather than verified progress.

Decomposition also changes statistical difficulty. Breaking a coherent task into subtasks may remove context that made the original problem solvable. Conversely, it can reduce distraction by exposing each worker to a narrower evidence set. A controlled experiment should distinguish these effects by comparing the same decomposition executed serially, in parallel without communication, and in parallel with communication. If only the communicating condition improves, evidence exchange is implicated. If serial decomposition already captures the gain, parallelism may primarily affect latency.

An important operating condition is interface stability. Delegation works best when a subtask produces a bounded artifact that can be checked independently of the worker’s narrative. A parsed dataset, executable patch, or evidence table has a clearer acceptance surface than a general recommendation. This does not make artifact verification trivial, but it constrains where errors can enter integration. Tasks requiring continuous negotiation of a shared latent interpretation are harder to decompose safely than tasks with explicit data dependencies.

The graph also needs an invalidation relation. If node consumed artifact digest from node , a later replacement of that artifact must mark and its affected descendants stale; graph reachability alone is insufficient when several artifact versions coexist. Reexecuting every descendant is conservative but potentially expensive. Reusing a descendant is justified only when its declared dependencies remain valid, or when an independently checked equivalence permits substitution. A model’s statement that a revision is minor is not such an equivalence. This turns the critical path into a versioned evidence path: parallel work reduces elapsed computation only to the extent that its outputs survive integration without invalidating subsequent work. Chapter applies the same dependency principle to deployed model, tool and memory updates.

Independent samples and collaborating agents answer different questions. If each independent attempt succeeds with probability , then the chance that at least one of attempts succeeds is . This expression assumes independence and an oracle that identifies a valid attempt. A practical selector can reject the successful attempt or accept a plausible failure. Therefore the expression is headroom under a stated model, not an end-to-end reliability prediction.

For averaging, positive pairwise correlation inflates variance under a fixed marginal model. For Bernoulli outcomes with common success probability , sample mean , and feasible common pairwise correlation , the variance of their mean is

The expression follows by expanding the covariance sum; it does not require full joint independence. When , the variance-equivalent effective sample size is . A zero bracket is a degenerate zero-variance case for which that finite effective-size interpretation is undefined. It is only a variance equivalence, not a complete description of team success. Two joint distributions can share pairwise correlations while differing in the probability of all agents failing together.

Assigning different role names does not guarantee low correlation. Workers can share training data, model family, prompt assumptions, retrieval sources, and tool failures. A critic primed with the original answer may anchor on it even when told to be independent. A more meaningful diversity intervention varies information access, initial hypothesis, retrieval strategy, or verification method, then measures whether these changes reduce harmful dependence. Diversity that increases disagreement without improving error detection is not automatically useful.

Communication can destroy independence. Once workers see a popular hypothesis, later agreement may reflect copying rather than independent confirmation. An evidence protocol can preserve initial private assessments before discussion. Record each worker’s claim, confidence interpretation, supporting observations, and falsification test; then permit exchange. Comparing pre-discussion and post-discussion judgments reveals whether communication corrects errors or amplifies consensus. The process remains an experiment rather than a proof that private reasoning is always preferable.

The causal baseline should spend the same total budget on a single agent, independent samples, and communicating teams. Equal call counts are insufficient when prompts, tool actions, and verifier work differ. Also report wall-clock under a declared concurrency limit. A team may reduce elapsed time while increasing total cost, which can be appropriate for time-critical work. The conclusion should state that tradeoff rather than describe parallelism as cost reduction.

A delegation message is an interface contract. Its payload should separate instructions, observations, inferences, proposed actions, and unresolved questions. Flattening them into one natural-language paragraph forces the receiving model to reconstruct authority and provenance. This is especially dangerous when a worker quotes untrusted material that contains instructions. The manager must not treat quoted source content as a delegated command merely because it arrived through an internal agent channel.

An evidence-bearing result contains a claim identifier, source references, the relevant observation, the transformation applied, uncertainty, and applicability conditions. For a code change it includes the artifact digest, tested revision, test selection, and known failures. For a research claim it includes paper version, result location, population, baseline, and limitation. The representation can be structured JSON or another schema; the important property is that integration can validate required fields and inspect the source behind them.

Schema validity does not establish semantic validity. A worker can provide a well-formed citation that does not support the associated claim. Therefore validation must be layered. Structural validation checks field presence and types. Referential validation resolves identifiers and versions. Evidential validation tests whether the cited observation supports the inference. Task validation checks whether the work product addresses the delegated objective. Conflating these stages makes a successful parser appear to be a scientific verifier.

Compression at handoff introduces an information bottleneck. Suppose a worker observes , emits message , and the manager chooses an action from . If two possible observations require disjoint correct actions but induce the same and the same other manager information, no rule on that information can be correct on both. Prior knowledge or a follow-up observation can change the information set; the claim is not that all omitted text is unrecoverable. The data-processing principle motivates preserving sufficient evidence rather than only conclusions. In practice exact sufficient statistics are unknown, so interfaces should expose provenance links and permit targeted follow-up retrieval.

A useful failure case is a worker reporting that the benchmark improved while omitting that the improvement used additional attempts or a different evaluator. The manager integrates the result as a method gain, and the final synthesis becomes incorrect even though neither agent invented a number. A required comparison field would have exposed the mismatch. This example illustrates why evidence loss at handoff is a distinct error class from hallucination and deserves separate measurement.

Message cost also affects scaling. For a round in which each of workers emits an -bit message to every other worker, payload volume is before protocol overhead. A star that sends those reports once to a manager and broadcasts an -bit summary uses bits, but holding fixed can discard task-relevant distinctions. The bound is an accounting model, not a measured speedup or a guarantee that the summary is sufficient. Hierarchical summaries reduce volume but introduce another compression layer and a potential single point of epistemic failure. Topic-based routing and shared artifact stores can reduce duplication, provided access control and version identity remain explicit. The appropriate topology depends on the dependency graph; a universal full-mesh conversation is rarely a neutral baseline.

Text is only one communication substrate. LatComm’s October 2026 preprint encodes a context once, without a question, into fixed-size hidden-state slots; a different frozen receiver reads them through learned cross-attention and prompt-dependent gates. Its two stages train the interface, then freeze the compressor while adapting reader-interface and gate parameters for question answering; both LLM backbones remain frozen . Interlat instead studies direct last-layer-state communication and learned compression, including heterogeneous sender–receiver configurations . These mechanisms require access below a typical text-only hosted API. They must not be inferred from ordinary agent handoff support.
