The identity follows from Bayes’ rule. It shows why an apparently accurate gate can produce unreliable accepted outputs when valid candidates are rare. It also shows why calibration measured on one candidate population cannot be transferred uncritically to another.

Repeated search changes that population. If an optimizer generates many candidates and retains one that passes, it increases exposure to the gate’s blind spots. Under an illustrative independent-invalid-candidate model, the probability of at least one false acceptance among candidates is . Independence rarely holds exactly, but the expression identifies the selection pressure. A gate evaluated only on ordinary samples can fail after adaptive optimization.
Adding another gate does not automatically multiply reliability. If gates share a model, prompt assumptions, or evidence source, their errors can be correlated. The joint false-acceptance rate is

It equals the product of the two class-conditional marginal rates only when conditional independence is justified. Diversity of implementation and observation can reduce shared failure modes, but that effect requires measurement.

An unresolved verdict is operationally useful. It allows the system to distinguish lack of evidence from detected failure. However, unresolved cases must remain in reporting denominators. A gate can achieve high precision by accepting almost nothing; whether that is useful depends on coverage and task consequences. Report accepted precision, valid-candidate recall, unresolved rate, cost, and residual failure severity together.

Gate evaluation should include adversarially selected candidates and naturally occurring failures. Seeded faults establish sensitivity to known defect classes; natural audits reveal unanticipated classes. Neither alone estimates deployment risk. The candidate generator, gate, and final adjudicator should have separate evaluation splits where possible. Otherwise the same held-out examples can leak into both optimization and assessment, creating an appearance of independent verification without actual independence.

TestJack audits benchmark-passing coding trials by generating tests tied to prompt requirements, checking them against a reference solution, and reviewing whether failures represent genuine requirement violations . Its distinction between insufficient tests and underspecified prompts is essential: disagreement with the reference is not enough to refute a candidate. The paper reports substantial refutations in its audited passing-trial corpus; that proportion is not a prevalence estimate for all coding-agent executions.

The method’s witness structure has three obligations. The test must correspond to a required behavior, pass on the reference, and fail on the candidate. The executable conditions are reproducible, but the requirement correspondence remains interpretive. A faulty reference or ambiguous prompt can invalidate the inference. A reviewer agent reduces some mistakes but does not become an oracle merely because its role is called reviewer.

A stronger causal ablation keeps the candidate set and execution environment fixed while varying requirement grounding, reference validation, and review. Measure how many proposed witnesses survive independent adjudication and what defect classes they expose. Also examine false refutations: a method that discovers many failures by imposing extra requirements can reduce a leaderboard score while making the evaluation less valid.

Witness sharing across trials can amortize cost. If several candidates fail the same requirement, one validated test can inspect them all. This changes the unit of evidence: outcomes share a task and a discovered witness, so they are statistically dependent. Uncertainty should reflect that clustering. Randomly auditing trials can estimate properties of the declared audit population, but adaptive witness reuse and selective follow-up require a carefully described sampling scheme.

The implementation path should preserve the original repository, candidate patch, reference patch, generated witness, native test runner, and adjudication record. An artifact link or algorithm description does not establish that all pieces are available at an immutable revision. Until the exact implementation is inspected and run, report the method and author results separately from reproduction. This is particularly important for evaluator evolution, where changing a prompt or test-generation model can alter the measured defect population.

Long computer-use trajectories challenge evaluators through observation volume, hidden state, and instruction-specific constraints. A judge may accept a visually convincing outcome while missing a wrong recipient, incorrect folder, or unrequested side effect. Conversely, it may reject a valid trajectory because the decisive evidence lies in an intermediate application state rather than the final image.

AgentHorizon uses paired instruction-trajectory relationships to probe these distinctions . Its design motivates evaluating false acceptance and false rejection separately rather than relying on a single agreement rate. A judge that accepts almost every plausible workflow can appear competent on a positive-heavy dataset. Balanced metrics help, but they do not replace a clear definition of the underlying positive and negative populations.

Evidence access should be controlled experimentally. Compare final-state observation, full trajectory, searchable artifact logs, and authoritative application queries. These conditions test different capabilities. Giving one judge an interactive tool harness and another only a fixed image sequence confounds model quality with evidence access. Tool-enabled judging also incurs latency and cost, and tools can fail or expose misleading state.

A useful implementation separates evidence retrieval from verdict generation. The judge identifies required predicates, retrieves supporting observations, and links each verdict to the corresponding evidence. This improves auditability but does not guarantee correctness. Evaluate whether cited observations actually establish the predicate and whether omitted constraints were checked. A verbose explanation can otherwise hide a shallow verdict behind extensive irrelevant evidence.

Trajectory compression is another treatment. Summaries can reduce evaluator cost while deleting the rare event that distinguishes success from failure. Compare compression methods on matched task families and include perturbations that move decisive evidence earlier or later in the history. Report the cost of reconstructing original observations. If the judge needs raw evidence after every difficult case, the summary’s apparent savings may not survive end-to-end accounting.

A verification study should predeclare the property, candidate population, observation interface, and adjudication process. It should also distinguish discovery from confirmation. Cases used to design a new gate belong to development; untouched cases test whether the gate generalizes. Repeatedly inspecting failures and adjusting the gate against the same holdout turns the holdout into a training resource even if no model weights change.

The implementation ledger links a source claim to an equation or algorithm, a versioned code path, configuration, dataset split, and observed result. For ROME, inspect the intervention and editing implementation separately; a successful edit does not validate every localization claim. For sparse autoencoders, inspect training, feature extraction, and downstream metrics separately. For executable witnesses, preserve the native test environment and the requirement argument. These boundaries prevent one successful component from lending unwarranted credibility to another.

Negative controls are particularly valuable. Patch a random activation site, use an irrelevant feature description, supply a test that distinguishes an incidental reference choice, or give a judge a trajectory for a related but incompatible instruction. A valid verification method should reject or limit these controls appropriately. Failing a negative control identifies a concrete weakness in causal interpretation or specification handling.

Uncertainty must follow the sampling unit. Multiple prompts for one fact, several features from one model layer, and many candidate patches for one task are not independent replications of the entire method. Use task-, fact-, model-, or repository-level grouping as appropriate. Report heterogeneity rather than only an aggregate mean, especially when rare errors have disproportionate consequences.

The practical implication is that verification is an evidence-producing system with its own model, tools, data, and failure modes. It should be versioned, monitored, and independently evaluated. Internal inspection can reveal useful mechanisms; executable checks can falsify artifacts; structured evidence can expose unsupported claims. Their combined strength comes from complementary observation and intervention, not from relabeling a second model as an infallible critic.

Consider a system that proposes a code change, obtains a test verdict, asks a model critic for approval, and publishes the accepted artifact for review. There are at least four distinct latent events: the patch satisfies the requirement, the test suite covers the relevant behavior, the critic interprets the evidence correctly, and the published artifact is the one that was checked. A failure at any stage can produce a misleading acceptance. Calling the arrangement a verification pipeline does not remove those events from the analysis.

Begin with the artifact-binding obligation. The test runner records digest , while the publication tool is about to send digest . If , the gate should reject or rerun regardless of the critic’s confidence. This is a deterministic check over recorded identities. If the digests match, the system has established that evidence and artifact correspond, but it has not established that the tests cover the specification. The distinction allows an engineering invariant to be enforced without claiming an unavailable semantic oracle.

Next consider a candidate that passes all visible tests by special-casing the tested examples. A model critic may notice the shortcut, but it may also infer that the behavior is acceptable because the benchmark passes. A requirement-grounded witness can target an untested input implied by the prompt. If the witness fails on the candidate and passes on the reference, the remaining question is whether its expectation actually follows from the task. An independent reviewer should be shown that question without being encouraged to treat the reference’s incidental choices as requirements.

Now add adaptive search. The agent sees a rejection and revises the patch. The resulting candidates are not independent draws from a fixed distribution: each can be optimized against prior feedback. A false-acceptance rate measured before this interaction may no longer apply. To obtain a union bound over attempts, one sufficient condition is a bound on the conditional probability of false acceptance at attempt given the entire previous search history. Then the probability of any false acceptance is at most . Marginal calibration on unrelated samples does not establish these conditional bounds.

The implementation consequence is to retain the search history and gate version. If a candidate generator is allowed to query the gate repeatedly, the evaluation must expose that access and include it in the budget. A final accepted artifact should identify how many candidates were considered and whether the gate’s feedback was visible during revision. Otherwise two systems with the same final test suite can have different effective opportunities to exploit it.

A holdout gate can reduce direct adaptation, but it introduces its own governance problem. If researchers repeatedly inspect holdout failures to improve the system, the holdout gradually becomes development data. Rotating tasks or using a genuinely untouched confirmation set can help, provided the task distribution remains relevant. A smaller untouched sample may yield wider uncertainty than a large heavily reused benchmark. Scientific reporting should preserve that uncertainty rather than prefer the larger but compromised number.

Threshold selection also depends on consequence. A gate used to prioritize human review has a different loss function from a gate that authorizes external publication. Let be the cost of false acceptance and the cost of false rejection. For conditional on the information actually available to that decision, accepting has expected error cost and rejecting has expected error cost under a simplified two-action model. Acceptance is favored when , with either decision permissible at equality. An estimated score requires validation in the corresponding decision population; marginal calibration on unrelated candidates does not supply this posterior when additional covariates change the costs or error distribution. The formula does not make either probability or cost available automatically.

An unresolved or review action changes that decision problem. Review can acquire additional evidence at cost, and the reviewer is also fallible. A rational policy compares expected residual loss after review with immediate acceptance or rejection. In practice these quantities are difficult to estimate, so applications often use hard rules for consequential effects and probabilistic gates for lower-impact filtering. The rules should be justified by the action boundary, not by an arbitrary global confidence threshold.

This analysis transfers to internal model monitors. Suppose a sparse feature is associated with a concerning behavior and triggers a warning. The feature’s activation can be a useful signal without being a complete causal explanation. Calibration depends on model revision, context distribution, and intervention history. If the deployment policy changes behavior in response to the monitor, the observed data distribution changes too. A monitor evaluated only before intervention can therefore become miscalibrated after it is embedded in a control loop.

The discriminating experiment has separate discovery, calibration, adaptive-attack, and confirmation phases. Discovery identifies candidate signals or tests. Calibration estimates their behavior on a declared population. Adaptive evaluation allows a bounded optimizer to search for accepted failures. Confirmation evaluates the final fixed configuration on untouched cases. Report how candidates, tasks, and model families overlap between phases. This makes the independence claim inspectable rather than relying on the label held out.

Finally, preserve the distinction between a falsifying witness and a comprehensive safety claim. One replayable counterexample can refute a universal assertion about a gate. The absence of a counterexample in a finite search cannot establish that no accepted failure exists. It can support a bounded empirical statement about the search procedure, budget, and task population. That statement is valuable when accurately scoped. Inflating it into certification makes the evidence less useful precisely because it hides the operating conditions under which the gate was actually examined.

The ROME implementation makes this separation concrete. Its published causal-tracing experiment exposes a patching routine and hidden-flow calculation, while the model-editing module exposes the function that applies ROME updates . These are distinct execution paths with distinct claims: restoring selected activations tests mediation under an intervention; applying an update tests whether a weight change produces the desired association and preserves specified neighboring behavior. A reproduction ledger should not mark both claims reproduced because only the editing demo ran. The sparse-autoencoder implementation likewise separates encoding and decoding in its Autoencoder class . Reconstructing activations through those functions establishes numerical behavior of the learned dictionary, while interpreting a feature and evaluating its downstream causal effect requires additional experiments. Record the model checkpoint, selected layer, activation normalization, feature selection rule, intervention magnitude and metric. These fields identify where two apparently contradictory analyses may actually differ. Code availability therefore strengthens inspectability without collapsing the distinction between a reachable function, an executed experiment and a supported scientific conclusion.

In particular, the inspected ROME source contains trace_with_patch, calculate_hidden_flow, apply_rome_to_model and execute_rome. Their presence was checked; no execution result is asserted here. Pinning these callables to a revision and running the associated controls is the implementation step required before an independent reproduction claim.

AgentHorizon and TestJack provide October 2026 examples of why evaluation logic belongs inside the scientific object being compared . A trajectory-aware computer-use judge and a coding witness-test auditor observe different evidence and target different mistakes. Their results should therefore alter the design of a comparison before they alter a leaderboard: define which property the instrument observes, audit its errors, and retain the configured execution that produced the artifact.

An evaluation harness is an experimental instrument. It constructs observations, constrains actions, allocates resources, records outcomes, and applies a scoring rule. Errors in any of those functions can change a measured capability claim. A benchmark name and a model name are therefore insufficient to identify an experiment. The evaluated object is the configured model-policy-harness-environment system under a particular sampling and scoring protocol.

This chapter develops the estimands, controls, implementation checks, and uncertainty analysis needed to interpret agent results. The aim is not to replace all benchmarks with one universal score. It is to make comparisons answer a precise question and to expose when apparently conflicting results concern different populations, information budgets, or evaluator behavior.

Let be a task distribution, a system configuration, a resource envelope, and a declared outcome. The primary estimand can be written . Formally, is a probability measure on an eligible task space , and is integrable under the joint task and execution randomness; a normalized success outcome has range . Every symbol carries a substantive choice. Tasks can be sampled by repository, user, domain, or time. Resources can constrain money, elapsed time, attempts, or tool access. Outcomes can measure final correctness, constraints, latency, or utility. A numerical ranking is uninterpretable without these choices.

Micro- and macro-averages answer different questions. A micro-average weights each task equally, so a large task family dominates. A macro-average gives equal weight to families, potentially giving a small noisy group disproportionate influence. Neither is universally correct. Report the weighting rule and family-level results, and avoid changing weights after seeing which system benefits. Where a deployment distribution is known, a workload-weighted estimate can be relevant, but its sampling uncertainty and drift remain material.

The system boundary should include model checkpoint or service identity, prompt and harness revision, tools, memory policy, evaluator, and environment. A benchmark score obtained with a newer parser or different hidden-test version is a different observation even if the headline labels are unchanged. Closed service revisions may be unavailable; then the result is a dated service evaluation rather than a fully reproducible checkpoint comparison.

The foundational 2022 HELM framework emphasizes multidimensional evaluation across scenarios and metrics . For agents, this perspective extends naturally to permission compliance, state consistency, external effects, and recovery. A system can improve success while worsening cost or security. A scalar utility can summarize those tradeoffs only after the weights and acceptable constraints are justified. It should not conceal a hard safety or authorization requirement inside a favorable average.

The practical first step is an evaluation contract that names the target population, eligibility rules, unit of analysis, allowed information, resource limits, stopping conditions, and outcome definitions. This contract supports later auditing because it makes deviations visible. It also prevents an experiment from drifting into a different question when difficult cases or infrastructure failures appear.
Figure contrasts selection feedback with the one-way transfer of a frozen artifact to sealed evaluation.

Two evaluation protocols with distinct feedback boundaries. Fresh sealed confirmation returns a report outside selection. Restricted reuse exposes only promotion decisions to the proposer; validity additionally requires the source protocol’s initial evaluation independence and history-wide error allocation. The feedback restriction alone is not an error-control proof. No experimental outcomes are depicted.

The harness controls initial state and evaluator access. For repository tasks, it selects the checkout, installs dependencies, exposes the issue description, and later runs tests. For browser tasks, it resets application databases and authentication state. For memory tasks, it decides what persists across episodes. Each reset policy can leak information or remove difficulty if implemented incorrectly.

The inspected language-model evaluation harness exposes evaluation entry points, while SWE-bench’s harness exposes instance execution and aggregation paths . These are concrete implementation anchors, not evidence that every downstream adapter is valid. An audit should follow one task through construction, action execution, result serialization, and score aggregation. Check that the scorer reads the artifact generated by that task rather than an old file, cached response, or another worker’s output.

Stable identifiers should connect task, attempt, environment, artifact, and verdict. A directory name alone is weak identity when workers reuse workspaces. Content digests and immutable manifests reduce ambiguity. The manifest should include test selection and evaluator configuration because a result can change when the same artifact is judged under a different rule. A successful container exit code does not establish that the intended tests ran.

Environment failures require explicit classification. Dependency installation can fail, a website can change, a tool can become unavailable, or the evaluator can crash. These failures affect operational reliability even when they do not diagnose model reasoning. Report both overall task success and conditional policy performance under valid infrastructure, with clear denominators. Removing failed setup cases after observing outcomes can bias comparisons if one system stresses infrastructure differently.

Sandbox isolation protects benchmark validity as well as deployment security. Hidden tests, reference artifacts, and scores must not be readable by the agent unless the protocol intentionally provides them. Shared caches and logs can create indirect leakage. A deterministic fixture should attempt to read forbidden paths and query evaluator state to verify the boundary. Such checks establish concrete isolation properties rather than relying on the phrase sandboxed environment.

Finding one successful answer among several attempts differs from succeeding reliably on repeated execution. Under independent identical success probability , the former is and the latter is . These formulas are illustrative models, not general laws for agent systems. Attempts can share task difficulty, memory, environment state, or sampling behavior, making their joint distribution substantially different.

For sampled candidates with successes, the familiar combinatorial pass-at- estimator is when the sampling and interpretation conditions apply . The domain is and , all integers, with when . It estimates discovery of a success among selected candidates, not a deployable selector’s performance. An actual system needs a gate that identifies a valid candidate without access to hidden labels. Selector false acceptance and false rejection belong inside end-to-end evaluation.

For a fixed realized candidate set, that expression is exactly the fraction of uniformly chosen size- subsets containing a success. Its interpretation as an unbiased estimate of fresh -attempt discovery additionally needs the corresponding exchangeable sampling model; adaptive revisions are not automatically such samples. Task heterogeneity introduces a separate distinction. If attempts are independent conditional on task with success probability , then

For integer and , Jensen’s inequality gives and . Thus even conditional independence does not justify raising a pooled mean to a power. These are analytical comparisons under the stated model, not estimates of any cited benchmark’s reliability.

Attempt budgets should count failed parsing, tool errors, and abandoned generations where they consume resources. The mini-swe-agent accounting change discussed in Chapter illustrates why this is implementation-sensitive. Equal nominal attempts can hide unequal token use or paid failed calls. Report measured cost and consumed resources rather than only configured maxima.

Repeated-run reliability should retain the benchmark’s exact definition. Some protocols ask whether every repetition succeeds; others measure average success or consistency of a required constraint. A paper using one definition cannot be compared directly with another merely because both use a superscript or similar label. State the aggregation rule in ordinary language and provide the underlying per-task outcomes when possible.

Adaptive selection increases the effective search budget. A system that repeatedly revises prompts, harnesses, or memory using benchmark feedback has used the benchmark as an optimization resource. RRSI explicitly addresses overfitting in harness evolution . The evaluation should preserve an untouched assessment set and record candidate counts, rejected changes, and evaluator access. Frozen weights do not imply absence of learning from test feedback.

An untouched confirmation set is one design; certified reuse requires a different protocol. REUSE permits feedback-adaptive proposals only through promotion decisions from an initially independent evaluation sample and allocates error across all possible promotion histories . Returning detailed scores or failure traces to the proposer breaks that theorem’s decision-only restriction unless the extra transcript is accounted for. A generic confidence sequence protects optional stopping under its assumptions; it does not erase information already leaked into candidate construction. The public report should therefore describe the feedback channel as precisely as the tested artifact.

Contamination is not a single binary property. A model may have seen the exact task, a near duplicate, the reference patch, a discussion of the solution, or a related repository version. A harness may leak hidden tests at runtime. Persistent memory can transfer answer-bearing information from previous evaluation episodes. Each channel requires a different control and supports a different inference about generalization.

Use task lineage to track duplicates and revisions. A later benchmark release can contain transformed versions of earlier public tasks. Deduplication based only on exact text can miss equivalent code changes or renamed entities. Semantic similarity is useful for screening but can also flag legitimately related tasks. Report the screening procedure and unresolved cases rather than claim complete decontamination from one similarity threshold.

Temporal holdouts reduce some exposure but do not guarantee novelty. A task first published after model training may depend on a public issue or patch that predates the cutoff. Conversely, a benchmark revision date does not make an old task new. Record first public availability of the task and solution separately when evidence permits. For proprietary models, unknown training data limits what can be established.

Runtime leakage should be tested directly. Keep evaluator credentials outside the agent environment, separate reference artifacts, and inspect tool access. A browser agent can inadvertently observe a success marker or database field intended only for grading. A coding agent can discover test files copied into the wrong layer. These are implementation defects that can be fixed without speculative claims about model memorization.

Memory experiments require explicit contamination boundaries. If one arm carries experiences across tasks while another resets, the information difference is the treatment and must be reported. If a learned skill contains a benchmark-specific answer rather than a reusable procedure, transfer gains can reflect memorization. Holdouts should test both new instances and changed task structure, with source and experience provenance available for audit.

A stateful benchmark generally does not admit independent per-task potential outcomes. Let be the task prefix, the memory generated by system on that prefix, and the next outcome. Changing the system at an early task changes later memory and therefore later outcomes even when the task list is fixed. A mean over tasks estimates performance of the complete stream policy under its order and feedback rules; it does not identify an isolated memory effect at every task.

Two experiments answer different questions. A frozen-prefix experiment initializes both arms from the same admissible state and varies the next decision mechanism. A full-stream experiment initializes a common starting state and lets each arm construct its own subsequent memory. The former isolates a conditional local effect; the latter measures accumulated adaptation and error propagation. Resetting memory after every task removes the longitudinal treatment, while copying the stronger arm’s evolved bank into both conditions changes the treatment again. Report the chosen intervention and cluster uncertainty by independently generated stream. Chapter develops the corresponding counterfactual controls and contamination boundaries.

An agent evaluation has several sources of variation: task sampling, model sampling, environment nondeterminism, evaluator error, and adaptive state. Treating every model call as an independent observation ignores most of this structure. The appropriate uncertainty analysis follows the unit to which the claim generalizes. Repository-level generalization needs variation across repositories, not merely many attempts on the same few issues.

Paired comparisons reduce nuisance variation by evaluating systems on the same task instances. Define and estimate its mean over the target population. Confidence intervals should preserve pairing. If tasks cluster by user, repository, or persistent session, resample clusters or use an explicitly justified hierarchical model. The choice should be declared before inspecting which interval is narrower.

Repeated seeds estimate stochastic execution variation conditional on the sampled tasks. They do not substitute for broader task coverage. Conversely, one run on many tasks can estimate a task-population average while leaving repeated-run reliability uncertain. Report both dimensions when the deployment depends on consistency. If compute prevents sufficient replication, narrow the claim rather than inventing stability from a positive mean.

Multiplicity matters when researchers compare many models, prompts, memory mechanisms, and metrics. Selecting the best configuration and reporting an ordinary confidence interval as if it had been fixed in advance understates uncertainty. Separate exploration from confirmation, report the selection procedure, and use untouched data for final comparison. A universal correction is not required for every descriptive analysis, but the inferential claim must reflect how the configuration was chosen.

Missing and censored outcomes need visible treatment. A timeout may indicate excessive latency, infrastructure failure, or an unfinished but promising trajectory. For a deadline-constrained task it is a failure to meet the deadline, regardless of possible eventual success. Additional analyses can examine completion-time distributions, but they should not erase the primary operational outcome. Report sensitivity to reasonable classification choices when the cause is ambiguous.

An ablation removes or changes a mechanism, but it can also change resources, information, and optimization opportunities. Removing a retrieval module may shorten the context and reduce cost; removing a critic may reduce model calls; replacing a hypergraph with flat retrieval may alter both representation and access policy. The observed difference identifies the combined treatment unless additional controls isolate the components.

HyperSkill provides a useful example. Its no-hypergraph condition replaces the structured retrieval pipeline with flat embedding retrieval, so the result does not isolate hyperedge representation alone . A stronger comparison keeps decomposition, candidate pools, ranking budget, and maintenance cost comparable while varying the storage relation. This does not invalidate the system result; it narrows the causal explanation supported by that ablation.

Oracle controls estimate headroom. Oracle retrieval tests whether downstream reasoning can use sufficient evidence; oracle state tests whether partial observation is the bottleneck; an oracle selector tests candidate-generation potential. These controls are deliberately privileged. Their performance cannot be described as deployable capability, but the gaps help prioritize engineering work. A large oracle-retrieval gap suggests retrieval deserves attention before increasing reasoning depth.

Negative controls test whether a supposed mechanism is doing meaningful work. Shuffle memory, provide irrelevant skills, randomize delegation messages, or replace a feature description with a plausible wrong label. Some controls can damage the system in several ways, so interpret them carefully. The aim is not to produce a dramatic drop but to distinguish a specific explanation from alternatives such as extra context, extra compute, or evaluator bias.

A mechanism claim requires explicit operating conditions and failure regimes. It identifies where the mechanism helps, where a simpler baseline matches it, and where it causes regressions. This is more useful than a universal superiority claim because deployments occupy particular workloads. Method comparisons should therefore preserve heterogeneity across horizon, task structure, evidence quality, and tool reliability rather than compress everything into one average.

Evaluators need their own validation set and error analysis. A benchmark can be well constructed while a particular grader accepts artifacts that violate requirements. AgentHorizon and TestJack expose different aspects of this problem: long-trajectory judgment and insufficient executable tests . The appropriate response is to audit the observation and scoring pipeline, not merely add another model judge and call the result verified.

October 2026 harness evaluations expose additional estimand boundaries. TraceTrial-Bench preserves raw operational states but resolves some unexercised criteria using the task outcome, so its semantic harness and task scores are coupled; its selected execution archive does not supply independent repetitions within every cell . ASAP’s frozen-base-model measurements include reference-prefix elicitation and bounded recovery, whereas Harness Scaling evaluates training exposure and transfer to withheld execution combinations . An audit must retain those interventions in its configuration ledger. Treating all three as ordinary backbone leaderboards would discard the variable each study is designed to examine.

Preserve raw verdicts, reason codes, evidence links, and subsequent adjudications. If an evaluator is corrected, publish both original and revised outcomes with the rule change. A moving grader can otherwise make historical comparisons impossible. Where legal or privacy constraints prevent releasing trajectories, provide a precise description of what remains inaccessible and what external investigators can still reproduce.

The reporting record should contain task manifest, environment construction, model and harness identities, prompts, tool schemas, memory policy, budgets, seed policy, evaluator revision, and complete outcomes. Logs should distinguish no response from empty response, unknown usage from zero usage, and incomplete work from completed failure. These distinctions affect both cost and capability estimates.

Reproducibility is graded rather than binary. Metadata verification establishes identity. Source inspection establishes an implementation path. Executed fixtures establish behavior under controlled conditions. Independent replication tests whether reported results recur. Cross-environment reproduction tests robustness to implementation and infrastructure differences. A survey should name the achieved level for each source rather than allow a verified title to imply verified experimental evidence.

The practical endpoint is a comparison whose conclusion can be reconstructed from its records. Another investigator should be able to identify what changed, which observations supported the score, how uncertainty was computed, and which failures remain unresolved. That standard does not require pretending that every proprietary component is transparent. It requires making opacity an explicit limit on inference rather than filling it with plausible assumptions.

Consider two coding systems evaluated on the same repository-task manifest. The manifest names the base commit, issue description, dependency environment, required tests, and allowed resource envelope. Each system produces one primary attempt and optional additional attempts under a separately declared budget. The experiment’s primary question is deadline-constrained verified completion, not whether a successful patch can eventually be found with unlimited retries. Defining this question before execution determines how timeouts and infrastructure problems enter the analysis.

The harness first constructs an isolated environment and records its identity. The system receives the task and permitted tools, but not the reference patch or hidden evaluator. At termination, the harness freezes the produced artifact, records its digest, and runs the evaluator against that digest. If the artifact changes during evaluation, the run is invalid and must be diagnosed rather than scored against a moving target. This sequence is directly auditable in the task construction, execution and scoring code paths.

The inspected SWE-bench execution module exposes run_instance and run_instances; the language-model evaluation harness exposes simple_evaluate and evaluate. These names identify concrete entry points for examining how tasks become outcomes . Their presence does not establish that a custom adapter passes the intended arguments or that an experiment used the inspected revision. The ledger must connect the callable to actual configuration and recorded execution before calling the result reproduced.
Table specifies the evidence needed at each boundary. The table contains no measured outcome. It is a testable contract for distinguishing model errors from deterministic evaluation defects.

Suppose some outcomes remain unresolved because the evaluator failed after execution. A success rate computed only over resolved runs is a conditional quantity. Without assumptions about missingness, it cannot identify the overall task success rate. If there are eligible runs, confirmed successes and unresolved outcomes, a simple identification interval is when all other outcomes are confirmed failures. The interval expresses missing information; it is not a confidence interval for task sampling.

This distinction matters when systems fail differently. One system may generate patches that stress the evaluator and cause more unresolved runs. Excluding them can make it appear better even if they are concentrated among difficult cases. Conversely, scoring every evaluator crash as a model failure mixes infrastructure and policy behavior. Report the overall operational outcome and a cause-stratified analysis, while retaining a sensitivity analysis for unresolved cases. Do not choose the classification after seeing which ordering it favors.

For paired comparison, preserve the outcome pair for each task. Tasks where both systems succeed contribute differently from tasks where only one succeeds. A test based on discordant pairs can be useful under its assumptions, but repository clustering or persistent memory can violate independence between pairs. A cluster-aware bootstrap or hierarchical analysis should then follow the declared task-generation structure. More attempts on the same repository do not create independent evidence about new repositories.

Resource matching requires another audit. If system A retries malformed outputs while system B stops, equal configured call limits can conceal different paid usage. Record actual model and tool consumption. If one arm receives more wall-clock because its environment starts faster, decide whether startup is part of the deployment comparison or a nuisance variable to control. Both choices can be legitimate; silently switching between them cannot. A complete report shows configured ceilings and realized consumption.

The evaluator should also inspect null and reference conditions. The unmodified repository reveals whether the benchmark’s tests already pass without a fix. The reference patch reveals whether the intended environment can represent the benchmark’s declared solution. A null pass can indicate inadequate tests; a reference failure can indicate environment drift or benchmark defects. Neither result should be attributed to the evaluated agent. These controls establish whether the instrument can distinguish the states it is intended to score.

Finally, add an independent audit of accepted patches. Dynamic witness tests can expose behavior missing from the fixed suite, while requirement review prevents incidental reference choices from becoming new obligations. Keep the original and audited scores separate, identify the sampled passing-trial population, and cluster uncertainty by task. A revised acceptance criterion changes the estimand; documenting that change makes the evidence more useful rather than less impressive. The result is a comparison whose limitations are concrete enough to guide the next experiment.

An additional distinction concerns cost per successful task. Dividing total cost by confirmed successes can be operationally informative, but it is unstable when success is rare and can hide differences in task mix. Report total eligible tasks, confirmed successes, unresolved outcomes and aggregate cost alongside the ratio. If a system fails quickly on hard tasks, it may have low average cost per attempt without being efficient at useful work. If it spends heavily to rescue difficult cases, its average attempt cost can rise while its cost per accepted deliverable improves. The relevant conclusion depends on which work the deployment must complete, not on whichever denominator yields the smaller number.

The benchmark should preserve outcome severity as well as success. A task that returns no patch, a patch that fails tests, and a patch that passes tests while changing access controls all count differently in an operational loss model. The primary benchmark can retain a binary completion definition for comparability, but a secondary failure taxonomy should record those distinctions. Severity weights require domain justification and sensitivity analysis. They should not be tuned to favor the preferred system after the failures are known. This analysis is particularly important when moving from isolated coding containers to tools that can affect external users.

Releasing the comparison also requires attention to provenance and confidentiality. A trace can contain credentials, private code, personal data or hidden evaluator material. Redaction should preserve event identity, timing, error categories and the evidence needed to reconstruct the score while removing content that cannot be shared. If redaction removes decisive evidence, state the resulting reproduction limit explicitly. A public summary and a private complete audit are different evidence products. Neither should be represented as the other. The scientific requirement is an honest account of which claims an independent reader can actually check from the released artifacts.
A signed manifest can bind the released task list, artifact digests and scoring configuration, reducing ambiguity about which experimental objects a later reproduction attempts to reconstruct.

InMind and MemCalib distinguish two failures that an explicit-recall score can conceal. InMind probes the recognition of indirectly relevant historical information, whereas MemCalib studies whether supplied memory influences an answer too little or too strongly . These 2026 studies do not establish indefinite retention or reliable autonomous operation. They motivate separate interventions on admission, retrieval, interpretation, and behavioral influence, followed by longitudinal tests of changing facts, policy, and consumer versions.

Long-horizon evaluation asks whether useful behavior persists as evidence accumulates, tasks change, memory evolves, and interruptions occur. A single successful episode cannot establish this property. A system may recall explicit facts while failing to apply them indirectly, improve on one task order while regressing on another, or preserve raw history while losing authorization and temporal validity. The evaluated object is therefore a trajectory of system states rather than a sequence of independent questions.

The objective is to distinguish retention, retrieval, interpretation, influence, adaptation, and operational continuity. These mechanisms interact, but they require different controls. This chapter develops a longitudinal experimental design and connects recent memory studies to the precise claims their evidence supports.

Horizon can mean model turns, tool actions, elapsed time, task count, or sessions. These quantities are correlated only under a workload model. A hundred short tool calls can be easier than a few actions separated by uncertain external events. An accelerated simulated clock can test temporal logic without establishing months-long deployment validity. Every study should declare which horizon is manipulated and which remains uncontrolled.

Continuity also has multiple units. A session can retain conversation history, a task can span several sessions, a user can have many tasks, and an organization can share a skill bank across users. The memory reset boundary determines the treatment. A fresh model call with a persistent external store is not a no-memory condition. Conversely, carrying raw conversation text without cross-session storage is not evidence of durable personal memory.

Represent a longitudinal unit by initial state, task sequence, environment-change schedule, model and harness versions, memory operations, and final outcomes. This record permits causal interventions on order, updates, and interruptions. It also exposes whether a claimed improvement is conditional on an implicit curriculum or on access to outcomes unavailable in deployment.

The two cited memory surveys provide complementary taxonomies of memory forms, functions, substrates, subjects, and dynamics . Their value here is conceptual organization and discovery of primary methods. A survey’s broad coverage does not independently validate the experiments it summarizes. Quantitative conclusions should return to the original method, exact version, and evaluation protocol.

The practical implication is to choose the unit of generalization before collecting runs. If the claim concerns new users, many episodes from one user do not suffice. If it concerns memory evolution, repeated calls against one fixed bank do not estimate variation in bank construction. If it concerns robustness after upgrades, a fixed-policy study cannot answer it. These distinctions determine both experimental cost and statistical uncertainty.

A memory pipeline writes records, organizes them, retrieves candidates, selects evidence, interprets it, and influences an action. Failure at one stage can look like failure at another. If a fact was never stored, improving the reader is irrelevant. If it is stored and retrieved but ignored, improving the embedding may not help. If it is applied too strongly after becoming stale, higher recall can worsen the result.

Use staged oracle controls. Supply the original record directly to test the reader’s ability to use it. Supply an oracle retrieval set to test selection and interpretation. Replace learned writing with complete raw logs to estimate extraction loss. Preserve the same action task and resource accounting. Oracle controls are diagnostic and may exceed deployable budgets, so their scores should not be presented as operational performance.

The evaluation should include negative transfer. A no-memory baseline reveals whether irrelevant or incorrect records reduce task quality. A shuffled-memory condition tests whether apparent benefit comes from generic additional text or task-specific information. A stale-memory condition tests conflict resolution. A revoked-memory condition tests authorization. These are different interventions and should not be combined into one noisy-memory score without retaining their separate outcomes.

Storage and retrieval metrics remain useful intermediate observations. Measure record coverage, provenance completeness, retrieval recall, rank quality, temporal filtering, and evidence packing. But none alone establishes useful behavior. A perfectly retrieved false record can harm the task, and a low-ranked record may be irrelevant to the action. Relate intermediate metrics to task-level outcomes through explicit ablations rather than assuming monotonic improvement.

Construction and maintenance cost belong inside the experiment. Include extraction calls, embeddings, graph updates, consolidation, deduplication, deletion, and reindexing. Report amortized cost over different reuse counts. A system that is efficient after extensive preconstruction may be unsuitable for cold-start users; another may have low initial cost but unbounded storage growth. The appropriate operating point depends on the actual longitudinal workload.

InMind tests a failure mode in which a memory is relevant through a knowledge bridge rather than lexical resemblance . Its paired controls distinguish storage, bridging knowledge, and query-conditioned retrieval. This is more diagnostic than asking only whether the agent can repeat a fact on demand. The benchmark is selective, however, and its authors identify domain coverage, shared answerer-judge identity, and missing negative controls against over-warning as limitations.

The mechanism suggests a concrete comparison. Hold the decisive memory and task fixed, then vary explicit recall queries, indirect application queries, direct in-context exposure, and retrieval-mediated exposure. A gap between the latter two implicates the access interface rather than necessarily the model’s knowledge. To test whether a proposed remedy overuses memory, add cases where a similar stored fact should not affect the answer. Without those negatives, more frequent warning or personalization can look like better judgment.

MemCalib isolates another stage: the amount of influence a supplied memory should have . It distinguishes over-use from under-use and studies training signals that balance the two. Because the relevant memory blocks are supplied, the result concerns memory-use behavior rather than complete storage and retrieval quality. Its counterfactual localization is a credit proxy with its own uncertainty, not a direct measurement of every token’s true causal contribution.

An influence evaluation needs context-dependent targets. A memory can be evidence, a preference, a constraint, or an obsolete observation. The proper response depends on provenance, current authority, and task scope. A simple rule to always prioritize memory is therefore inadequate. Test contradictory updates, exceptions, and cases where a retrieved instruction lacks authority to modify the user’s objective.

These studies jointly motivate separating recall from decision use. Better retrieval can expose more relevant evidence while a poorly calibrated reader overweights it. Better memory-use training can improve interpretation while retrieval still misses implicit relevance. A complete experiment crosses retrieval policy with reader policy and reports their interaction. This factorial design can reveal whether an improvement transfers across memory engines or depends on a particular writer-reader pairing.

An evolving memory makes task order part of the treatment. Early episodes determine which procedures and mistakes enter the bank; later episodes determine whether those records are useful. A default dataset order may contain an implicit curriculum, grouping related tasks or increasing difficulty. Improvement along that sequence does not establish order-robust learning.

The fragility study reevaluates memory-based self-improving agents across multiple runs and shuffled orders, identifying substantial sensitivity to variance, order, and underspecification . Its findings apply to the tested methods and environments, not every possible self-improvement architecture. The methodological implication is strong: one cumulative curve under one order is insufficient evidence for a stable improvement mechanism.

Use several independently constructed memory trajectories for each experimental condition. Within a trajectory, tasks share an evolving bank and are dependent. Across trajectories, randomize order and model sampling as declared. If a common initial bank is used, treat its construction as another factor rather than assume it is representative. Report variation across banks and orders, not only average task accuracy pooled over all calls.

Curriculum effects can be studied directly. Compare random order, grouped order, reversed order, and an explicitly designed curriculum while holding the task multiset fixed. A curriculum that improves performance is a legitimate result if named as such. The error is presenting that conditional benefit as spontaneous general improvement. Also test new task families that do not share the procedures learned early in the sequence.

Underspecified tasks can contaminate memory with misleading lessons. If a failure arose from an ambiguous objective or unavailable tool, the agent may store an incorrect procedural correction. Later reuse then amplifies the original ambiguity. Memory construction should record failure attribution and uncertainty, and evaluations should distinguish environment failure from policy failure. Additional rubrics can improve specification while also giving the learner more supervision; that information difference belongs in the treatment description.

A persistent memory must cope with facts becoming false, permissions changing, and representations drifting. Static recall benchmarks cannot test these transitions. A useful longitudinal suite includes explicit corrections, contradictory sources of unequal authority, expired preferences, deletion requests, user separation, and model or embedding upgrades. The required behavior is not always to retain more: sometimes it is to stop using a previously useful record.

Define the validity interval of a fact separately from its observation timestamp. A record can remain historically true while becoming inapplicable to the current decision. Retrieval should expose this distinction, and the reader should not treat a recent ingestion time as evidence of recent event time. Inject delayed reports and backdated corrections to test whether the system confuses the two.

Deletion tests must follow derivatives. Raw events can generate summaries, embeddings, graph edges, skills, caches, and copied subagent context. Removing one row does not establish complete erasure. A test should enumerate the lineage, verify retrieval exclusion, and check whether reconstruction can reintroduce deleted content. Physical deletion, logical exclusion, and retention under restricted audit policy are different outcomes.

Migration changes memory meaning. A new embedding model can alter nearest neighbors; a new policy can interpret the same skill differently; a schema conversion can drop provenance or confidence. Compare pre- and post-migration behavior on held-out tasks and known conflict cases. A successful database migration does not establish behavioral compatibility. Retain the old representation where permitted so failures can be traced and rollback can be assessed.

Authorization is particularly sensitive to restored state. A checkpoint can contain a historical grant, but a resumed session must consult current authority. The experiment should revoke access while the task is paused and then resume from the old checkpoint. Measure whether the forbidden record remains in model-visible context and whether new effects are blocked. This tests context-memory-policy consistency rather than storage persistence alone.

Long tasks can be analyzed through time to a defined failure event. Let be the first step at which a required invariant is violated and the survival probability through horizon . The hazard at step is . Then under the corresponding discrete-time definitions. Here , , the empty product is one, and is defined only while . The identity does not assume a constant hazard.

This representation distinguishes cumulative exposure from worsening policy. A system with constant small per-step risk can have declining long-horizon success without becoming less competent at each step. Conversely, memory contamination or context loss can make the hazard increase over time. Stratify failures by cause and inspect their relationship to compaction, retrieval, updates, and interruptions. A single final completion rate cannot distinguish these explanations.

Censoring requires care. If a run ends because the budget expires before failure or completion, the censoring mechanism may depend on task difficulty. Standard survival estimators require assumptions about that dependence. Report budget exhaustion explicitly and avoid treating censored trajectories as successful survivors indefinitely. Competing events, such as authorization failure, evaluator outage, and task completion, may require cause-specific analysis rather than one undifferentiated stopping time.

In particular, successful completion removes a run from exposure to further task actions. To distinguish this event from failure, let be the first absorbing stopping time under the study protocol and its cause. For each cause , define while the risk set is nonempty. Then

Here the causes are mutually exclusive, , and is the cumulative incidence of that stopping cause. Treating completed tasks as ordinary independent censoring can instead estimate a hypothetical continued-exposure process. Faster completion and lower failure hazard are different interventions; report completion incidence, failure incidence, and unresolved budget stops separately. The identity is a probability decomposition, not a claim that a particular survival estimator is justified for the available logs.

Recovery changes the event definition. A transient tool failure that is correctly reconciled may not count as task failure, while an undetected duplicate effect may violate an invariant even if the final artifact looks correct. Declare whether the study measures first fault, unrecovered fault, constraint violation, or final failure. Each is useful, but they answer different operational questions.

Uncertainty should cluster by longitudinal unit, not by step. Thousands of steps from one evolving bank do not provide thousands of independent observations about population reliability. Report the number of independent users, sessions, task streams, and bank constructions. Where the data are limited, present the observed trajectories and conditional conclusions rather than fitting an elaborate hazard model whose parameters are weakly identified.

The evaluator needs a clock, task scheduler, environment-change injector, memory snapshotter, and artifact verifier. These components should be separate from the agent’s own tools. Otherwise the agent can observe future tasks, change the evaluation clock, or inspect outcomes intended only for grading. A simulated environment can provide controlled interventions, but its simplifications must be identified when generalizing to deployment.

For every memory operation, record writer identity, source event, model and harness version, record type, validity scope, permissions, and affected derivatives. Read operations should record candidate sets and selected evidence where feasible. This enables failure attribution: a missing fact, bad ranking, inappropriate influence, and stale authorization leave different traces. Privacy constraints may limit released content, but event structure and redaction policy can still be documented.

The baseline set should include no memory, raw-log retrieval, simple lexical or dense retrieval, curated factual records, procedural memory, and an oracle evidence condition. Match task streams and budgets, and include construction cost. A complex system should demonstrate benefit over a strong simple baseline, not only over an intentionally weak store. Report where simpler methods win and whether the difference survives shuffled orders.

The October 2026 audit of MemoryAgentBench’s conflict-resolution split supplies a more specific baseline: a frozen parser and last-write resolver that directly executes the benchmark’s newest-statement rule . The parser was developed on one fact list and held fixed on three others. The audit separates parser or path-composition residuals from items whose released answer is unreachable in its frozen parser’s final last-write graph. This operational classification does not itself prove that the released label is wrong: a fuller parser or a different grounding rule can change reachability. Its principal item-level model comparisons retain one scored outcome per item, without mechanism traces, and do not run learned or structured memory systems. Thus an apparent failure can reflect a label–rule conflict, rather than evidence that an agent failed selective forgetting; the audit does not establish how a particular memory mechanism reasons internally.

This case changes the experimental unit. Hundreds of questions sharing four fact lists do not constitute hundreds of independent histories. Answer-level uncertainty is conditional on those lists; generalization across history construction is limited by the small number of distinct streams. A proposed extension generates independent update streams from a versioned state machine, derives answers by replay, and verifies the gold graph independently of the agent’s parser. Include first-write, last-write, valid-time, and authority-aware resolvers as distinct baselines only where the task semantics warrant them. Blindly applying last-write order to real organizational evidence would be incorrect when a later source has lower authority or reports an earlier valid-time interval. Benchmark-rule correctness and deployment conflict semantics must remain separate.

HyperSkill’s sequential fixed-order evaluation, extra LLM maintenance calls, and gold-outcome main setting illustrate why these fields matter . Its structured memory mechanism is substantive, while concurrency, order robustness, and deployment feedback availability require additional evidence. Similarly, context-management results that retain raw offloaded history should not be interpreted as indefinite usable memory without testing retrieval and decision preservation .

The practical output is a trajectory-level evidence record that supports both mechanism analysis and operational decisions. It should show what the system retained, what it retrieved, how it used the evidence, what changed, and which constraints survived. This is a more demanding standard than a recall score, but it is necessary when memory is expected to influence long-running agents across users, tasks, and versions.

Consider a technical assistant supporting a software team over a sequence of repository tasks. Early sessions establish that one service uses a particular deployment command, that production changes require review, and that a diagnostic document belongs to a restricted project. Later sessions change the command, introduce an exception for a sandbox environment, revoke one user’s access, and ask an indirect question whose answer depends on the old experience. The test is not whether the assistant can repeat each fact. It is whether it uses the correct record, scope and authority when choosing an action.

Construct independent task streams from templates with controlled entity substitutions, dependency structures and change schedules. The substitutions prevent exact-string memorization from explaining transfer, while the dependency structure preserves the reasoning required. Separate streams should not share answer-bearing memory unless cross-user sharing is explicitly the treatment. The evaluator retains the authoritative event sequence and can query the environment, but the agent sees only observations available at each step.

Table lists interventions that distinguish the relevant mechanisms. Each row specifies what changes and what observation would diagnose the failure. The table is an experimental design, not a set of reported measurements.

The baseline conditions should preserve information and budget as carefully as possible. A direct-context oracle can consume more prompt space than a retrieval system, so reserve equivalent context capacity or report the difference. A full-history baseline can become infeasible at long horizons; report the horizon at which it ceases to fit rather than silently switching its truncation policy. A simple raw-log retriever provides an important control because it avoids extraction errors while retaining the same source evidence.

Writer and reader policies should be crossed. A high-quality writer paired with a weak reader may produce accurate records that are misapplied. A strong reader paired with an aggressive summarizer may never receive the decisive constraint. Crossing these components identifies interaction effects and prevents a memory engine from receiving credit for a better backbone. The experiment should also vary whether outcome feedback is gold, self-judged, delayed or unavailable. A method that relies on immediate correct labels has a different deployment requirement from one operating without them.

Task order needs independent replication. Generate several permutations of the same multiset and several independently sampled streams. The first comparison isolates curriculum effects conditional on the tasks; the second supports broader generalization. Preserve the entire evolving memory for each run so failures can be traced to prior updates. Reusing a bank built under one order across all conditions would remove an important source of variation and could favor methods compatible with that bank’s organization.

The primary outcomes include verified task completion, constraint adherence, temporal correctness, authorized evidence use and recovery after interruption. Intermediate outcomes include write coverage, retrieval of decisive records, correct rejection of obsolete records and calibrated influence. These outcomes should be linked rather than pooled indiscriminately. For example, a retrieval improvement with no action improvement can reveal a reader bottleneck; an action gain accompanied by unauthorized context use is not an acceptable solution to the stated task.

Negative controls are essential. Include tasks where the remembered deployment command is irrelevant, where the restricted document is unnecessary, and where the sandbox exception should not generalize. Otherwise an agent that always emits warnings or always retrieves every memory can receive undeserved credit. Measure over-application and under-application separately, as motivated by MemCalib, while retaining the end-to-end storage and retrieval components that its supplied-memory setting intentionally isolates.

Failure adjudication should use the event history and artifact state, not the agent’s explanation alone. A stored memory can claim that a tool failed because credentials were invalid when the actual cause was a temporary outage. If this explanation becomes a procedural rule, later tasks may avoid a useful tool unnecessarily. The evaluator should identify the original observation, the inferred lesson and the later consequence. This causal chain distinguishes bad experience attribution from simple forgetting.

Finally, report the maintenance workload as the bank grows. Track raw and derived storage, index updates, compaction, merge operations, deletion propagation and retrieval latency. A sublinear skill count does not imply bounded total memory if raw trajectories and subtask nodes continue to grow. Nor does a compact bank guarantee low decision cost if each query invokes extensive reasoning. The study should expose which resource grows with episodes, which is amortized across reuse, and which can be bounded only by discarding information. Those operating conditions determine whether a promising memory mechanism can support sustained agent execution.

The public HyperSkill implementation provides a concrete separation between the hypergraph core and the per-task provider interface . A reproduction should instrument both: the core determines candidate reachability and maintenance, while the provider determines when retrieval and ingestion occur relative to task execution. Logging only final skill counts would miss a provider that ingests outcome information too early. Logging only model context would miss a maintenance operation that changes the interpretation of later records. Attach task and memory-version identifiers to each operation so the two traces can be joined.

The implementation audit should also verify that the evaluator’s gold outcome is unavailable to deployment-style variants before they commit their own interpretation. A gold-feedback experiment is useful for estimating mechanism potential, but it should not be confused with a self-judged agent. When switching to self-judgment, measure the resulting memory-label errors and their downstream accumulation rather than reporting only final success. A modest immediate error rate can have a disproportionate longitudinal effect if the same mistaken lesson is reused repeatedly.

The fragility study’s published code and InMind’s released diagnostic resources offer additional primary anchors for this audit . Their existence improves inspectability but does not establish that the experiment described here has run. The appropriate next record is an immutable implementation revision, complete stream manifest and trace of the actual interventions. Until those observations exist, the proposed factorial and counterfactual tests remain a research design with explicit rejection criteria, not evidence of achieved lifelong reliability.

The inspected provider exposes provide_memory and take_in_memory; instrumentation at these boundaries can establish whether evidence was supplied before a decision or incorporated only after the task outcome.

Replaying logged actions under a changed memory policy does not by itself estimate that policy’s end-to-end performance. Once a changed context induces another action, the future tool results, environment and memory writes can diverge. Continuing to supply the original observations then evaluates a hybrid trajectory that neither policy would necessarily generate. The problem is particularly acute for recoverable effects: an original successful write cannot be assumed to exist after a counterfactual policy chose a read instead.

A frozen-prefix test can legitimately compare next-action distributions from the same recorded state, provided both contexts contain only information available at that boundary. This identifies local sensitivity, such as whether a revoked instruction changes a proposal, rather than full task success. A full counterfactual test must rerun the environment from a valid checkpoint or use a justified transition model, exposing model error and replay limits. Importance weighting requires logged behavior probabilities and support for the alternative actions; deterministic tool logs do not supply those conditions automatically. Thus paired prefix diagnostics, complete reruns and model-based counterfactuals should be reported as distinct evidence products rather than interchangeable forms of replay.
