The boundaries of exact verification differ between tokens, model calls, observations, and external effects.

Continuous batching admits and retires sequences between decode steps, reducing the waste of static batches with heterogeneous lengths. Prefill and decode can nevertheless interfere because they stress different resources and have different service times. Chunked prefill limits how much a long prompt delays interactive decode. Disaggregation places prefill and decode on different workers, trading interference against KV transfer, coordination, and potentially duplicated state.

For a request with prefill time , decode time , transfer time , and scheduling delays , disaggregation improves latency only if the reduction in interference and queueing exceeds and added coordination. It can improve throughput while worsening a short request’s latency. An experiment must compare offered load and quality, not merely the best isolated run on each architecture. SGLang’s structured execution and prefix-sharing design provides another implementation perspective on serving programs with related prompts .

Little’s law relates stable long-run averages: for average population , admitted throughput , and mean residence time under the corresponding boundary. It does not require exponential service, but it does require consistent accounting and a stable system. A more restrictive M/G/1 model with Poisson arrivals, identically distributed independent service times independent of those arrivals, finite , and first-come-first-served scheduling gives
The second moment makes service variability important. The model is a diagnostic approximation for isolated stages; continuous-batching GPU service does not literally satisfy its assumptions .

Retries can increase offered load precisely when service is degraded. If every attempt independently succeeds with probability and retries have no cap, expected attempts are . With a cap of attempts, the expected count is ; at the capped count is and an uncapped process never succeeds. These are counts, not latency formulas when attempt durations depend on outcomes. When timeouts depend on congestion, independence fails and the feedback can be worse: queueing causes timeouts, which cause retries, which increase queueing. Idempotency prevents duplicate effects but does not eliminate duplicate compute. Retry budgets, jitter, admission control, and reconciliation should be evaluated as part of the serving policy.

The experimental unit is a trace-defined session with declared model, tokenizer, harness, and memory behavior. Record input and output lengths, reused prefix, cache tier, context edits, tool waits, retries, and termination. Run both open-loop offered-load tests and closed-loop concurrency tests, because closed-loop clients reduce arrivals when latency increases and can hide overload. Separate cold starts, warm kernels, cold caches, warm prefixes, and resumed sessions on different replicas.

Report time to first token, inter-token latency, request completion, session completion, throughput, rejection, timeout, and failure. Provide p50, p95, and p99 where sample size supports them, with the number of observations and a clear treatment of censored requests. A percentile from completed requests alone can look better when the slowest requests fail. Include tool time and memory maintenance in task-level results even when engine-only timing is also reported.

The ablation sequence should isolate one mechanism at a time: no prefix reuse versus reuse, uniform versus hybrid allocation, cache offload disabled versus enabled, fixed versus adaptive speculative budget, and monolithic versus disaggregated execution. Hold the action-output quality criterion fixed. If an optimization changes context policy or truncates evidence, report that as a behavioral intervention rather than an invisible serving improvement.

A negative result is informative. Tiered caching may lose on low-reuse traffic; speculation may lose with weak acceptance; a larger batch may improve aggregate throughput while delaying critical tool actions; compressed KV may preserve average language quality while corrupting rare arguments. The deployment decision follows from the joint quality, latency, cost, and reliability envelope. Peak throughput is one coordinate of that envelope, not a sufficient description of an agent-serving system.

Deploying a new model endpoint does not by itself deploy a new agent system. The release also includes tokenizer and serialization rules, prompts, context transformations, memory schemas, embedding indexes, skills, tools, permissions, validators, and runtime behavior. A change can be compatible at the API level while incompatible at the level of meaning. A field that remains a string can change from an absolute path to a workspace-relative path; an old skill may then direct a valid call to the wrong location.
Define a release manifest

with versions for the model, tokenizer, decoder, context constructor, memory schema, index, harness, tools, authorization, and validators. The decoder reference binds sampling configuration and versioned constrained-decoding rules; actual per-call settings are retained alongside the model input when runtime-selectable. A comparison claiming fixed decoding holds that configuration fixed. Parsing, stopping, and retries remain part of the versioned harness. A session is pinned to a manifest or governed by an explicit migration rule. Compatibility is a predicate over configuration and retained state, not merely a comparison of version strings. It can require schema validation, representation conversion, regenerated embeddings, restored cache dependencies, reauthorized tools, and revalidation of procedures extracted under an older policy.

A deployment dependency graph has an edge when the interpretation or safety of component depends on the contract supplied by . Changing a tokenizer can invalidate token offsets, cache keys, and learned interface adapters. Changing an embedding model can invalidate nearest-neighbor comparability. Changing authorization can invalidate queued actions and retrieved procedural instructions. The affected closure is the set of reachable dependents. A release gate should examine that closure instead of treating each changed file as an independent patch.

This graph need not be acyclic in its full behavioral form. A policy writes memory that later conditions the policy; a verifier changes the training data that alters the executor. For deployment planning, use a versioned snapshot and a declared update order to break the operational cycle. Record which old artifacts can be read during transition and which new artifacts can be written. A system that writes new-schema records before all readers are compatible has introduced a mixed-version state that rollback may not be able to interpret.

Current framework documentation illustrates the need to distinguish persistence mechanisms. LangGraph’s October 2026 persistence documentation separates thread-scoped checkpointers from cross-thread stores and warns that in-memory implementations do not survive process restarts . Those documented roles do not establish an end-to-end durability guarantee. The application must select a persistent backend, define retention, verify recovery, and reconcile external effects independently.

A trace suitable for diagnosing an agent must connect a decision to the observations that conditioned it and to the effects it actually caused. A useful event envelope contains run, session, branch, model-call, tool-call, operation, and parent identifiers; timestamps with clock-domain information; the release manifest; context and memory versions; authorization decisions; result status; and links to evidence artifacts. Content may be redacted or retained separately, but the links must preserve the ability to distinguish absent evidence from inaccessible evidence.

Wall-clock order alone is insufficient in a distributed system. Two workers can observe different memory versions and log events with skewed clocks. Use causal identifiers and explicit read/write versions to reconstruct which state each worker consumed. A trace that records only the latest memory snapshot cannot establish whether a stale record influenced an earlier action. Similarly, a final tool success log cannot reveal whether the model first attempted several invalid operations that were blocked by policy.

Separate four event states: proposed, authorized, submitted, and reconciled. Proposed means the model or deterministic planner produced an action. Authorized means a policy accepted the operation under a specific authority epoch. Submitted means the request crossed the execution boundary. Reconciled means the system has evidence about the external outcome. A timeout between submission and reconciliation must remain an unknown outcome, rather than being relabeled as failure and retried blindly.

Monitoring every prompt verbatim is neither necessary nor sufficient for observability. Raw content can contain credentials, personal information, proprietary documents, or malicious instructions. A design can retain hashes, typed state transitions, retrieval identifiers, and separately protected evidence while exposing only the minimum content needed for diagnosis. Redaction must preserve semantic distinctions important to a failure: removing every destination string, for example, can make an authorization bug impossible to reconstruct. The retention policy therefore belongs in the threat and debugging model rather than being an afterthought.

Sampling also changes what can be inferred. If traces are sampled only for successful requests, incident analysis will miss failure paths. If rare violations are oversampled for diagnosis, their raw frequency in the sample is not a deployment rate. Record selection probabilities or maintain a separate denominator stream so that operational metrics can be interpreted correctly. A dashboard without a defined observation process can produce precise-looking but misleading numbers.

A canary compares a new release with a baseline on a declared traffic population. For stateless requests, random assignment can often occur per request. For agents with persistent memory, assignment should usually occur at a level that prevents state contamination, such as user, repository, or session lineage. Switching versions turn by turn can make the new policy read memories written by the old policy and vice versa, confounding both treatment and safety interpretation.

Let denote treatment assignment for independent cluster , and its outcome under release . The estimand can be mean task success, violation probability, completion time, or a vector of operational metrics. A release decision should specify acceptable changes before reading the results. A quality improvement cannot automatically compensate for an authorization regression. Delayed outcomes require waiting or explicitly handling censoring; early completion rates can favor the release that abandons difficult tasks quickly.

Shared retrieval indexes create interference even when sessions are assigned independently. If canary runs write new procedures into a global skill bank that baseline runs can retrieve, the baseline has been treated indirectly. Possible designs include isolated memory namespaces, frozen read-only shared evidence with separate write stores, or cluster-level assignment that includes the shared state. Each has a different cost and external-validity tradeoff. The experimental report must state which information crossed treatment boundaries.

Sequential monitoring creates repeated looks at the same data. Declaring success as soon as any metric crosses a conventional threshold inflates false positives. Use a predeclared stopping rule, a valid sequential procedure, or a fixed observation window appropriate to the estimand. Operational emergency stops are different: a serious violation can justify containment without first establishing statistical superiority or inferiority. The corresponding incident should be retained in the comparison rather than erased by restarting the experiment.

A proposed canary design uses four arms: baseline policy with baseline memory, new policy with baseline memory, new policy with migrated memory, and new policy with an isolated empty derived bank but the same raw evidence access. The first pair estimates a policy intervention at fixed retained state; the second and third isolate migration under the new policy; the third and fourth assess dependence on inherited derived state. These are conditional contrasts within the specified configurations, not a complete decomposition of all interactions. If the new policy cannot consume the baseline representation, that arm requires a declared compatibility adapter or controlled replay and cannot isolate a pure policy effect. No outcome is asserted. Additional cross-pairings can diagnose incompatibility, while real-effect exposure requires the corresponding operating authority and isolation.

Rollback restores a prior software or logical state. Compensation attempts to counteract an external effect using another operation. Neither necessarily reconstructs the world that existed before the original action. Deleting a published object may not undo its disclosure; reversing a financial transaction may not remove fees or downstream actions; restoring a database snapshot can erase legitimate concurrent writes. An agent runtime must classify which effects are reversible, compensatable, or irreversible under the actual service contract.

Consider a hypothetical enterprise agent that prepares a report, uploads it, then records the uploaded identifier in memory. The service accepts an idempotency key. The following failure sequence is possible:

The correct recovery cannot be inferred from a natural-language summary that says upload failed. It requires operation identity and reconciliation semantics. If the service lacks idempotency and lookup, a global exactly-once claim is unsupported. The application may need conservative escalation, an outbox pattern with a specialized delivery service, or a bounded duplicate-risk policy. These are explicit changes to the operating contract.

Idempotency is a scoped service property. The same logical operation must retain its identity across retries, and reuse of an identifier with different arguments must follow a declared conflict rule. Deduplication retention, namespace, concurrent submission and crash behavior determine how long the protection holds. Expiry of a deduplication record can make an old delayed retry appear new. HTTP’s idempotent-method semantics concern the intended effect of repeated identical requests, not a universal exactly-once execution or identical-response promise . A client therefore needs the actual application’s operation contract before retrying a non-idempotent effect. A local outbox can durably retain intent while delivery remains repeated; the receiving service still determines whether those deliveries become duplicate effects.

Memory rollback must preserve authority monotonicity. Suppose a credential was revoked after a checkpoint. Restoring that checkpoint must not restore the old credential’s authority. Revocation information should be applied from an authoritative current source even when task state is rolled back. The same principle applies to deletion tombstones and legal retention boundaries: an old backup is not permission to resurrect information for use. Recovery is a compatibility-preserving reconstruction under current authority, not unconditional time travel.

The three contracts in Chapter apply at different points in this reconstruction. A byte-faithful checkpoint may preserve old proposal conditioning while violating current authority. A permission-filtered restoration may preserve authority while changing proposal probabilities. Reconciliation may legitimately update an unknown effect status after obtaining new service evidence; that update must be distinguished from the preceding representation-only restoration. The recovery trace should therefore record restoration, current-authority filtering, and external reconciliation as separate typed transitions. Testing only equality with the old snapshot would reward the wrong behavior after revocation.
For a rollback from to , the required condition is not simply that old code starts. There must be an admissible conversion such that

while external effects and current authorization remain reconciled. A lossy forward migration may have no inverse. The release procedure must then retain a recoverable representation or declare the rollback boundary before deployment. Pretending every schema migration is reversible converts a known design limitation into an incident.
Figure isolates the mechanism and its stated information boundaries.

Recovery retains operation identity and distinguishes submission from commitment evidence. A missing receipt does not prove absence. Only the service contract can justify a confirmed effect or a final negative outcome; otherwise the ledger stays unresolved. Configuration rollback does not reverse an external effect.

Agent failures include model errors, invalid tool calls, stale observations, context loss, memory poisoning, authorization mistakes, service outages, evaluator failures, and infrastructure faults. The same outward symptom can have several causes. A missing artifact may result from no attempted write, a permission rejection, a transport failure, a successful write in the wrong workspace, or a stale listing. Diagnosis should use discriminating observations rather than repeatedly asking the model to try harder.

A recovery policy is a decision rule over failure evidence and remaining budget. Let be a recovery action with expected task value , expected resource cost , and specified risk . Define the admissible set
where excludes actions without current authority or required state, and is a declared risk limit in the units of . For a nonempty finite set and , one possible decision rule is

The coefficient converts resource cost to the utility units of ; ties require a declared selection rule. For general infinite action sets, attainment needs additional assumptions. An empty admissible set means that this optimization supplies no recovery action; cancellation or escalation is available only if separately admissible. Estimated values and risks remain uncertain. Conservative policies can prefer reconciliation when effect status is unknown. A retry count is not a substitute for a recovery model, because repeated identical attempts can be positively correlated and can worsen overload.

Budget exhaustion should produce a typed terminal state. Distinguish completed, failed, cancelled, waiting for external input, and outcome unknown. A model-generated success statement does not override the runtime’s effect ledger. Conversely, a timed-out worker may have produced a valid artifact that can be recovered and verified. The termination protocol should specify which partial outputs are retained, who may resume them, and whether their authority or evidence has expired.

Bounded local recovery does not imply bounded external resolution. A timeout cannot by itself distinguish a failed remote service from a delayed one. If receipts remain unavailable, the runtime can stop spending its local budget and durably return an unresolved outcome, but cannot manufacture evidence that the effect is absent. An eventual-resolution claim requires explicit assumptions about service recovery, message delivery, identity retention and continued reconciliation access. Test those premises separately from restart success. In particular, expiring credentials can make a previously available status query inadmissible; escalation must then obtain current authority rather than replay the old grant.

Failure injection tests these claims directly. Crash immediately before submission, after submission, after remote commit, after local reconciliation, and during derived-memory updates. Introduce delayed duplicate responses, stale index replicas, broken validators, schema changes, and worker partitions. Check invariants about duplicate effects, unauthorized operations, lost writes, and eventual terminal state. These tests should run against controlled fixtures or isolated services; a successful test supports the tested contract, not an unrestricted guarantee.

The proposed instrumentation should record recovery-induced changes in the policy distribution. Offloading a failed tool output, replacing a summary, or retrieving a different skill can change the model’s next decision. A recovery that eventually succeeds may have introduced a hidden regression in a rare constraint. Evaluate the complete recovered trajectory rather than treating recovery as an infrastructure event independent of cognition.

An operational objective needs a denominator, boundary, and observation window. Examples include the fraction of admitted tasks that complete under the specified verifier and deadline, the probability of a duplicate external effect per submitted operation, and the time from a detected compatibility failure to containment. Aggregate availability can hide a system that responds quickly but returns unusable artifacts. Report task success and effect correctness separately from endpoint availability.

Mean recovery time is sensitive to incident definition and censoring. A system that labels unresolved incidents as abandoned can appear faster. Time-to-recovery distributions should retain unresolved cases and distinguish restoration of service from reconciliation of residual effects. The latter may continue after the model endpoint is healthy. Cost accounting should include repeated model calls, tool requests, memory repair, reindexing, and human intervention according to the declared boundary.

Incident learning creates another feedback channel. A failure trace can reveal a benchmark answer, a confidential record, or an attacker payload. Automatically adding the trace to a shared memory or training corpus can contaminate future evaluation or persist the attack. Curate incident-derived records with provenance, scope, authorization, and a statement of the tested lesson. Preserve the raw restricted evidence separately when needed for audit. A procedure extracted from one incident should identify the conditions that made it appropriate.

The AgentOps research proposal provides a vocabulary for observing and optimizing agent systems, but its historical publication date and conceptual role must be distinguished from current 2026 platform capabilities . Current SDK and managed-agent documentation can establish available tracing, state, and recovery interfaces; they do not independently establish reliability in a particular workload . An operational assurance claim requires evidence from that workload and the actual release manifest.

A defensible deployment sequence begins by freezing the candidate manifest and enumerating its dependency closure. Validate state migrations and authority handling in an isolated replay environment. Run deterministic contract tests and stochastic task evaluations with matched baselines. Include long histories, memory conflicts, interrupted sessions, concurrent writers, tool schema drift, and previously observed incidents. Record both improvements and regressions rather than selecting a favorable subset of tasks.

Next, deploy to an isolated canary population with declared state-sharing rules and stopping criteria. Monitor task outcomes, constraint violations, latency distributions, resource consumption, and unknown external effects. A rollback rehearsal must demonstrate that the retained state can actually be read by the previous release or converted safely. Rehearsing only a container restart does not test restoration of policy-compatible memory.

Let be the frozen candidate manifest and its dependency graph. If contains the changed components, the affected closure is , explicitly including the changed components themselves. Define Boolean migration, current-authority, and deletion predicates , , and . For initial retained state and authority epoch ,

The operator runs the isolated regression and fault tests; retains every outcome and known limit. The marker means that failed preconditions prevented this test stage. The predeclared release predicate does not inspect a selected favorable subset. The manifest, closure, predicate outcomes, results, and limits are appended to the release journal before any canary decision.

Only when is the candidate eligible for an isolated canary assignment . A migration predicate does not execute a migration: the canary initializer must construct and check the compatibility relation before admission. Here is the tested conversion into the candidate’s isolated state namespace; failure prevents admission. Let be the canary transition kernel and the observations available to monitoring by time . A predeclared adapted stopping rule defines

The convention leaves monitoring incomplete rather than inventing a terminal outcome. The reconciliation operator uses external-service evidence to update the release-relevant effect ledger , including relevant production and canary operation identities; unsuccessful reconciliation preserves uncertainty. The kernel’s namespace isolation and the stopping rule’s information restrictions are implementation obligations, not properties established by their notation.

At a finite stopping time, let denote the recorded decision to roll back, hold, or promote, and let be the rollback target. Obtain a fresh production snapshot , containing its manifest, retained state, and concurrency version. With separately checked guards and , the admissible transition request is

The guards require current authority, deletion compliance, and reconciled effect status acceptable under the declared transition contract. The maps and are declared retained-state conversions with compatible outputs, respectively and . The rollback conversion follows Section ; a target that starts but cannot interpret the state is inadmissible. These guards inspect production state, not the isolated canary snapshot.

The request neither migrates state nor activates a manifest. Its implementation must revalidate the production concurrency version, authority epoch, effect-ledger freshness, and transition guards when committing the state conversion and manifest activation. A changed precondition requires a hold and renewed validation. Atomicity within the deployment state store does not supply atomicity for external services. Failed admission, incomplete monitoring, or a rejected request supplies no promotion. The equations specify evidence order and admissibility, not a guarantee that a named deployment platform satisfies the contract.

The procedure is an original implementation contract, not a claim that any named product performs these steps automatically. Its purpose is to make deployment assertions testable. A system can expose excellent components and still fail at their boundaries. Monitoring, rollback, and recovery become part of agent intelligence when they determine what the policy knows, which effects are possible, and whether learned state remains meaningful after change.

A component-level improvement can disappear when composed with the rest of an agent. A retriever can return more relevant material while increasing prompt length enough to force a harmful compaction. A model can generate more valid tool calls while increasing the fraction that target stale objects. A faster serving backend can change which parallel branch finishes first and therefore which artifact a selector adopts. Cross-layer analysis asks whether the composed system preserves the assumptions under which each mechanism was evaluated.

The cases in this chapter are worked analytical designs, not reported deployments or newly measured experiments. They combine mechanisms examined in earlier chapters into explicit state transitions, resource calculations, and falsification tests. Each case specifies the observation and authority boundaries, the information that must persist, the role of model inference, and the evidence required before an external effect or scientific conclusion is accepted. Their purpose is to make interaction failures concrete.

Let a workflow be a directed graph whose vertices are model decisions, retrievals, tool operations, state commits, or verification steps. Edges represent causal prerequisites, not merely visual order. Each vertex has an execution contract , resource cost , duration , and possible failure events . The global task requirement follows from local contracts only if the contracts include all relevant coupling conditions:

A collection of passing local tests does not establish the antecedent if omits state-version consistency, authority, or external effects. This is the formal reason that integration testing cannot be replaced by component leaderboards.

If violation of implies at least one enumerated failure event, a union bound gives . Independence is not required. The premise is strong: unenumerated failure modes and invalid coupling assumptions destroy the guarantee. Multiplying apparent component accuracies is even less defensible when all components rely on the same model-generated interpretation. Shared uncertainty does not become independent evidence because it passes through several boxes.

Consider an agent asked to repair a regression in an unfamiliar repository and return a tested patch. The environment is a pinned checkout with isolated dependencies and a protected evaluator. The model may inspect files, search code, edit permitted paths, and run tests. It may not modify the protected evaluator, fetch hidden answers, or publish changes externally. This is an evaluation contract: whether a real benchmark enforces all these restrictions must be checked separately. SWE-agent and SWE-bench supply concrete historical interfaces and task structures, while the harder SWE-bench Pro material motivates examining repository diversity and contamination .

The privileged run state contains the repository commit, dependency-image digest, writable path set, tool schemas, remaining budget, and test-result identities. Working context contains the issue, relevant source excerpts, the current hypothesis, and selected tool evidence. Persistent procedural memory may supply a debugging strategy, but it cannot supply a hidden patch or override writable-path restrictions. A skill retrieved because it solved a similar error must be rechecked against the current repository and test environment.

Suppose the agent observes a failing parser test, inspects the parser and its callers, and proposes changing a branch condition. The decisive evidence is not the model’s statement that the change is safe. A useful sequence is to preserve the pre-change failure, apply a minimal patch, run the targeted test, then run relevant regression tests under the same dependency image. If a dependency update is also made, its effect must be separated from the code change. Otherwise the experiment has changed two causal variables and cannot identify which one repaired the failure.

Context compaction can introduce a specific failure. The original issue says that an error must be raised before any output file is created. A summary preserves the expected error message but drops the ordering requirement. The agent produces a patch that raises the error after creating an empty file. A string-based test passes, while the specified side-effect condition fails. The appropriate counterexample test checks both the exception and the absence of the file. This case distinguishes answer retention, requirement retention, and behavioral verification.

A stored procedural lesson should therefore say more than check the error message. It should identify the applicability condition, the ordering requirement, and the test that distinguishes the correct implementation from a plausible shortcut. If later tasks use a different output contract, the lesson’s preconditions prevent indiscriminate reuse. The memory record should retain its source trajectory and verifier scope, so a later failure can invalidate the procedure without erasing unrelated debugging knowledge.

An evaluation of the complete design would compare no procedural memory, unstructured reflections, typed procedures, and retrieval with applicability checks. Keep the model, repository set, token and tool budgets, and grading access fixed. Randomize task order if memory evolves, and include held-out repositories. Record successful repairs, incorrect accepted patches, invalid edits, tool failures, and complete cost. This is a proposed experiment; the case supplies no fabricated outcome.

A contemporary reported case demonstrates the difference between tested and architectural contracts. Terminal-RSI’s revised Rust–C evaluator case passes protected wrapper and output-equivalence checks in its final trials, yet one trial delegates expression evaluation to Python despite producing a statically linked Rust executable. The authors explicitly separate these observations from proof of the requested native evaluation path or memory safety . This is author-reported trajectory evidence, not a reproduction here. It shows why an output oracle and an implementation requirement need separate witnesses: successful observable behavior does not entail that the specified internal mechanism produced it.

Now allow four isolated workers to investigate different hypotheses. They share a read-only task prefix but have independent writable worktrees. A coordinator receives evidence and candidate patches rather than raw unbounded histories. The meaningful comparison is not simply four agents versus one. Compare against a single agent with the same total budget and four independent samples without communication. Otherwise gains from additional search can be misattributed to coordination.

A precise resource example uses the hypothetical homogeneous model from Chapter , with 128 KiB of KV state per retained token. Suppose each worker uses a common 32,768-token prefix followed by a private 8,192-token continuation. Without sharing, four sequences retain 163,840 token positions, consuming 20 GiB of KV state. With exact read-only prefix sharing and private suffix pages, the unique retained positions are , consuming 8 GiB before overhead. The 12-GiB difference is calculated storage sharing, not a measured speedup or a guarantee that an engine implements it.

Sharing is valid only while the common prefix computation remains compatible. If one worker’s context constructor rewrites an early shared observation, its dependent state must diverge. Copy-on-write protects other workers’ pages but does not make the edited worker’s old suffix valid. A coordinator that changes the common instruction midway through execution creates another compatibility boundary; workers must receive a versioned update or remain explicitly pinned to the old task state.

The wall-clock lower bound is the duration of the longest dependency path, while total resource consumption sums work across branches. A slow branch may contain the only evidence that exposes a constraint violation. Cancelling it solely because another branch produced a plausible patch trades latency against coverage. The selector should know which checks remain incomplete and whether its chosen candidate was examined by an independent validator. A vote among models that all missed the same requirement is not independent verification.

Selection also changes the outcome distribution. Let indicate that worker has produced an eligible candidate, its completion time, and a true contract violation by that candidate. Conditional on at least one eligible candidate, define with a fixed tie rule. Then

This identity does not allow the conditional risk to be replaced by each worker’s marginal risk. Fast shortcuts, early termination, and validation cost can correlate quality with selection. A serving change that changes completion order can therefore change the delivered-artifact distribution even when every worker’s policy is fixed. Compare selectors on identical saved candidate sets when isolating selection, and compare full executions when measuring the deployed system. Cancelled branches have unobserved counterfactual completions; counting them as successful or failed would invent outcomes.

The final merge is a separate operation. Two individually passing patches can conflict or invalidate each other’s assumptions. Preserve each branch’s base commit and diff, merge in an isolated worktree, and rerun integration checks on the merged artifact. If the coordinator adopts only one patch, it should retain the rejected branches’ relevant counterevidence. Discarding all unsuccessful trajectories can create a memory bank that remembers only apparent successes and loses the information needed to avoid repeating failed hypotheses.

Consider a system that answers questions and prepares reports from a changing collection of internal records. It has multiple sessions per user, shared organizational evidence, role-dependent permissions, and a persistent memory of prior work. Its central problem is not simply document retrieval. The same claim can be true at one time, superseded later, restricted to one audience, or derived from a source whose access has been revoked.
Use a typed assertion record

where identifies the subject, the proposition, the fields its asserted validity interval, the recording time, the evidence source, its access scope, and its derivation lineage. Valid time and record time differ: a correction recorded today can say that yesterday’s claim was wrong. A retrieval system that sorts only by ingestion time can answer a historical question incorrectly, while one that ignores corrections can repeat superseded information.

The answer pipeline first determines the question’s temporal and authority scope, then retrieves permitted source records, resolves relevant conflicts, constructs working context, generates an attributed answer, and verifies citations and requested output constraints. Derived memory may accelerate this process, but raw evidence remains necessary for contested or high-consequence claims. A retrieved summary is a claim about evidence, not a replacement for the evidence’s provenance.

The following constructed sequence exposes a cross-session failure. Session A reads that a project owner is Maya and stores a semantic memory. Later an authoritative update names Ravi, and a deletion policy removes the old personnel record from active use. Session B retrieves an old summary that still names Maya. A semantically similar answer can be fluent and well cited to an obsolete derived artifact. Correct handling requires propagation of the update or revocation through summaries, indexes, caches, and procedural assumptions, together with an access-time validity check.

This is not solved by globally replacing every occurrence of Maya. The name may be correct in historical reports or unrelated projects. Deletion and correction semantics need subject and lineage identity. A tombstone can block future reads while physical cleanup proceeds, but the system should state whether backups, cached prompts, and downstream artifacts remain. A restored old checkpoint must not erase the authoritative revocation epoch. Chapter explains why rollback and authority restoration must be separated.

A memory can be retrieved and still have no appropriate effect on behavior. Suppose a user’s prior instruction says that externally shared reports must omit a confidential appendix. A later request asks for a concise project update without explicitly mentioning confidentiality. A memory test that asks what the confidentiality instruction was measures explicit recall. The operational test asks whether the agent applies it when preparing the report. InMind’s distinction between explicit recall and implicit application motivates this separation, while memory-writing and consolidation systems such as RecMem address different parts of the lifecycle .

An influence experiment can intervene on a memory while holding the current task and evidence fixed. Compare a valid relevant instruction, an irrelevant record, a superseded instruction, and an adversarially injected instruction. The desired policy responds differently to these cases. Measuring only whether any memory was used rewards over-influence. Measuring only answer accuracy can hide an unauthorized disclosure that does not affect the nominal answer key.

The evaluation unit should be a user or organizational task stream with declared persistence. Freeze the post-history memory before testing explicit recall and implicit application so that the first test does not teach the answer to the second. Randomize task order or use independent cloned states. Preserve the exact accessible evidence and authority epoch. These controls distinguish a useful memory mechanism from leakage through the evaluation conversation.

The deployment architecture also needs a correction path. When a user disputes an answer, the system should identify whether the error came from source truth, retrieval, conflict resolution, context packing, model interpretation, or output attribution. Updating the answer text alone may leave the faulty derived memory intact. A correction should invalidate the appropriate descendants and record the reason, while avoiding a global overwrite that destroys legitimate historical information.

The research agent performs experiments in a sandbox and proposes changes to its own harness. The mutable objects include prompt templates, search strategy, context management, memory access, and tool orchestration. The evaluator contains protected tasks and graders. The candidate may inspect its search evidence but not final evaluation artifacts. This configuration resembles the bounded mechanisms studied by RRSI, Harness2, and AIDE2, with important differences in feedback and update targets .

Separate three artifact classes: the executor under test, the improver that proposes and selects changes, and the measurement system that scores them. Store immutable snapshots of all three at each accepted update. A proposal that changes a test must be classified as a measurement intervention, not quietly accepted as an executor improvement. A discovered evaluator bug can be real and worth repairing, but results before and after the repair need a consistent rescoring policy.

Suppose the current agent repeatedly overflows context and drops experiment configurations. A candidate harness offloads raw logs and retains a typed experiment record containing hypothesis, code revision, data split, random seed, metric definition, and result artifact. This may preserve scientific continuity with fewer active tokens. Its success should be tested on tasks where a later decision requires an earlier configuration, including changed metrics and failed runs. A summary that retains only the best score can create selection bias even if its memory use is efficient.

The candidate should be evaluated against a fixed-summary baseline, raw-log retrieval, and a no-change harness under matched total resources. Include the cost of creating and maintaining the structured records. If the candidate receives a stronger external critic, that critic’s contribution must be separated. If the improver selects among many candidates, the final held-out evaluation should be independent of the selection stream. The relevant claim is transferable state management, not the ability to search longer on the same tasks.

The protected-evaluator design here should not be imputed to every cited method. Harness2 uses execution contrasts and model judgment for its task-level edits rather than ground-truth verifier access; its limitation section explicitly allows shared model bias and failed transfer . When repeated promotion reuses a benchmark, REUSE instead proves an admission guarantee under restricted decision-only feedback and an independent initial sample . Revealing raw protected traces to the proposer violates that particular information restriction. Independent confirmation, adaptive reuse, and proxy-guided editing are distinct experimental contracts.

Now consider model post-training on the collected trajectories. If the retained record exposes information that the behavior policy did not see at a prior decision, training on a naively flattened history can change the conditioning problem. MemoryWalker identifies exact and approximate ways to address compaction-induced inconsistencies . The research system must record transform lineage and behavior inputs during collection; a later attempt to reconstruct them from a final summary may be impossible. The same memory design that helps execution can therefore create invalid training data if its information boundaries are ignored.

Across the three cases, an accepted artifact should be associated with a claim record containing the objective, applicable population, configuration, intervention, baseline, evidence, resource boundary, failure observations, and limits. This is not a generic success label. A passing patch, a grounded report, and an evolved harness require different validators, but each needs a trace from the delivered artifact to the evidence that supports it.

The interventions are narrow enough to falsify mechanism explanations. They also expose where an observed improvement is underdetermined. If a structured-memory system changes storage, retrieval, prompting, and maintenance simultaneously, an end-to-end gain does not identify which component caused it. Factorial ablations or staged replacements can locate the contribution, while a complete system comparison remains useful for deployment decisions. Mechanistic attribution and engineering utility are different questions.

Cross-layer work should report the simplest baseline that survives these tests. An event log plus deterministic metadata can outperform an elaborate reflective memory on tasks dominated by exact state. A reactive policy with a strong tool interface can outperform search when observations are reliable and actions cheap. A single agent can outperform a team when coordination consumes the available context and latency budget. These are conditional possibilities to test, not universal rankings. The value of the system formulation is that it makes those conditions visible and turns a broad claim about autonomy into a set of specific, reviewable technical propositions.
Figure isolates the mechanism and its stated information boundaries.

The constructed workflows require different witnesses: protected behavior checks, source-level review, or held-out evaluation. Each claim record binds the delivered artifact to its versioned state, current authority and actual witness scope. A passing local check does not certify the complete workflow.

The evidence supports a system-level account of agent competence. Model architecture and training determine a conditional policy, but context construction, tools, memory, runtime, and evaluation determine which policy is actually executed and which outcomes are credited. This is not an argument that model quality is secondary. It is an identification statement: when several layers change together, an outcome difference cannot be attributed to the model or to a named memory mechanism without additional controls.

The current frontier also changes which implementation assumptions are reasonable. FlashAttention-4, current hybrid cache managers, and low-precision architectures make hardware and model layout part of any performance claim. V-JEPA 2.1 and contemporary world-model work sharpen representation questions but do not collapse predictive quality into control validity. Context Language Models, MemoryWalker, RecMem, InMind, HyperSkill, and 2026 compaction studies expose different failure points in retained state: writing, consolidation, access, implicit relevance, influence, conditioning, and lifecycle maintenance. A survey that treats them all as larger memory misses the distinctions needed to design experiments .

The strongest practical conclusion is conditional. Reliable execution requires that decision-relevant evidence, procedural applicability, authorization, and effect status remain interpretable across the system’s state transitions. Longer windows and larger stores can help, but neither establishes those properties. A persistent archive can coexist with failed retrieval. Correct retrieval can coexist with inappropriate influence. A valid procedure can coexist with revoked authority. An authorized call can coexist with an unknown external outcome. Each transition needs its own evidence.

No single benchmark or finite improvement trajectory establishes unrestricted AGI. Generality remains a profile over declared task families, resources, adaptation, and risk. Recursive self-improvement remains a set of bounded mechanisms whose executor gains, improver gains, and evaluator dependence must be separated. Negative evidence, including task-order sensitivity, evaluator false acceptance, and limited transfer, is part of the scientific account rather than an inconvenience to remove from an aggregate score.

Fixed-policy interface changes and learning across interfaces also answer different questions. Harness decision geometry separates an interface’s regularized optimum from the deployed policy’s mismatch under finite-state assumptions; the coding experiments use a teacher proxy rather than access to the true optimum. Harness Scaling instead tests training across structured harness combinations and held-out compositions . Together they motivate measuring compatibility and adaptation separately. Neither a mismatch decomposition nor successful transfer among sampled interfaces establishes robustness to arbitrary future tool semantics, memory transformations, or authority changes.

A central research target is to minimize retained computation while preserving decisions that matter. The wrong objective is an unqualified maximize recall: some records should expire, some should never influence a given user, and some are irrelevant to the current task. The testable target is a constrained tradeoff between useful information, authority, cost, and loss.

Let be a memory/context mechanism, a declared task-stream distribution, its complete cost, and a vector of task and constraint losses. Let contain mechanisms satisfying the declared access and lifecycle constraints. Their feasible set is

The Pareto frontier is the nondominated subset of : no other feasible point has no greater cost and no greater loss on every coordinate, with a strict improvement on at least one coordinate. Empirical dominance requires uncertainty to be assessed jointly rather than inferred from favorable point estimates alone. A method that saves tokens while increasing violations is not unconditionally more efficient. A method that retains everything but requires unaffordable reconstruction is not a useful memory optimum.

One discriminating experiment uses paired histories that differ in a rare action-changing qualifier. Examples include a revoked permission, a temporal exception, a requirement about side-effect ordering, or a procedure valid only under one tool version. Compare raw history, fixed summarization, selective retrieval, typed memory, and learned editing at matched complete budgets. Hold the downstream policy fixed initially, then repeat after a controlled policy update. The estimands are the action-distribution change, constraint loss, task utility, and cost, not only a recall score.

The competing explanations are explicit. If a method succeeds only when the qualifier is repeated in the current prompt, it has not solved persistent retrieval or implicit relevance. If it retrieves the qualifier but fails to act on it, access is not the bottleneck. If it applies obsolete qualifiers, influence calibration or temporal validity is wrong. If success disappears after changing the model while retaining the same memory bank, the representation may encode policy-specific workarounds. These outcomes identify different next interventions.

An improved benchmark should expose the same latent facts through several surface forms and several future decision contexts. It should include irrelevant and contradictory memories, not only supportive ones. Evaluation queries must not update the frozen memory used by subsequent paired tests. The unit of uncertainty should include independent histories and task streams. This design can falsify broad claims of memory usefulness while preserving the cases in which a simple store or raw log is sufficient.

Context editing, memory maintenance, and policy training can create incompatible conditional distributions. The failure is structural: an action generated under one information set is later trained as though it had been generated under another. Better final-answer supervision does not restore the missing behavior history. MemoryWalker supplies concrete exact and approximate corrections, while the broader system question is how to retain the evidence required to apply or validate those corrections .

A falsifiable hypothesis is that recording and respecting transform lineage improves deployment behavior after compaction beyond what can be explained by additional training compute. Test exact rollout-history conditioning where feasible, a naive flattened reconstruction, and an approximation with matched update budgets. Include a no-compaction control, vary the number and location of edits, and measure behavior log-probability diagnostics alongside held-out task outcomes. An approximation should not be called equivalent merely because its average reward is close on one suite.

Joint updates require another factorial test. Train or evolve context policies and memory banks separately and together, then evaluate all cross-pairings with frozen policy checkpoints. Estimate interaction terms and migration failures under independent task streams. If joint gains disappear when component combinations are crossed, the system may have learned a useful but narrow compatibility relation. That is valuable engineering evidence, but it differs from a portable improvement to memory or reasoning.

Frozen cross-pairings measure compatibility of the resulting artifacts. They do not by themselves identify the causal benefit of joint training: separately trained checkpoints can differ in task exposure, optimization, or selection. That claim requires controlled training interventions with matched resources and independent training runs, followed by the same protected evaluation. More test trajectories for one trained checkpoint reduce evaluation uncertainty but do not create additional independent training runs.

Compatibility validation also has a resource constraint. Let be the amount of new compatibility work introduced by releases and derived-state changes during interval , and the work actually validated. A simple backlog identity is

If long-run required work exceeds validation capacity and no sound compositional shortcut is available, unresolved compatibility obligations accumulate. This is an accounting deduction, not a stochastic performance theorem. Possible responses include slower promotion, version-pinned sessions, narrower update scopes, or stronger contracts that reduce what must be retested. Silently assuming that old memories remain valid does not remove the obligation.

The research opportunity is to discover contracts that are both checkable and behaviorally meaningful. Syntactic schemas are easy to validate but weak about semantics. Full behavioral equivalence is generally intractable for open-ended stochastic agents. Intermediate invariants, such as provenance preservation, authority monotonicity, exact cache dependency identity, and restricted procedure applicability, can reduce risk without pretending to solve all semantic compatibility.

Agent progress depends heavily on the quality of evaluators. A verifier can miss a requirement, reward a shortcut, crash selectively, or share the executor’s mistaken interpretation. Increasing the number of judges does not guarantee independent evidence. The research target is to quantify the conditions under which a verifier’s acceptance predicts the intended outcome and to detect when those conditions change.

TestJack’s adversarial auditing and AgentHorizon-style evaluator inspection motivate a useful separation between an artifact’s tested behavior, specification interpretation, and grading implementation . A witness test that fails a candidate and passes a reference is evidence of a difference; whether that difference violates the task still depends on the requirement. Reference agreement alone is not a complete oracle.

A discriminating verifier experiment inserts known fault classes into artifacts while preserving plausible surface quality. Vary the fault’s visibility, execution path, and relationship to the written specification. Compare deterministic checks, model judges, adversarial test generation, and combinations. Report false acceptance, false rejection, abstention, cost, and fault-family transfer. Keep the final fault families hidden from verifier optimization. If the verifier is updated, independently reevaluate its errors before using it to select a stronger executor.

The unresolved problem is adaptive evaluator exploitation. A static false-acceptance estimate may not apply after an improver repeatedly searches for artifacts that the verifier accepts. Evaluation should therefore include an adaptive attacker constrained to the same information and resources available to the optimizer, followed by an independent audit. This does not produce a universal guarantee, but it tests the distribution shift induced by the very process the verifier is meant to supervise.

Statistical validity and semantic validity must be checked separately. REUSE controls erroneous promotions on its declared population under an independent initial sample and restricted decision-only feedback . That guarantee concerns the supplied score; it cannot establish that the score measures the complete specification. Conversely, a semantically strong test set can still yield invalid statistical comparisons after unrestricted adaptive reuse. A credible improvement claim needs both a justified outcome definition and an evaluation protocol valid for the optimizer’s actual information access.

Predictive representations can improve perceptual and temporal structure while still omitting distinctions necessary for action. A visually coherent rollout can be wrong about a tool’s side effects; a compact latent can predict typical observations while losing a rare precondition. The relevant research question is which representation preserves consequences under interventions, not merely which representation supports a strong passive probe.

Use controlled environments with known interventions to compare reconstructive, contrastive, JEPA-style, and action-conditioned representations at matched data and compute. Measure downstream planning or control with both frozen and adapted encoders. Include actions outside the behavior distribution and require uncertainty or abstention rather than extrapolation by default. Finally, validate selected plans through actual environment execution. A simulator-only gain can result from exploiting model error.

For tool environments, a world model can represent operation preconditions, possible effects, durations, and failure states rather than generate pixels. This typed model should be compared with direct execution, a learned unstructured predictor, and an oracle simulator in a controlled test bed. Replacing only the predictor with an oracle while holding the planner, representation interface, query budget, and evaluation population fixed estimates the effect of predictive error within that system; it is not a context-free decomposition of all errors. Comparing oracle-assisted planning with reactive control estimates a joint policy-and-information advantage under the declared budgets. Without these controls, a negative result cannot tell whether the model, planner, or task simply made planning unnecessary.

Generated imagery has no special evidential status. It can explain a mechanism or propose a possible future observation, but it cannot supply measured results. Diffusion and flow-based systems used as simulators need temporal, physical, and task-specific validation. Representation quality and generative realism are intermediate properties. Their practical importance depends on the decisions and failure events they change.

Recursive self-improvement should be evaluated through independent outer-loop runs, held-out task populations, and complete resource accounting. RRSI, Harness2, AIDE2, MASS, Self-HPO, and skill-memory methods vary in update target, feedback, and persistence. Their results are informative precisely when those differences remain visible. A single label such as self-evolving agent does not define a comparable algorithmic class .

The first hypothesis is that improvement of an executor transfers to improvement of an improver. Fix an initial executor, an outer-loop resource budget, and an independently measured task-utility functional . For improver , define

where the expectation includes independent search runs and their declared task sampling, and all proposal and selection costs fall within the fixed budget. Prespecify a meaningful advantage and a confidence interval for valid under that search and evaluation design. A lower endpoint above supports that advantage; an upper endpoint at or below rules it out at the interval’s stated coverage. An interval crossing is inconclusive. Failure to demonstrate improvement is not proof of its absence. AIDE2’s inconclusive ignition test shows why executor transfer is insufficient. The second hypothesis is that jointly evolving policy and harness yields robust interaction gains. Test cross-pairings, multiple update rounds, task-order variation, and held-out environments; a gain tied to one checkpoint pair is a narrower result.

The third hypothesis is that co-evolving feedback improves alignment with the intended task rather than merely agreement between executor and evaluator. Evaluate the pair with an independent, fixed external audit and adversarial fault families. The fourth is that persistent procedural experience improves future adaptation without accumulating invalid assumptions. Test memory removal, shuffled evidence, stale schemas, model migration, and revocation. Each hypothesis has a different unit of intervention and should not be inferred from the same final leaderboard score.

Complete accounting includes failed proposals, discarded trajectories, evaluator calls, environment setup, memory construction, training, serving, and human review when used. Report the distribution across improvement runs and the regressions of selected artifacts. A method that produces one exceptional artifact after a large search can still be useful, but its scientific claim is search efficiency under that budget, not reliable autonomous acceleration.

The October 2026 ecosystem makes persistence, tools, skills, and orchestration accessible through increasingly explicit protocol and runtime interfaces. The unresolved boundary is the evidence needed when these mechanisms are composed and updated. MCP conformance describes protocol behavior; it does not certify source truth or permission. Durable execution interfaces describe state management; they do not make every external effect reversible. Serving optimizations improve a resource envelope; they do not guarantee preserved task behavior after context or precision changes. The same distinction applies to scientific agents: an autonomous software loop does not establish autonomous physical experimentation, and a changed assay result does not isolate a changed reasoning policy.

Domain transfer also changes the admissible experiment. Cybersecurity capability in a controlled target environment does not grant authority over another system. Evidence from a noninfectious molecular-discovery sandbox does not establish clinical efficacy or the conditions for a different biological workflow. These boundaries belong to the task definition and evidence record; a larger model, longer session, or successful API call cannot discharge them.

The final research standard is therefore an auditable chain from problem formulation to delivered artifact: define the information available to each decision, identify mutable state and authority, derive the mechanism under explicit assumptions, connect it to an implementation, compare against controlled alternatives, and preserve failures and uncertainty. Where evidence is missing, the conclusion narrows. Where a simple baseline survives, complexity needs a measured justification. Where a current method improves only one layer, its cross-layer consequences remain part of the claim.

Generality will be better understood through experiments that discriminate these mechanisms than through broader labels. The technically productive questions are specific: which distinctions must a memory preserve, which histories a policy was trained on, which cache state remains valid, which operation committed, which verifier requirement was actually tested, and which improvement survives an independent task stream. Answering those questions is the path from a collection of model capabilities to reliable, adaptable agentic systems.
Figure isolates the mechanism and its stated information boundaries.

State continuity separates the information used by a policy, current dispatch authority and evidence of external effects. Permission does not establish source truth, and an authorized dispatch can leave the effect ledger unknown. Compatibility and independent evaluation are obligations for updates, rather than guarantees inherited from one component score.
